questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The barium swallow image shows a characteristic appearance of the esophagus. In which condition is this finding typically observed?
questions.explanation: The barium swallow image shows a characteristic “corkscrew” or “rosary bead” appearance of the esophagus. This pattern is produced by multiple simultaneous, uncoordinated contractions of the esophageal muscles, which is typical of diffuse esophageal spasm (DES). In DES, normal peristalsis is replaced by non-propulsive, high-amplitude contractions, leading to the segmented, irregular outline seen on imaging. Patients may present with intermittent dysphagia and chest pain, often mimicking cardiac pain. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Esophageal carcinoma : Shows irregular narrowing (“rat-tail” or “shouldering”), not a corkscrew pattern (C) Esophageal ulcer: Appears as localized mucosal defects, not diffuse contractions (D) Achalasia cardia : Shows “bird-beak” narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter with proximal dilation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common feature of third nerve palsy, in a case of long-standing, uncontrolled diabetes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ptosis

The most common feature seen in diabetic oculomotor palsy among the given options is ptosis.

In the anatomical arrangement of the nerve fibers of the 3rd cranial nerve, the fibers controlling the pupillary reflex are present superficially and are thus spared from diabetic ischemia-induced injury which starts from the central nerve fibres. Thus, pupil sparing is commonly seen in diabetic patients.

The etiology of diabetic neuropathy is hyperglycemia-induced damage to nerve cells and neuronal ischemic change due to microvascular angiopathy.

Involvement of the third cranial nerve is most common and it often presents with early features of ptosis and diplopia with pupil sparing.

The involvement of levator palpebrae superioris muscle of the eyelid manifests as ptosis and the involvement of extraocular muscles such as medial rectus,inferior rectus and inferior oblique presents as opthalmoplegia with diplopia. All the muscles mentioned above are supplied by the Occulomotor nerve.

Note: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery is an important cause of isolated third nerve palsy with involvement of the pupil. This is because the aneurysm impinges on the superficial pupil nerve fibres of the 3rd cranial nerve.

questions.text: Upon reactivation of VZV, the virus is transported through the nerve axon to the skin. Which of the following proteins is most likely involved in the transport process leading to disease recurrence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kinesin

During reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the virus travels from the dorsal root ganglion along the axon to the skin.

Axonal transport mechanisms:

●  Anterograde transport (cell body → axon terminal/skin): mediated by kinesin along microtubules.

●  Retrograde transport (axon terminal → cell body): mediated by dynein.

During VZV reactivation, the virus moves anterogradely toward the skin, causing herpes zoster (shingles).

Other proteins:

C. Lamin: structural protein of the nuclear lamina.

D. Selectin: adhesion molecule involved in leukocyte rolling during inflammation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which hormone is responsible for producing the characteristic ferning pattern seen when cervical mucus dries?
questions.explanation: The "ferning pattern" refers to the microscopic appearance of cervical mucus when it is allowed to dry on a glass slide. This pattern, which resembles the leaves of a fern, is caused by high concentrations of sodium chloride in the mucus. This phenomenon is exclusively under the influence of Estrogen (Option A) and is most prominent during the mid-cycle (pre-ovulatory) phase. Progesterone (Option B), which dominates the luteal phase after ovulation, inhibits the ferning pattern and causes the mucus to become thick and cellular (beading). This is known as a negative fern test. Prolactin (Option C) and 17-ketosteroids (Option D) (adrenal androgens) do not have a direct effect on the crystallization properties of cervical mucus. The presence of ferning is a reliable clinical indicator of estrogenic activity and is used to monitor follicular development and determine the timing of ovulation in infertility assessments

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for the past 20 days, along with gingival hyperplasia and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin 11 g/dL, platelet count 95,000/mm³, and white blood cell count 45,000/mm³. Bone marrow examination reveals 100% cellularity with numerous blast cells that are peroxidase negative and non- specific esterase positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and laboratory findings provide several definitive clues. The presence of gingival hyperplasia and bleeding gums is a classic physical sign associated with the monocytic subtypes of leukemia. Hepatosplenomegaly and leukocytosis ( cells/mm3) further indicate an acute proliferative malignancy. The critical diagnostic hallmark is the bone marrow biopsy result: blasts that are peroxidase negative but non-specific esterase (NSE) positive. According to the FAB classification, AML M5 (acute monocytic leukemia) is defined by its strong NSE positivity and its clinical propensity for extramedullary involvement, such as in the gums. AML M2 (Option A) is typically peroxidase positive. AML M0 (Option B) is undifferentiated. AML M7 (Option D) is megakaryoblastic and would not typically be NSE positive. Therefore, the specific combination of gingival infiltration and NSE positivity confirms the diagnosis of AML M5
questions.learning: The clinical and laboratory findings provide several definitive clues. The presence of gingival hyperplasia and bleeding gums is a classic physical sign associated with the monocytic subtypes of leukemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which method is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway of coagulation?

PT-Prothrombin time

APTT-Activated partial thromboplastin time

CBC-Complete blood count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. APTT

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway, i.e. factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Liver disease
• Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
• Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
• A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
• Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII (since it is part of the extrinsic pathway)
• APTT is also moderately prolonged in patients taking oral anticoagulant drugs and in the presence of vitamin K deficiency

APTT is also moderately prolonged in patients taking oral anticoagulant drugs and in the presence of vitamin K deficiency (in which factors II, VII, IX, and X will fail to activate). A patient with previously undiagnosed haemophilia or another congenital coagulation disorder can also present with an isolated prolonged APTT.

Other options:

Option A: Prothrombin time evaluates the extrinsic pathway, i.e. factors VII, X, V, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen. It measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin).

Causes of prolonged PT:

• Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs (vitamin K antagonists)
• Liver disease, particularly obstructive jaundice
• Vitamin K deficiency
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Rarely, a previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect

Isolated prolonged prothrombin time occurs due to the deficiency of clotting factor VII.

Option C: Fibrinogen levels are used for measuring clotting.

Option D: Complete blood count is used to measure total RBC count, WBC count, and Platelet count.
questions.learning: APTT Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway, i.e. factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient undergoing evaluation for suspected mitochondrial dysfunction has various mitochondrial structures assessed. Cardiolipin is a characteristic phospholipid of which mitochondrial location?
questions.explanation: Cardiolipin is a unique phospholipid that is found almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It accounts for approximately 20% of the total lipid composition in this membrane. Cardiolipin is essential for the structural integrity and optimal function of various mitochondrial proteins, including those involved in the electron transport chain (such as Complex IV) and the ATP synthase complex. It is not a significant component of the outer mitochondrial membrane (Option A), the cytosol (Option B), or the mitochondrial matrix (Option D). Because of its specific location and role in bioenergetics, cardiolipin is often a target of investigation in cases of mitochondrial dysfunction. For example, abnormalities in cardiolipin metabolism are associated with Barth syndrome, a rare X-linked disorder characterized by cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle weakness. Its unique structure, consisting of four fatty acid tails, allows the inner membrane to maintain the tight curvature necessary for forming cristae
questions.learning: Cardiolipin is a unique phospholipid that is found almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It accounts for approximately 20% of the total lipid composition in this membrane.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Determine the rhythm displayed in the provided ECG rhythm strip.
questions.explanation: The ECG strip shows features consistent with Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR): Key features visible: 1. 1. Regular R-R intervals — complexes appear evenly spaced 2. 2. P wave before every QRS — normal atrial depolarization 3. 3. Heart rate ~60–100 bpm — within normal range 4. 4. Narrow QRS complexes — normal ventricular conduction 5. 5. Consistent morphology throughout the strip Why other options are wrong: (A) Atrial Fibrillation : AF shows irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no distinct P waves, replaced by chaotic fibrillatory baseline. This ECG shows regular rhythm with clear P waves : ruling out AF completely. (B) Atrial Flutter : Flutter shows a characteristic "sawtooth" pattern of flutter waves (F waves) at ~300 bpm with regular ventricular response. No such sawtooth baseline is seen here. (D) AV Block : AV block would show prolonged PR interval (1st degree), dropped QRS beats (2nd degree), or complete dissociation between P waves and QRS (3rd degree). None of these features are present here

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following renal histological features is characteristically seen in diabetic nephropathy but not typically seen in other glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kimmelstiel-Wilson

The “signature lesion”: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules

• Nodular, PAS-positive mesangial expansion
• Located in glomerular tuft
• Strongly associated with long-standing diabetes mellitus

These are pathognomonic of diabetic nephropathy, representing nodular mesangial expansion.

Mesangial sclerosis and GBM thickening can be seen in other chronic glomerulopathies, and foot process effacement is nonspecific.

Thus, nodular glomerulosclerosis uniquely points to diabetic nephropathy.

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| GBM thickening | Early change

| Mesangial expansion | Diffuse

| K-W nodules | Nodular, pathognomonic

| Hyaline arteriolosclerosis | Both afferent & efferent (important!)

| Proteinuria | Nephrotic range

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Instrument assisted delivery is not indicated in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cephalo pelvic disproportion

Instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated in cephalo pelvic disproportion. Ruling out CPD is a prerequisite before attempting instrument-assisted delivery.

Cephalo-pelvic disproportion (CPD) is a condition in which the baby’s head is too large, or the pelvis is too small, for the baby to pass through the birth canal. In such cases, instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated because vaginal birth is not feasible. The appropriate management for CPD is usually a cesarean section to avoid complications for both mother and baby.

Conditions where instrument-assisted delivery may be indicated:

1. Fetal distress: If the baby is showing signs of distress (such as decelerations in the heart rate), an instrument-assisted delivery may be needed to expedite delivery and reduce the risk of further harm. (Option A)
2. Maternal exhaustion: In cases of maternal fatigue, particularly after a prolonged second stage of labor, instruments may be used to assist in delivery if the mother is unable to continue pushing effectively. (Option B)
3. Prolonged second stage of labor: If the second stage of labor (when the cervix is fully dilated and the baby is descending) is prolonged, instruments can be used to assist in the delivery of the baby, especially if there are signs of fetal distress or maternal exhaustion. (Option C)

Prerequisites for instrumental vaginal delivery:

• Ruptured membranes vertex presentation
• Cephalopelvic disproportion not suspected
• No fetal coagulopathy or bone demineralization disorder
• Completely dilated cervix
• Precisely assessed fetal head position
• Engaged head
• Experienced operator
questions.learning: Cephalo pelvic disproportion Instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated in cephalo pelvic disproportion. Ruling out CPD is a prerequisite before attempting instrument-assisted delivery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases primarily involves the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paralysis agitans

The structure marked in this transverse section of the brain at the level of superior colliculus is substantia nigra. Degeneration of substantia nigra is seen in Parkinson's disease, also known as paralysis agitans.

Substantia nigra is pigmented due to the presence of neuromelanin granules, which help in the synthesis of dopamine. In Parkinson's disease, there is an absence/reduced pigmentation of the substantia nigra.

Bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor are classic features of Parkinson's disease. Because of motor disability, it is also referred to as paralysis agitans.

Other options:

Option B: Depression is often a comorbid finding with Parkinson's disease, but is not due to damage to the substantia nigra.

Option C: Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. It is due to atrophy of the entorhinal cortex, located in the medial temporal lobe.

Option D: Huntington’s chorea is an autosomal dominant disorder of movement and cognition primarily involving the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).
questions.learning: Paralysis agitans — The structure marked in this transverse section of the brain at the level of superior colliculus is substantia nigra. Degeneration of substantia nigra is seen in Parkinson's disease, also known as paralysis agitans.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate was brought with a history of frothiness from the mouth and respiratory distress. An X-ray of the neonate is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Esophageal atresia with tracheo-esophageal fistula

The given symptoms of frothiness and respiratory distress and an X-ray showing a nasogastric (NG) tube in proximal esophagus and stomach distended with gas are suggestive of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF).

Longitudinal furrow separates the trachea from the esophagus during development. Deviation or altered growth in this septum results in the formation of an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea called a tracheoesophageal fistula. It is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb) anomalies.

The newborn has excessive drooling and frothing soon after birth. On feeding, the baby develops choking and cyanosis. Regurgitation of secretion and feed through the fistulous tract into the lungs results in aspiration pneumonia.

Type C consists of proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF is the commonest. Here the air enters into stomach causing gastric distention which is seen as an air bubble. There is an inability to pass an NG tube for more than 7-10 cm, and a coiling in the proximal esophagus helps in the diagnosis.

Other options

Option A - Transient tachypnea of newborn is due to delayed clearance of lung fluid. They have tachypnea with minimal or no respiratory distress. Chest X-ray may show hyper-expanded lung fields, prominent vascular marking and prominent interlobar fissure.

Option B: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of the failure to close the pleuroperitoneal membrane. Intestinal loops enter the thorax and compress the developing lung causing pulmonary hypoplasia. They present with respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Chest X-ray would show multiple air-filled spaces in the thorax, a shift of mediastinum, and the absence of an outline of the left diaphragm.

Option D: Respiratory distress syndrome/Hyaline membrane disease occurs primarily in premature infants due to a deficiency of surfactant in the alveoli. Clinical features include tachypnea, retractions, grunting, cyanosis, and decreased air entry. X-ray shows reticulogranular pattern, ground glass opacity, low lung volume, air bronchogram, and white-out lungs in severe disease.

Pearl PF1361: Types of Tracheo-esophageal Fistula/Esophageal Atresia

Abbreviations:

* EA: Esophageal atresia

* TEF: Tracheoesophageal Fistula

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CAD Prophylaxis

Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated in coronary artery disease prophylaxis. There is currently insufficient evidence to recommend the initiation or continuation of either estrogen therapy (ET) or estrogen-progestin therapy (EPT) for the prevention of primary or secondary coronary heart disease (CHD).

In an 18-year reevaluation of WHI (women health initiative) participants, it was found that cardiovascular, cancer, and all-cause mortality rates were essentially the same in both the hormone therapy (HT) and placebo groups.

Currently, hormone therapy (HT) is only indicated for the treatment of bothersome vasomotor symptoms (VMS) and genitourinary symptoms, prevention of osteoporosis, and treatment of hypoestrogenism caused by hypogonadism, surgical menopause, or premature ovarian insufficiency.

Estrogen should not be used in women with the following conditions:

• undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding
• known, suspected, or history of breast cancer
• known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia
• active or prior venous thromboembolism
• active or prior stroke, myocardial infarction, or transient ischemic attack (TIA)
• known thrombophilia, liver dysfunction, or disease
• untreated hypertension
• known hypersensitivity to the ingredients of the estrogen preparation
• known or suspected pregnancy

Risks of HRT:

• Endometrial cancer
• Breast cancer
• Ovarian cancer
• Thromboembolism
• Lipid profile dysfunction
• Gall stones, liver dysfunction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman presents for counseling shortly after unprotected sexual intercourse and inquires about available methods of emergency contraception. Among the following options, which method is not recommended for use as emergency contraception?
options: OCP 2 tablets within 24 hours, repeat dose after 14 days
questions.explanation: The Yuzpe regimen for emergency contraception involve taking specific doses of combined OCPs (Ethinyl Estradiol and Levonorgestrel). The standard protocol involves an initial dose taken as soon as possible after intercourse, followed by a second identical dose exactly 12 hours later. Stating that the second dose is repeated after 14 days (Option D) is inaccurate and would be medically ineffective; therefore, this is the not recommended method. LNG (Levonorgestrel) 0.75 mg (Option A) is a standard emergency method, taken either as a single 1.5 mg dose or two 0.75 mg doses 12 hours apart. Ulipristal acetate (Option C) is currently the most effective oral emergency contraceptive available. Ethinyl Estradiol (Option B), while part of the Yuzpe regimen, is not used alone for this purpose. The 14-day delay mentioned in Option D is longer than a standard luteal phase, making it entirely useless for preventing implantation. The IUCD remains the most effective overall emergency contraceptive method

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A blood sample from a patient with diabetes is collected and stored in the container shown. Which substance is added to the blood sample in this container?
questions.explanation: The container shown is a grey-top vacutainer, which is specifically used for blood glucose and lactate estimation. The additive in this tube is Sodium fluoride (NaF), which serves as a potent antiglycolytic agent. It inhibits the enzyme enolase in the glycolytic pathway, preventing red blood cells from consuming the glucose in the sample post-collection. This ensures that the measured glucose level accurately reflects the patient's state at the time of the draw. EDTA (Option B) is in purple-top tubes for hematology. Sodium citrate (Option C) is in light blue-top tubes for coagulation studies. Heparin (Option D) is in green-top tubes for clinical chemistry and arterial blood gases. Without NaF, blood glucose levels drop by approximately 5-10% per hour at room temperature due to cellular metabolism. This additive is essential for the accurate diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes mellitus in clinical practice
questions.learning: The container shown is a grey-top vacutainer, which is specifically used for blood glucose and lactate estimation. The additive in this tube is Sodium fluoride (NaF), which serves as a potent antiglycolytic agent.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In relation to the orbital wall, where are the canaliculi located as they open into the lacrimal sac?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal drainage system is strategically located at the medial aspect of the orbit. Tears enter the system through the superior and inferior puncta, travel through the canaliculi, and eventually empty into the lacrimal sac. The lacrimal sac sits within the lacrimal fossa, which is formed by the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla, both located on the medial orbital wall. The canaliculi typically join to form a common canaliculus before entering the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac, but this entire complex is situated at the medial canthus. The lateral wall (Option A) contains the lacrimal gland, which produces tears, but not the drainage sac. The superior (Option C) and inferior (Option D) walls form the roof and floor of the orbit, respectively, and do not house the primary lacrimal drainage structures. Clinically, knowledge of this medial location is vital during procedures like dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) or when managing medial canthal trauma to avoid permanent damage to the tear drainage pathway
questions.learning: The lacrimal drainage system is strategically located at the medial aspect of the orbit. Tears enter the system through the superior and inferior puncta, travel through the canaliculi, and eventually empty into the lacrimal sac.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought with extensive burn injuries affecting the entire head, neck, and upper limb. Based on this distribution, what is the estimated percentage of total body surface area burned?
questions.explanation: Burn area in children is calculated differently than in adults due to their larger head-to-body ratio. According to the adjusted Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck of a child account for approximately 18% of the total body surface area (TBSA). Each individual upper limb accounts for 9% of the TBSA. In this case, adding the 18% for the head and neck to the 9% for one upper limb results in a total of 27%. This value falls within the 25–30% range provided in Option A. Option B (40–44%) would imply much more extensive injuries, such as both arms or parts of the trunk. Option C (18–20%) only accounts for the head and neck without the upper limb. Option D (5–10%) is a severe underestimation. Therefore, 27% (rounded to the 25–30% range) is the accurate clinical estimation for this 3-year-old child
questions.learning: Burn area in children is calculated differently than in adults due to their larger head-to-body ratio. According to the adjusted Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck of a child account for approximately 18% of the total body surface area (TBSA).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The most likely cause is accidental endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus, resulting in ventilation of only the right lung and subsequent collapse (atelectasis) of the left lung.
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to positive pressure ventilation
questions.explanation: The absence of breath sounds on the left side with sounds heard only on the right immediately following intubation strongly supports a diagnosis of right endobronchial (mainstem) intubation. This occurs because the right mainstem bronchus is more vertically oriented than the left, making it the most likely path if an endotracheal tube is advanced too far. This results in selective ventilation of the right lung only, while the left lung collapses due to lack of air entry. Mucus secretions (Option B) would typically cause bilateral decreased air entry or generalized poor air movement rather than such distinct unilateral findings. Left-sided pneumothorax (Option C) could cause unilateral sound loss but would usually feature additional signs like hyperresonance and tracheal deviation. Bronchospasm (Option D) presents with bilateral wheezing and increased airway pressures rather than complete unilateral absence of breath sounds. Withdrawing the tube slightly usually resolves the issue
questions.learning: The absence of breath sounds on the left side with sounds heard only on the right immediately following intubation strongly supports a diagnosis of right endobronchial (mainstem) intubation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain.On examination, the infant has a scaphoid abdomen and breath sounds are decreased on both sides. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bochdalek hernia

The given clinical picture of respiratory distress, intermittent abdominal pain, scaphoid abdomen, absent breath sounds in both sides of the chest, and an X-ray image showing bowel loops in the thoracic cavity is diagnostic of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), the most common variant being Bochdalek hernia.

If the defect is posterolateral it is called Bochdalek hernia and if it's anteromedial it is called Morgagni hernia.

Clinical features :

* Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

* Early respiratory distress, within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign.

* Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter.

* Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest, with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds.

* The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred.

* Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect. If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including the stomach may herniate.

Diagnosis:

* Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis.

* CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation)

* High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion.

Differential diagnosis:

* Diaphragmatic eventration

* Cystic adenomatoid malformation

* Bronchogenic cyst

* Cystic teratoma

Treatment:

Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair. Immediate respiratory support should be provided, including rapid endotracheal intubation and sedation.

Bag and Mask Ventilation is contraindicated in newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia because it causes distension of the stomach which in turn may limit the expansion of the already hypoplastic lung.

During surgery, the viscera are reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is closed using interrupted, nonabsorbable sutures.

In most cases (80%-90%), a hernia sac is not present. If identified, it is excised at the time of repair.

Conventional mechanical ventilation, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are the 3 main strategies to support respiratory failure in the newborn with CDH.

Good relative indicators of stability are as follows:

* Requirement for conventional ventilation only

* Low peak inspiratory pressure

* Fi-O2 <50

If the defect is too large, a porous polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) patch is used.

Other options:

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

* Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain

* Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus

* Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the structural composition of the outer nose?
options: Upper 1/2 is bony, and lower 1/2 is cartilaginous
Upper 2/3rd is bony and the lower 1/3rd is cartilaginous
questions.explanation: The structural framework of the external human nose is composed of both rigid bone and flexible cartilage. The upper one-third of the nose is supported by bone, specifically the paired nasal bones and the frontal process of the maxilla. The lower two-thirds of the nose is composed of hyaline cartilage, which includes the major alar cartilages, lateral nasal cartilages, and the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum. This arrangement provides stability at the root while allowing for flexibility and airway regulation at the tip and nostrils. Option A and Option B provide incorrect proportions for these components. Understanding this specific 1:2 ratio of bone to cartilage is essential in plastic and reconstructive surgery (rhinoplasty) and in managing nasal fractures. Fractures typically involve the upper bony bridge, whereas trauma to the lower portion often results in cartilaginous deviation or septal hematoma. Consequently, the correct anatomical description characterizes the upper third as bony and the lower two-thirds as cartilaginous
questions.learning: The structural framework of the external human nose is composed of both rigid bone and flexible cartilage. The upper one-third of the nose is supported by bone, specifically the paired nasal bones and the frontal process of the maxilla.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Surgery where nostrils are partially or completely occluded is done for which condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrophic rhinitis

Complete closure of the nostrils (Young's operation) or partial closure of the nostrils (Modified Young's operation) is done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

In Young's operation, both nostrils are closed completely by raising flaps within the nasal vestibule. They are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa becomes normal, and the crusting is reduced.

In Modified Young's operation, the procedure has been modified to avoid discomfort from complete closure of the nostrils. Here the nostrils are only partially closed. The results are the same when compared to Young's operation.

Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is a chronic inflammation of the nose with atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. Roomy nasal cavities with foul-smelling crusts are seen. The patient presents with a foul smell from the nose, marked anosmia (merciful anosmia), and paradoxical nasal obstruction (nasal obstruction despite wide nasal passages). Paradoxical nasal obstruction occurs due to degenerative changes in the sensory nerves of the nasal mucosa, leading to an inability to sense airflow.

Medical management includes nasal irrigation and removal of crusts. 25% glucose in glycerine, antibiotics (quinolones or metronidazole), estradiol nasal spray, and mucolytics can be used.
questions.learning: Atrophic rhinitis Complete closure of the nostrils (Young's operation) or partial closure of the nostrils (Modified Young's operation) is done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which finding on pleural fluid analysis would be indicative of an exudative pleural effusion?
options: pleural:serum ratio >0.5 pleural:serum LDH ratio>0.6 or pleural LDH>2/3
Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and glucose = 30mg%
Pleural fluid LDH = 90IU and glucose = 30 mg%
Pleural fluid protein = 3.5gm% and glucose = 90 mg%
questions.explanation: Light's criteria are the gold standard for differentiating between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. An effusion is classified as an "exudate" if it meets at least one of the following: "pleural-to-serum protein ratio >0.5," "pleural-to-serum LDH ratio >0.6," or "pleural fluid LDH >2/3" of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH. Options B, C, and D provide single laboratory values which, while suggestive (e.g., protein >3 gm% in Option B), do not satisfy the formal, comprehensive definition of Light's criteria. Exudative effusions are typically caused by inflammatory, infectious, or malignant processes (e.g., pneumonia or cancer) that increase capillary permeability. Transudates, by contrast, are caused by imbalances in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure (e.g., heart failure or cirrhosis) and do not meet these criteria. Accurately categorizing the effusion is the first essential step in determining its underlying cause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maternal component of placenta would be
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decidua Basalis

The decidua basalis, also known as the basal plate, is the portion of the endometrium (uterine lining) that lies beneath the conceptus (embryo/fetus) and contributes to the formation of the maternal component of the placenta. It forms the maternal part of the placenta by coming into direct contact with the chorionic villi, allowing for the exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste products between the maternal and fetal circulations.

The definitive placenta (see image) consists of the chorionic plate on the fetal aspect and a basal plate on the maternal aspect with the intervillous space between them. The structures in each of these parts are as follows:

Fetal side: Chorionic plate

* Amnion

* Primary (extraembryonic) mesoderm with fetal blood vessels

* Cytotrophoblast (Langhan's layer)

* Syncytiotrophoblast

Maternal side: Basal plate

* Stratum spongiosum of decidua basalis containing maternal blood vessels

* Outer layer of syncytiotrophoblast (Nitabuch’s layer)

* Outer shell of cytotrophoblast

* Inner layer of syncytiotrophoblast (Rohr’s fibrinoid stria)

Between basal plate and chorionic plate

* Intervillous space

* Maternal blood flowing in the intervillous space

* Stem villi

* Fetal blood flowing within the fetal villi
questions.learning: Decidua Basalis — The decidua basalis, also known as the basal plate, is the portion of the endometrium (uterine lining) that lies beneath the conceptus (embryo/fetus) and contributes to the formation of the maternal component of the placenta.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presenting with hypercalcemia is found to have multiple pancreatic lesions on evaluation. Further assessment is performed to identify an underlying inherited genetic syndrome. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations
There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells
Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients
Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13. It is classically characterized by tumors of the Parathyroid glands, Pancreatic islet cells, and Pituitary gland (“3 Ps”). In a patient with hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism) and multiple pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, MEN 1 should be strongly suspected.

Why not the other options?

• A. Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations: RET mutations are associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B, not MEN 1.
• B. There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells: MEN 2 is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from parafollicular C cells, not follicular cells.
• C. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients: Recommended in RET mutation carriers (MEN 2) to prevent medullary thyroid carcinoma; not indicated in MEN 1.
questions.learning: Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1 Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer are commonly prescribed to chronic kidney disease patients because of their property of binding to which one of the following electrolytes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Potassium

Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) and patiromer are potassium-binding resins used to treat hyperkalemia, which is particularly common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).

• Patiromer exchanges calcium for potassium in the gastrointestinal tract → binds K⁺ → increases fecal potassium excretion.
• Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate selectively traps potassium ions in the gastrointestinal tract in exchange for sodium and hydrogen ions → increases fecal K⁺ elimination.

Both therefore lower serum potassium without directly increasing urinary potassium excretion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Calcium: Patiromer uses calcium as an exchange ion but does not primarily bind calcium therapeutically.
• B. Sodium: SZC exchanges sodium/H⁺ for potassium; sodium is not the target electrolyte.
• D. Phosphate: These are not phosphate binders. Drugs such as sevelamer, calcium acetate, and lanthanum are used for hyperphosphatemia in CKD.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 80-year-old man developed right-sided calf muscle pain and swelling. He was bedridden following a right inter-trochanteric fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deep vein thrombosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of deep vein thrombosis. It occurs due to immobilization and venous stasis.

It most commonly occurs in the calf veins and less often in the proximal veins of the thigh and pelvis. It is caused due to Virchow's triad:

* Hemodynamic changes (stasis or turbulence)

* Hypercoagulabilty

* Endothelial injury/dysfunction

It is usually asymptomatic. Some patients may present with pain in the calf or thigh. There may be an increase in temperature and pulse rate. Calf swelling and tenderness may be noted. Increased pain on passive dorsiflexion of the foot (Homan's test), although frequently used is now regarded as an unreliable sign.

Pearl PF1167: Prophylaxis for DVT

Mechanical prophylaxis

Early ambulation

Acts by activating the calf pump mechanism

Pneumatic compression stocking

Prevents stasis by periodically compressing the calves

Pharmacological prophylaxis

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin

Fondaparinux

Prevent thrombus formation by inhibiting factor Xa

Apixaban

Rivaroxaban

Oral factor Xa inhibitors

Unfractionated heparin (UFH)

Prevents action of factors VIII - XII and production of thrombin/fibrin.

Used in renal insufficiency

Warfarin

Inhibits hepatic production of factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.learning: Deep vein thrombosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of deep vein thrombosis. It occurs due to immobilization and venous stasis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with weight loss, fever, and a painless swelling of the jaw. Histopathological examination of the biopsy shows the features depicted in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of a rapidly growing painless jaw swelling, weight loss, and fever in a young child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt Lymphoma. The provided biopsy image confirms this with the classic "starry sky" appearance—this pattern is created by sheets of medium-sized, dark-staining B-lymphocytes (the "sky") with interspersed pale, "tingible-body" macrophages containing cellular debris (the "stars"). Kikuchi disease (Option A) and Infectious mononucleosis (Option B) typically involve painful lymphadenopathy and show different histological patterns . Hodgkin's lymphoma (Option C) is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, not a starry-sky pattern. Burkitt lymphoma is associated with the Epstein-Barr Virus and involves a translocation of the c-myc gene on chromosome 8. It is one of the fastest-growing human tumors, requiring immediate aggressive chemotherapy. The pathognomonic histology and jaw location make Burkitt lymphoma the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical combination of a rapidly growing painless jaw swelling, weight loss, and fever in a young child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt Lymphoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male was on maize as a staple diet for a prolonged period. He presented with diarrhoea and lesion over his neck as shown in the image below. The condition occurs due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra. Corn/Maize has low levels of niacin and tryptophan. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of Niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

* Diarrhea

* Dermatitis

* Dementia

The lesion in the neck is characteristic Casal’s necklace pattern, seen in pellagra. The Casal collar or Casal necklace is a clinical sign in which there is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar (dermatomes C3 and C4).

Other options:

B. Zinc: Zinc deficiency can cause various symptoms, but it does not typically present with the specific symptoms described in the case.

C. Thiamine (Vitamin B1): Thiamine deficiency can lead to a condition called beriberi, which primarily affects the nervous system and cardiovascular system. It does not typically present with skin lesions or diarrhea as described in the case.

D. Iron: Iron deficiency can result in anemia and other symptoms, but it does not cause the specific symptoms described, including skin lesions and diarrhea.
questions.learning: Niacin — The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: When the pH = pKa of a drug, which of the following statements is true?
options: Concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50 % non-ionic
Concentration of the drug is 90% ionic and 10% non-ionic
Concentration of the drug is 75% ionic and 25 % non-ionic
Concentration of the drug is 25% ionic and 75 % non-ionic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50 % non-ionic

When the pH = pKa of a drug, the concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50% non-ionic.

pKa is defined as the pH at which a drug exists as 50% ionized (hydrophilic) and 50% unionized (lipophilic).

For e.g., phenobarbitone is an acidic drug with a pKa of 7.2. At a pH of 7.2, 50% will be unionized. In a more basic plasma (pH=7.4), a lesser fraction (around 40%) will be unionized.

Small changes in pH near pKa of a drug may cause large variations in the degree of ionization.
questions.learning: Concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50 % non-ionic When the pH = pKa of a drug, the concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50% non-ionic. pKa is defined as the pH at which a drug exists as 50% ionized (hydrophilic) and 50% unionized (lipophilic).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the lungs, which type of cells are responsible for the secretion of surfactant?
questions.explanation: The alveolar epithelium consists of two main cell types. Type 2 pneumocytes are cuboidal cells that serve as the "caretakers" of the alveoli; they are responsible for the synthesis, storage, and secretion of pulmonary surfactant. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that reduces surface tension at the air-liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at the end of expiration. Type 1 pneumocytes (Option A) are thin, squamous cells that cover about 95% of the alveolar surface and are optimized for gas exchange. Alveolar macrophages, also known as "dust cells" (Options B and C), are the primary immune cells of the distal airway, responsible for phagocytosing inhaled particles and pathogens. Clinically, a deficiency in surfactant production by Type 2 pneumocytes in premature infants leads to Infant Respiratory Distress Syndrome (IRDS). Furthermore, Type 2 cells act as progenitor cells; following lung injury, they proliferate and differentiate into Type 1 cells to restore the alveolar lining
questions.learning: The alveolar epithelium consists of two main cell types. Type 2 pneumocytes are cuboidal cells that serve as the "caretakers" of the alveoli; they are responsible for the synthesis, storage, and secretion of pulmonary surfactant.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient develops enophthalmos and periorbital ecchymosis after being struck by a ball. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma from an object like a ball causes a sudden rise in orbital pressure, often fracturing the thin orbital floor. This results in the herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus, which causes enophthalmos (sunken eye). Patients also classically present with periorbital ecchymosis and potential infraorbital nerve anesthesia. Zygomatic fractures (Option B) typically present with cheek flattening and trismus rather than isolated enophthalmos. Nasal bone fractures (Option C) cause deformity and epistaxis but do not affect orbital position. Le Fort I fractures (Option D) are horizontal maxillary fractures involving the upper jaw and teeth. A classic radiographic sign for a blowout fracture is the "hanging drop" or "tear drop" sign on a Water's view X-ray or CT. Thus, the mechanism and enophthalmos confirm the orbital blowout diagnosis

questions.text: A patient was referred by a doctor to a radiologist for a CT scan and the doctor was given money for the referral. What is this unethical act called?

Correct answer: A. Dichotomy

This unethical act of receiving a commission for referring a patient is referred to as Dichotomy.

Dichotomy is an unethical act wherein a doctor receives a gift, commission or money for referring, recommending, or procuring a patient for any medical, surgical or other treatments. Fee splitting is unethical in India.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient comes with active variceal bleeding. Which of the following is not done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Platelet transfusion

Platelet transfusion is not done in the case of active variceal bleeding unless coagulopathy is confirmed as the cause. Platelet transfusions are indicated only in patients with a platelet count of <50,000/microL  or in patients with evidence of microvascular bleeding.

Variceal hemorrhage is a medical emergency. Varices usually present with the acute onset large-volume haematemesis, the lower esophagus being the most common site for variceal bleeding.

The sites for portosystemic anastomosis are:

• Left gastric vein to distal oesophageal veins: oesophageal and gastric variceal bleeding
• Superior rectal veins to Middle and inferior rectal veins: hemorrhoids and rectal bleeding
• Left branch of the portal vein to Periumbilical veins: caput-medusae
• The right branch of the portal vein to retroperitoneal veins draining into azygos, hemiazygos, lumbar, intercostal, and phrenic veins
• Omental and colonic veins near hepatic and splenic ﬂexures to Retroperitoneal veins near hepatic and splenic ﬂexures

Medical management of variceal bleeding includes blood transfusion (option B) and drug therapy with somatostatin analogs like octreotide (option C). Short-term antibiotics like ceftriaxone are known to decrease bacterial infection and increase survival.

Surgical measures are preferred if medical management fails. They include balloon tamponade, endoscopic banding (option D), transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), portosystemic shunts, splenectomy, and gastric revascularization

Note: Sugiura procedure is the non-shunt surgical management of refractory oesophageal variceal bleeding. It is a procedure of de-vascularizing the distal esophagus and stomach.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 67-year-old diabetic patient presented with swelling around the knee, restriction of movement and minimal or no pain. The x-ray of the knee is given below. The diagnosis is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Charcot arthropathy

The x-ray depicts severe joint destruction and instability, seen on (a) varus stress (b)Neutral (c) valgus stress on the patient's knee joint. There is h/o diabetes and minimal pain , which indicates a neuropathic cause like Charcot arthropathy.

Charcot arthropathy is a neuroarthropathy commonly associated with diabetes.

Though the exact pathogenesis of this disease is unclear, it is speculated that vascular, neurological, and metabolic changes associated with diabetes lead to this condition.

Points in favor of a diagnosis of Charcot arthropathy are:

* Swelling of ankle joint  associated with foot ulcer (possible diabetic foot ulcer)

* Instability of movement

* Movements beyond normal limits and a loose bag of bones feel

* X-ray that shows obvious bone destruction and the presence of irregular calcified masses

Charcot's arthropathy can also be caused by the following conditions:

* leprosy

* dialysis

* chronic alcoholism

* spinal cord injury

* syringomyelia

* meningomyelocele

* syphilis

Treatment for this condition is usually decided upon by a multidisciplinary team of health care professionals such as a physician, a rheumatologist, an orthopedician, and a physiotherapist.

Other options:

Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthropathy present with pain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the cells secrete surfactant in lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type 2 pneumocyte

Type 2 pneumocytes secrete surfactant in the lungs.

Alveolar Lining Epithelial Cells

Two types

* Type I cells – The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium); Helps in gas exchange

* Type II cells  – Granular pneumocytes produce surfactant

Type II cells make 60% of epithelial cells in alveoli but type I cells form 95% of the total surface area because of its flat surface.

Type II cells are stem cells which help in replenishing damaged Type 1 pneumocytes in conditions like drug-induced pulmonary toxicity by amiodarone, bleomycin etc.

Other cells – Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells), lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells (APUD cells-Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation), and mast cells.

Clinical correlate :

* Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm neonates is due to insufficient surfactant production.

* Lung maturity of the fetus can be assessed by determining the ratio of lecithin to sphingomyelin (L:S ratio) in the amniotic fluid. A ratio of >2 indicates maturity.

* Shake test/Bubble test/Clement test: Formation of stable foam in the presence of surfactant.

* Phosphatidylglycerol levels in Amniotic fluid.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Reservoir for Kala azar is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human

In India, humans are considered the main reservoir for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis).

Kala azar or visceral leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection, mainly affecting the reticuloendothelial system. It is caused by the Leishmania donovani complex that includes L. donovani and L. infantum. These organisms are transmitted by sandflies.

Clinical features of kala-azar:

* Moderate- to high-grade fever with chills and rigors

* Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly

* Anemia

* Lymphadenopathy

* Pedal edema, ascites, due to hypoalbuminemia

* Epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleed, and retinal hemorrhages, due to thrombocytopenia

The gold standard test for the diagnosis is the demonstration of amastigotes in the smears of tissue aspirates. Another commonly used modality is the detection of antibodies to a recombinant antigen called rK39 by rapid immunochormatographic test.

Amphotericin B is the first-line drug used in India. Other drugs useful in treating the condition are sodium stibogluconate, meglumine antimoniate, paromomycin, and miltefosine.
questions.learning: Human — In India, humans are considered the main reservoir for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). Kala azar or visceral leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection, mainly affecting the reticuloendothelial system.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a 2–3 month history of reduced hearing, and the otoscopic findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of chronic, painless hearing loss over several months and the otoscopic image of a dull, retracted eardrum with visible air bubbles are hallmark features of Serous Otitis Media (SOM), also known as Otitis Media with Effusion (OME). SOM is common in children and results from Eustachian tube dysfunction, leading to fluid accumulation in the middle ear without signs of acute infection. Acute otitis media (Option C) would present with sudden pain, fever, and a red, bulging eardrum. Hemorrhagic Myringitis bullosa (Option A) is a painful viral condition characterized by blood-filled blisters on the external surface of the eardrum. Myringitis granulosa (Option D) involves the presence of granulation tissue on the outer layer of the drum, usually as a result of chronic irritation. Therefore, given the subacute timeline and the classic "glue ear" appearance, Serous Otitis Media is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical history of chronic, painless hearing loss over several months and the otoscopic image of a dull, retracted eardrum with visible air bubbles are hallmark features of Serous Otitis Media (SOM), also known as Otitis Media with Effusion (OME).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following congenital heart diseases are associated with a split second heart sound? 1. ASD 2. VSD 3. PDA 4. TOF
questions.explanation: Split second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure becomes asynchronous. Conditions causing increased right heart volume/flow delay pulmonary valve closure, producing wide splitting of S2. 1 ASD Causes fixed wide splitting of S2 — the hallmark finding. Increased right heart volume delays pulmonary valve closure consistently throughout respiration. 2 VSD Increased pulmonary blood flow delays P2 closure, producing wide splitting of S2. 3 PDA Increased pulmonary circulation delays P2, causing wide splitting of S2. Why TOF is excluded: 4 TOF is incorrect because in Tetralogy of Fallot, severe pulmonary stenosis causes markedly diminished pulmonary blood flow. P2 becomes so soft it is virtually inaudible, resulting in a single S2 rather than split S2. The aortic component dominates completely, making splitting absent. Why other options are wrong: (B,C) are incorrect because they include TOF which characteristically produces single S2, not split S2. (D) is incorrect because TOF does not produce split S2, making "all correct" invalid
questions.learning: Split second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure becomes asynchronous. Conditions causing increased right heart volume/flow delay pulmonary valve closure, producing wide splitting of S2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes of light and floaters. Ocular examination reveals a deep anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of myopia, sudden flashes (photopsia), and floaters is highly suggestive of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). In highly myopic eyes, the elongated globe leads to retinal thinning and lattice degeneration, predisposing the patient to retinal tears. These breaks allow liquefied vitreous to pass into the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the pigment epithelium. A deep anterior chamber is common in high myopia due to the increased axial length. Exudative detachment (Option A) is characterized by "shifting fluid" without tears. Tractional detachment (Option C) occurs due to vitreoretinal bands pulling the retina, often without flashes or floaters. Central serous retinopathy (Option D) typically presents with metamorphopsia and central blurring in young males, rather than flashes. Therefore, RRD is the most probable diagnosis given the risk factors and acute symptoms

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the hospital with multiple fractures of the humerus secondary to a fall from height. On examination, there is difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, and associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm. Which is the nerve most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Musculocutaneous nerve

The given clinical vignette in a patient with difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, with associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm, is suggestive of injury to the musculocutaneous nerve.

Fall from a height on an outstretched hand is one of the main causes of humerus fractures.

Course:

The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7) is a branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. It emerges at the lower border of the pectoralis minor and pierces coracobrachialis. It then descends between biceps brachii and brachialis where it supplies a branch to the shaft of the humerus. Then it enters the elbow and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

It innervates all the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm i.e.,

• Biceps brachii - involved in flexion of elbow and supination of the forearm
• Brachialis -  involved in the flexion of the elbow
• Coracobrachialis - flexes the arm at the glenohumeral joint

Cutaneous innervation of the lateral aspect of the forearm is by a branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, namely, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C5, C6).

Hence, injury to the musculocutaneous nerve results in weakness of supination of forearm (biceps brachii), weakness in flexion of the elbow (biceps brachii, brachialis), and loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm).

The below image shows the anterior compartment of the arm

Other options:

Option A:

Median nerve injury is characterized by sensory loss over the radial 3 1/2 fingers and loss of thumb abduction. In high lesions, the long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, the radial wrist flexors, and the forearm pronator muscles are also paralyzed. Wasting of the thenar eminence is seen in long-standing cases.

Option B:

Radial nerve injury can present with wrist drop, thumb drop, and finger drop. Extension of the elbow will be spared in lesions below the elbow. The extension of the IP joints is intact due to the action of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Loss of sensation over the first dorsal web space is observed.

Option D:

Ulnar nerve injury is characterized by ulnar claw hand, wasting of the hypothenar muscles and intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensory loss over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the hand and medial 1 1/2 fingers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The type of fibers present in the fornix are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Association and commisural fibers

The fibers present in the fornix are association fibers except for the hippocampal commissure of fornix which has commissural fibers. Hence the most appropriate answer is option A. i.e both association and commissural fibers.

Association fibers connect various cortical regions within the same hemisphere whereas commissural fibers connect corresponding regions of two hemispheres.

Fornix arises from the hippocampus and ends in the mamillary body of the hypothalamus. It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

Note: The function of the commissure of the fornix is to connect the hippocampal formations of the two sides.
questions.learning: Association and commisural fibers — The fibers present in the fornix are association fibers except for the hippocampal commissure of fornix which has commissural fibers.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Researchers conduct a randomized controlled trial to evaluate whether adding tranexamic acid (TXA) to routine oxytocin prophylaxis reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) after vaginal delivery. The study reports a relative risk (RR) of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.66–0.96) for PPH in the TXA group compared with the control group. Which of the following best interprets these findings?
options: TXA increases the risk of PPH by 20%.
TXA reduces the risk of PPH by 80%.
TXA reduces the risk of PPH by 20%.
The absolute risk of PPH with TXA is 0.8%.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TXA reduces the risk of PPH by 20%.

Relative Risk Reduction = 1 − RR = 1 − 0.80 = 0.20 (20%). Since the confidence interval does not cross 1, the reduction is statistically significant.
questions.learning: TXA reduces the risk of PPH by 20%. Relative Risk Reduction = 1 − RR = 1 − 0.80 = 0.20 (20%).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following would have no effect on the function of the protein product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glutamine replaced by asparagine

When glutamine is replaced by asparagine, there is no change in the function of the protein product.

This is due to the concept of conservative or homologous replacement of amino acids. Asparagine and glutamine are both uncharged polar (hydrophilic) amino acids. Thus, when glutamine is replaced with asparagine there is no change in the polarity or the charge of the peptide/protein.
questions.learning: Glutamine replaced by asparagine When glutamine is replaced by asparagine, there is no change in the function of the protein product. This is due to the concept of conservative or homologous replacement of amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
What is the repair mechanism associated with CRISPR-Cas9?

CRISPR- Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-homologous end joining

The repair mechanism associated with CRISPR-Cas9 is non-homologous end-joining.

Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) is a mechanism by which a group of proteins mediates the recognition, processing, and direct ligation of the ends of two DNA fragments where a double-strand break in DNA has occurred. This is in contrast to homologous recombination (HR), another mechanism to repair a double-strand break, where DNA repair needs an undamaged homologous DNA template to replace an adjacent damaged one.

Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated gene 9 or CRISPR-Cas9 is a DNA editing/gene regulatory system. It involves two essential components, Cas9, an endonuclease that causes a double-stranded DNA break, allowing modifications to the genomic DNA to be made; and a synthetic single guide RNA or sgRNA responsible for guiding Cas9 to its target.

Once the sgRNA has directed the Cas9 to the section of the genomic DNA to be edited, the 3’ end of the sgRNA comes to lie across a specific sequence of DNA adjacent to the editing side called the protospacer adjacent motif or PAM. The Cas9 now causes a double-stranded break in the DNA at the PAM site which is then repaired by a non-homologous end-joining.

The following image shows CRISPR-Cas9 system

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient complains of loss of appetite and dysphagia. He lost around significant amount weight in the last few months. The clinician suspects an esophageal condition. Which of the following is the gold standard investigation method in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

This patient with a significant weight loss and other symptoms of cachexia and anorexia most likely has esophageal carcinoma. Endoscopy and biopsy of the lesion (gold standard) are performed to diagnose esophageal carcinoma.

Esophageal carcinoma is more commonly seen in men. Tobacco use and alcohol are strong risk factors. Adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus are the two most common types. The squamous cell variant usually affects the upper two-thirds and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower third. The incidence of adenocarcinoma is increasing.

Clinical features include:

* Dysphagia (most common)

* Regurgitation

* Vomiting

* Odynophagia

* Weight loss

In the advanced stage, there can be hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, horner’s syndrome, chronic spinal pain, and diaphragmatic paralysis.

Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Other investigations include barium swallow, which shows a rat-tail appearance due to irregular narrowing or ulceration. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumor invasion and lymph node metastasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anemia. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by a classic clinical triad: iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, and glossitis or cheilosis. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) and cheilosis (cracking at the mouth corners) are physical signs resulting from severe, chronic iron deficiency. This condition is most common in middle-aged women and carries an increased risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Esophageal cancer (Option B) may be a long-term complication but is not the primary diagnosis for this triad. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a motility disorder that causes dysphagia but is not associated with anemia or iron-deficiency skin signs. Tylosis palmaris (Option D) is a genetic condition involving thickened skin on the palms and soles, which is also linked to esophageal cancer risk but unrelated to anemia. Therefore, the described findings are diagnostic of Plummer-Vinson syndrome
