questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following options best describes the characteristic clinical features seen in a patient bitten by the snake shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The snake shown in the image is characteristic of a viper (most commonly Russell’s viper), which is highly venomous and responsible for severe systemic and local toxicity. Why option (D) is correct Viper venom is predominantly hemotoxic and vasculotoxic, but Russell’s viper venom also has neurotoxic components, making its clinical picture mixed. Typical manifestations include: 1. 1. Bleeding – due to venom-induced coagulopathy (DIC-like state, bleeding from gums, wound, hematuria) 2. 2. Paralysis – especially with Russell’s viper, which can cause ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and respiratory muscle weakness 3. 3. Amputation – severe local tissue necrosis, gangrene, and compartment syndrome may necessitate surgical debridement or amputation Why other options are incorrect (A) Non-poisonous, dry bite – incorrect; the snake is venomous (B) Severe edema, necrosis and bleeding – partially correct but misses neurotoxicity (C) Severe muscle necrosis, rhabdomyolysis – typical of sea snake, not viper
questions.learning: The snake shown in the image is characteristic of a viper (most commonly Russell’s viper), which is highly venomous and responsible for severe systemic and local toxicity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the finding marked by the arrow in the below image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vossius ring

The finding given in the image is that of a Vossius ring.

Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

It usually has about the same diameter as the contracted pupil. The force of the blow drives the cornea and iris backward and thus producing an impression of the iris on the lens. The resorption of the pigment results in discrete subcapsular opacities.

Other options:

Option B: Weiss ring is a floater which may be seen by the patient as a circle or other large solitary lesion. It is the detached former attachment to the margin of the optic disc. It is seen in posterior vitreous detachment and is not confirmatory. It is seen in the image below.

Option C: A Fleischer's ring is usually observed in keratoconus, representing epithelial iron deposits. It is seen best with a cobalt blue filter.

Option D: Kayser-Fleischer ring is observed in Wilson's disease, due to intraocular deposition of copper. A brownish-yellow zone is seen in the peripheral Descemet membrane of the cornea. Anterior capsular cataract, also knowns as a sunflower cataract may be seen in some patients.
questions.learning: Vossius ring — The finding given in the image is that of a Vossius ring. Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with low-grade fever, headache, and malaise for the past 2 weeks. Lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals lymphocytic predominance and low glucose levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tubercular meningitis

Differentiate the common causes of meningitis based on CSF analysis. Tubercular meningitis (TBM) typically presents with a subacute onset (days to weeks) of fever, headache, and malaise. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, reflecting chronic granulomatous inflammation caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bacterial meningitis: Usually presents acutely with neutrophilic predominance, markedly low glucose, and very high protein.
• B. Viral meningitis: CSF shows lymphocytic predominance, but glucose is usually normal with only mildly elevated protein.
• D. Fungal meningitis: Can also show lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose, but it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis), whereas the clinical presentation here is most typical of TBM.

High-yield Pearl

| Type of Meningitis | Cells | Protein | Glucose

| ------------------ | ----- | ------- | -------

| Bacterial | Neutrophils ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓↓

| Viral | Lymphocytes ↑ | Mild ↑ | Normal

| Tubercular | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓

| Fungal | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑ | ↓

Exam Tip:

• Subacute meningitis + Lymphocytic CSF + Low glucose = Think Tubercular meningitis.
• Acute meningitis + Neutrophils + Very low glucose = Bacterial meningitis.
questions.learning: Tubercular meningitis Differentiate the common causes of meningitis based on CSF analysis. Tubercular meningitis (TBM) typically presents with a subacute onset (days to weeks) of fever, headache, and malaise.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the half-life of lithium?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a widely used mood stabilizer in the management of bipolar disorder. In adults with normal renal function, lithium has an average elimination half-life of approximately 24 hours. Because a drug typically requires about 4–5 half-lives to reach steady-state levels, lithium concentrations usually stabilize after 4–5 days of regular dosing. This is why serum lithium levels are generally checked after 5 days of initiating therapy or changing the dose. Lithium is excreted entirely by the kidneys, and its half-life can be prolonged in certain situations—up to 36 hours or more in elderly patients or those with renal impairment. Therefore, renal function has a major impact on lithium pharmacokinetics. Options A (8 hours) and B (12 hours) are too short, while Option D (48 hours) is longer than the typical half-life in healthy adults. Because lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (≈0.6–1.2 mEq/L), regular serum level monitoring is essential to avoid toxicity, which can manifest as tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, or coma
questions.learning: Lithium is a widely used mood stabilizer in the management of bipolar disorder. In adults with normal renal function, lithium has an average elimination half-life of approximately 24 hours.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following disease results in weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leprosy

Leprosy could result in paresis of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness.

Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids. This can be due to the involvement of the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve (as in leprosy). Other causes of lagophthalmos include extreme proptosis and symblepharon. The decreased corneal sensation seen is due to the involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve which innervates the cornea.

Leprosy or Hansen disease is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by infection with Mycobacterium leprae. Ocular features in leprosy occur due to bacterial invasion and include corneal anesthesia, lagophthalmos, corneal ulceration, episcleritis, and iris atrophy. Other features seen are:

• Keratitis with thickened, beaded corneal nerves, punctate subepithelial lesions, pannus, and vascularization
• Chronic low-grade anterior uveitis
• Miosis
• Iris atrophy
• Iris pearls
• Retinal pearls

Option B: The most common ocular manifestation in Lyme's disease is conjunctivitis. Other manifestations like keratitis, iridocyclitis, retinal vasculitis, choroiditis, optic neuropathy, and uveitis occurs very rarely.

Option C: Ophthalmia neonatarum also called neonatal conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva occurring in an infant <30 days after birth. The clinical features include conjunctival redness, eyelid edema, and ocular discharge (purulent or mucopurulent).

Option D: In trachoma, the symptoms include lacrimation, scanty mucoid discharge and foreign body sensation. Conjunctival congestion and follicles, papillary hyperplasia, Herbert follicles (seen in the limbal area), and progressive pannus are the characteristic features.
questions.learning: Leprosy Leprosy could result in paresis of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness. Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following microorganisms cannot be grown on artificial culture media?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium leprae, the causative agent of leprosy, is an obligate intracellular pathogen. A hallmark of this organism is its total inability to grow on any artificial or cell-free culture media. For experimental purposes, it is cultivated in animal models, such as the footpads of mice or the nine-banded armadillo. Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) grows easily on standard media like blood agar. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option C) is slow-growing but cultivable on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) media. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option D) is fastidious but grows on enriched media. The failure of M. leprae to grow in vitro is attributed to its massive gene decay, having lost many essential metabolic pathways. Therefore, it remains the classic example of a bacterium that cannot be cultured using standard microbiological techniques
questions.learning: Mycobacterium leprae, the causative agent of leprosy, is an obligate intracellular pathogen. A hallmark of this organism is its total inability to grow on any artificial or cell-free culture media.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presents with blurred vision and headaches. Retinal examination reveals flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and disc edema. According to the Keith-Wagener classification, which grade of hypertensive retinopathy does this patient have?
questions.explanation: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification is used to grade the severity of hypertensive retinopathy based on ophthalmoscopic findings. The presence of disc edema (papilledema), along with the signs of severe retinal damage like flame-shaped hemorrhages and cotton wool spots, is the defining feature of Grade IV retinopathy. This grade signifies malignant hypertension and is a medical emergency, as it indicates significant end-organ damage and a high risk of cardiovascular or neurological events. Grade III (Option C) includes hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates (often in a "macular star" pattern) but lacks disc edema. Grade II (Option B) is characterized by more pronounced arteriolar narrowing and AV nipping. Grade 1 (Option A) involves simple generalized arteriolar narrowing and "silver-wiring". Management of Grade IV retinopathy requires immediate but controlled reduction of blood pressure, usually in an intensive care setting, and urgent neurological evaluation to rule out hypertensive encephalopathy. Retinal findings often improve significantly once blood pressure is stabilized

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following procedures has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Highly selective vagotomy

Highly selective vagotomy (HSV) has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers among the given options.

HSV retains the vagal innervation to the antrum, pylorus, and the remaining abdominal viscera while cutting off the vagal nerve supply to the proximal two-thirds of the stomach, which houses nearly all of the parietal cells. As a result, the procedure reduces overall gastric acid secretion by around 75%, and GI side effects are uncommon. However, HSV has not had great success treating type II (gastric and duodenal) and type III (prepyloric) gastric ulcers, possibly as a result of hypergastrinemia brought on by prolonged antral stasis and gastric outlet obstruction.

Option A: Resective procedures like gastrectomy have the least rates of recurrence but are less preferred nowadays due to higher rates of morbidity and mortality.

Option C: Unlike HSV, vagotomy and drainage is widely accepted as a successful definitive operation for complicated PUD, with lower rates of recurrence.

Option D: Gastrojejunostomy is a good choice in patients with gastric outlet obstruction or a severely diseased proximal duodenum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following barium swallow is suggestive of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia cardia

Image shows markedly dilated esophagus and characteristic bird's beak appearance suggestive of achalasia cardia (dilated esophagus with distal narrowing).

In achalasia cardia, the lower esophagral spinchter (LES) is hypertensive and fails to relax appropriately in response to swallowing. Sphincter spasm and delayed emptying through LES are also seen. Esophageal manometry is the gold standard for establishing the diagnosis of esophageal achalasia.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy
questions.learning: Achalasia cardia Image shows markedly dilated esophagus and characteristic bird's beak appearance suggestive of achalasia cardia (dilated esophagus with distal narrowing).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with facial palsy, as depicted in the image. Which anatomical structure is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows clear facial asymmetry, including drooping of the corner of the mouth and incomplete eye closure on the affected side, which is characteristic of a 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve) palsy, commonly known as Bell's palsy. This lower motor neuron lesion affects all muscles of facial expression on the same side. Regarding the distractors, a 3rd nerve palsy (Option B) would present with ptosis (eyelid drooping) and abnormal eye deviation, but would not cause a drooping mouth. Erb's palsy (Option C) is a brachial plexus injury affecting the arm's "waiter's tip" position, not the face. An isolated orbicularis oculi palsy (Option D) would only affect the ability to close the eye and would not explain the lower facial drooping seen here. Therefore, the global hemifacial weakness confirms 7th nerve involvement
questions.learning: The clinical image shows clear facial asymmetry, including drooping of the corner of the mouth and incomplete eye closure on the affected side, which is characteristic of a 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve) palsy, commonly known as Bell's palsy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old male diagnosed with carcinoma of the larynx is scheduled for treatment and has undergone the procedure shown in the image below. At what level is the incision made for this procedure?
options: At the level of the 2nd tracheal ring
At the level of the 1st tracheal ring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. At the level of the 1st tracheal ring

The clinical scenario describes a 50-year-old male with carcinoma of the larynx undergoing a tracheostomy, as shown in the image. The incision is made at the level of the first tracheal ring, above the isthmus, in a patient with laryngeal carcinoma, and this procedure is referred to as a high tracheostomy.

Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy. It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea. High tracheostomy is performed above the level of the thyroid isthmus (the Isthmus lies against the II, III, and IV tracheal rings). The only indication for high tracheostomy is carcinoma of the larynx.

It provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
It uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood.

Indications of tracheostomy:

* Respiratory obstruction due to infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria).

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures.

* Neoplasms.

* Foreign bodies or edema.

* Retained secretionsInability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles.

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions.

* Painful cough.

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Steps of Tracheostomy:

* Incision: Make a vertical incision in the midline from the cricoid cartilage to above the sternal notch. For a better cosmetic outcome for elective procedures, a 5 cm transverse incision two fingers' breadth above the sternal notch can be used.

* Dissection: Dissect tissues in the midline. Displace or ligate any dilated veins encountered to control bleeding.

* Muscle separation: Separate and retract the strap muscles of the neck laterally to expose underlying structures.

* Thyroid isthmus management: Displace the thyroid isthmus upwards or divide and ligate it with sutures.

* Local anaesthesia: Inject a few drops of 4% lignocaine into the trachea to suppress coughing.

* Tracheal incision: Fix the trachea with a hook and make a vertical incision between the third and fourth tracheal rings(Option D), converting it into a circular opening. Avoid dividing the first tracheal ring to prevent perichondritis and stenosis.

* Inserting the tube: Insert a tracheostomy tube of appropriate size into the tracheal opening and secure it with tapes.

* Avoid tight suturing: Avoid tightly suturing or packing the skin incision to prevent subcutaneous emphysema.

* Dressing: Place a gauze dressing between the skin and the flange of the tracheostomy tube around the stoma to absorb secretions, provide a barrier against infection, and allow air to escape, promoting proper healing.

Pearl PF1486: Types of Tracheostomy

High tracheostomy

* Done through the 1st tracheal ring

* An opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

* Done in case of malignancy of the larynx

* Increased risk of perichondritis and subglottic stenosis

Mid tracheostomy

* Done through the 2nd - 3rd rings

* Most commonly done tracheostomy

* Isthmus has to be retracted or divided

Low tracheostomy

* Done through the 4th - 5th tracheal ring

* Done below the isthmus

* Done when the airway is blocked at an upper airway level

* Risk of injuring the great vessels of the neck

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, diffuse erythematous rash, hypotension, and shock. She started menstruating 3 days ago and reports using superabsorbent tampons. Which of the following is the most likely reason responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superantigen like TSST-1

The presentation is classic for toxic shock syndrome associated with tampon use.

It is caused by TSST-1 produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which acts as a superantigen.

Superantigens cause non-specific activation of a large number of T cells with massive cytokine release.

This cytokine storm leads to fever, rash, hypotension, and shock.

TSST-1 (superantigen)

↓

Bridges MHC II and TCR (non-specific)

↓

Massive T-cell activation

↓

Cytokine storm:

• IL-1 → fever

• IL-2 → T-cell proliferation

• TNF-α → hypotension, shock

↓

Toxic Shock Syndrome

| Feature | Normal Antigen | Superantigen

| ------- | -------------- | ------------

| Processing | Required | Not required

| T-cell activation | Specific (\~0.01%) | Massive (20–30%)

| Binding | Specific peptide-MHC | Direct MHC–TCR binding

| Cytokines | Controlled | Explosive (storm)
questions.learning: Superantigen like TSST-1 — The presentation is classic for toxic shock syndrome associated with tampon use. It is caused by TSST-1 produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which acts as a superantigen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abductor pollicis brevis

The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such as the "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely and consistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptible to dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of the median nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the "OK" sign.

Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers.

Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome.
questions.learning: Abductor pollicis brevis — The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: No. of live births/1000 women in reproductive age group?
questions.explanation: In demography, the General Fertility Rate (GFR) is defined as the number of live births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group (typically 15 to 44 or 49 years) in a given year. It is a more refined measure of fertility than the Crude Birth Rate (Option D), which uses the total population as the denominator. The Total Fertility Rate (Option A) represents the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime based on current age-specific rates. The Net Reproduction Rate (Option C) measures the number of daughters a newborn girl will bear, accounting for maternal mortality before the end of her reproductive years. GFR is superior to CBR because it only considers the segment of the population capable of giving birth. However, it does not account for the age distribution within the reproductive group, which is why age-specific fertility rates are also used for more detailed demographic analysis and planning
questions.learning: In demography, the General Fertility Rate (GFR) is defined as the number of live births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group (typically 15 to 44 or 49 years) in a given year.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23 yr old gravida 1, para 0 at 25 weeks gestation, presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting for the past 2 days. BP-104/72mm Hg, PR-72bpm. There is generalized edema. Peripheral smear shows hemolysis. Lab values are given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Leukocyte count: 10,500/mm3 Platelet count: 62000/mm3 Hematocrit: 26% AST: 90 IU/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HELLP Syndrome

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is HELLP syndrome.

The typical presentation of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, lab findings of thrombocytopenia, low hematocrit, and peripheral smear finding of hemolysis, point towards a diagnosis of  HELLP ( Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome.

Although related to preeclampsia, hypertension and proteinuria may be absent or minimal in HELLP syndrome.

Tennessee criteria used in the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome :

* Platelet count <1 lakh,

* AST >70 IU/L,

* LDH >600 IU/L

Risk factors for HELLP syndrome include

* Preeclampsia

* abnormal placentation

* family history of HELLP syndrome

* elevated levels of fetal mRNA for FLT l (vascular endothelial growth factor rfi receptor 1) and

* Multiparity

* Maternal age >34 years

* European descent

* History of previous poor pregnancy outcomes

Laboratory evaluation in HELLP:

* Complete blood cell (CBC) count: Thrombocytopenia, anemia with possible reticulocytosis

* Coagulation studies: Normal prothrombin time, 50% may have prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time

* Peripheral smear: Schistocytes, helmet cells, and burr cells secondary to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

* Serum aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase (AST/ALT) levels: Elevated secondary to liver dysfunction

* Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level: Elevated secondary to liver dysfunction or hemolysis

* Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN)/creatinine with acute renal failure

* Bilirubin level: Increased secondary to hemolysis

* Haptoglobin level: Decreased secondary to hemolysis

* Fibrinogen levels: Low secondary to increased coagulation

* D-dimer: Increased due to fibrinolysis/DIC

HELLP syndrome may lead to the development of DIC which manifests as increased fibrin split products and decreased fibrinogen levels.

Other options:

Disorder

AST (SGOT) U/L
Bilirubin (mg/dL)

Cholestasis of pregnancy
Up to 200

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. On examination, the uterus is tense and tender, and fetal parts are not easily palpable through the abdominal wall. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of significant abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender, board-like uterus in the third trimester is highly diagnostic for Abruptio placenta. This condition involve the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall. The difficulty in palpating fetal parts occurs due to the extreme uterine hypertonicity and tenderness associated with retroplacental hemorrhage. In contrast, placenta previa (Option B) is characteristically associated with painless vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. Uterine rupture (Option C) is rare in a primigravida and usually presents with the recession of the presenting part and easily palpable fetal parts under the maternal skin. Polyhydramnios (Option D) involves excessive amniotic fluid and would present with an oversized but non-tender uterus without acute bleeding. Abruptio placenta is an obstetric emergency that carries high risks of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and fetal distress, necessitating immediate stabilization and often urgent delivery to ensure both maternal and fetal safety
questions.learning: The clinical triad of significant abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender, board-like uterus in the third trimester is highly diagnostic for Abruptio placenta.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be used for pre-operative management in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha adrenergic blockers

Alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine are given pre-operatively to manage hypertension in pheochromocytoma. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved.

The drug of choice to control blood pressure prior to surgery is oral phenoxybenzamine at 0.5–4 mg/kg of body weight. It is a non-specific α-blocker and is preferred due to its long action (3-4 days).

Pheochromocytoma:

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

It can be sporadical or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1.

Clinical features:

It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness.

Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants.

Investigations:

* Biochemical screening test - measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms.

* Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy, DOPA- or FDG- PET scan are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases.

Treatment:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma.

Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers.

Postoperatively, lifelong yearly follow-up should be done.
questions.learning: Alpha adrenergic blockers Alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine are given pre-operatively to manage hypertension in pheochromocytoma. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding scleredema?
options: The dermis is 3–4 times thicker than normal
Erythema and peau d’orange appearance of the skin can be seen
Can occur in association with diabetes
Associated with sclerodactyly or Raynauds phenomenon
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Associated with sclerodactyly or Raynauds phenomenon

Scleredema is not associated with sclerodactyly or Raynauds Phenomenon. Scleredema and scleroderma are different entities. In contrast to systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), scleredema is not associated with sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon, nail fold capillary changes, or serum autoantibodies.

In scleredema, the dermis is 3–4 times thicker than normal due to an increase in type 1 collagen synthesis by dysfunctional fibroblast. However, fibroblast proliferation is not seen.

Erythema and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin are commonly observed. The hands and feet are characteristically spared.

Diabetic scleredema is the most common type. In diabetic scleredema, the accumulation of collagen may be due to irreversible non‐enzymatic glycosylation of collagen and resistance to degradation by collagenase. It can also occur post-streptococcal infections.
questions.learning: Associated with sclerodactyly or Raynauds phenomenon Scleredema is not associated with sclerodactyly or Raynauds Phenomenon. Scleredema and scleroderma are different entities.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The Truelove–Witts criteria are used to define acute severe ulcerative colitis. All of the following are components of the Truelove–Witts criteria, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Presence of jaundice and pruritus

The Truelove–Witts criteria are used to identify acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) and guide the need for hospitalization and intensive therapy.

Criteria include:

• ≥6 bloody stools/day
• Plus ≥1 systemic sign of toxicity:

o    Pulse ≥90/min

o    Temperature >37.8°C

o    Hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL

o    ESR >30 mm/hr

Not included:

• Jaundice and pruritus, which are features of hepatobiliary disease (e.g., primary sclerosing cholangitis) rather than severity criteria for ulcerative colitis.
questions.learning: Presence of jaundice and pruritus — The Truelove–Witts criteria are used to identify acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) and guide the need for hospitalization and intensive therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with hypoxemia and a normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. What can be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoventilation

All of the given options can cause hypoxemia out of which the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) remains normal in hypoventilation.

The A-a gradient or the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient refers to the difference between the oxygen concentration in the alveoli (PAO2) and oxygen concentration in the arterial system (PaO2).

A-a gradient= PAO2 - PaO2

In hypoventilation, patients lack oxygen tension in the respiratory system as well as their arterial system. This results in a decrease in both PAO2 and PaO2 and A-a gradient remains normal. Hypoventilation can be seen in CNS depression, neuromuscular diseases such as myasthenia gravis, kyphoscoliosis, vertebral fractures, etc.

Other options:

Option A- In a right-to-left shunt, a portion of the pulmonary blood flow gets shunted away from the alveoli. This results in ventilation without perfusion which causes a higher V/Q ratio. Here, diffusion between capillaries and alveoli is unaffected,  but the arterial PaO2 is decreased due to the lack of oxygenation of the shunted blood. This results in hypoxemia and an increased A-a gradient. In the cases of the shunt, oxygenation does not improve hypoxemia.

Option B- Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia.

Low V/Q mismatch occurs in chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD), asthma, interstitial lung disease, etc. In these cases, the A-a oxygen gradient is increased due to a defect in diffusion resulting in hypoxemia.

A high V/Q ratio is seen in pulmonary embolism (PE) where there is wasted ventilation. The alveolar oxygen is normal but there is decreased perfusion resulting in increased A-a gradient.

Inspiratory hypoxia, seen at high altitudes, can cause a V/Q mismatch. The decreased atmospheric pressure causes a decreased PAO2. There is normal diffusion which suggests a normal A-a gradient while the arterial PaO2 decreases, leading to hypoxemia.

Hypoventilation is the better answer as the cause of the V/Q mismatch is not specified.

Option D: Alveolar membrane damage affects diffusion between the alveoli and capillaries. The oxygen levels in the arterial blood decrease even though alveoli are being ventilated. This leads to an increased A-a gradient.
questions.learning: Hypoventilation All of the given options can cause hypoxemia out of which the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) remains normal in hypoventilation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following sensory receptors undergoes hyperpolarization rather than depolarization during sensory transduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Photoreceptors of the retina

Photoreceptors are unique because exposure to light causes hyperpolarization. Light activates rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase, reducing intracellular cGMP. Closure of cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels decreases inward current, resulting in hyperpolarization and reduced glutamate release.

Other options:

• B. Cochlear hair cells: Depolarize when mechanically gated K⁺ channels open.
• C. Taste receptor cells: Most taste modalities produce depolarization.
• D. Olfactory receptor neurons: Odorants cause depolarization via cAMP-mediated Na⁺/Ca²⁺ influx.
questions.learning: Photoreceptors of the retina Photoreceptors are unique because exposure to light causes hyperpolarization. Light activates rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase, reducing intracellular cGMP.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A tall male presents with sparse pubic and axillary hair, underdeveloped genitalia, and laboratory findings of elevated LH and FSH levels. Karyotype analysis reveals an XXY chromosomal pattern. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a tall stature, signs of androgen deficiency (scant hair, small genitalia), and the pathognomonic 47, XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B). This is the most common cause of primary hypogonadism in males. The elevated LH and FSH levels occur due to the lack of negative feedback from the failing testes (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A) would result in a similar hormonal profile but would lack the specific XXY genetics and tall stature. Noonan syndrome (Option C) presents with characteristic facial features and heart defects, usually with a 46, XY karyotype. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Option D) typically presents with ambiguous genitalia in females or precocious puberty in males. Therefore, the specific chromosomal finding of XXY confirms Klinefelter's syndrome as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of a tall stature, signs of androgen deficiency (scant hair, small genitalia), and the pathognomonic 47, XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the sign given in the image below:
questions.explanation: The image shows the "Double Ring Sign," also known as the "Halo Sign" or "Double Target Sign," which is a bedside test for identifying cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. When blood mixed with CSF is dropped onto filter paper, the CSF, being less viscous than blood, spreads further outward, creating a clear outer ring around a central red blood spot. This is commonly used in cases of CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea following head trauma. Beta-2 transferrin (Option A) is the biochemical gold standard test for CSF but requires laboratory analysis. The "handkerchief sign" (Option C) refers to the fact that CSF does not stiffen a handkerchief when dry, unlike nasal mucus. The "teardrop sign" (Option D) is an imaging finding in orbital floor fractures. Although useful, the halo sign is not 100% specific, as other fluids can also create similar patterns
questions.learning: The image shows the "Double Ring Sign," also known as the "Halo Sign" or "Double Target Sign," which is a bedside test for identifying cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are measuring a patient's blood pressure at a primary health center when the sphygmomanometer fell and broke and mercury was spilled onto the ground. How will you clean the mercury?
options: Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar
Collect it by sweeping it with a broom and throw it outside
Collect it by sweeping it and flush it in the toilet
Collect it by hand and then wash hands with water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar

Mercury is cleaned by collecting it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and putting the mercury into a jar.

After a mercury spill, the following steps should be followed:

• Isolation of the spill and ventilation of the area
• Collection of items to clean the spill: zipper-top plastic bags, trash bags, gloves, paper towels, cardboard or squeegee, eye dropper, tape, flashlight, and powdered sulfur.
• Clean up the spill.
• After putting on the gloves, the glass pieces are picked and placed on a towel, rolled and disposed of into a zipper-top plastic bag, and finally sealed.
• The beads of mercury are cleaned by using cardboard or a squeegee. They are rolled onto a sheet of paper, disposed into the zipper bag, and sealed.
• Powdered sulfur may be used to absorb small beads that are not visible
• Looking for any missed spill using a flashlight
• Remove other mercury contaminated items and wipe off any mercury beads with a wet towel into a plastic trash bag
• Proper disposal of contaminated clean-up materials.
• Keep the area well ventilated for 24 hours, keep pets and children away from the area

The use of a vacuum cleaner or broom to clean the spill should be avoided. This will break the mercury into smaller droplets and spread it further. Mercury should not be poured down any drain. Do not use a washing machine to clean the clothes contaminated with mercury. This can contaminate the water and sewage. Mercury-contaminated shoes or clothing should not be worn.
questions.learning: Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar Mercury is cleaned by collecting it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and putting the mercury into a jar.

questions.text: During labor, a fetus is found to be in face presentation. Which fetal skull diameter presents to the maternal pelvis in this position?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Submento-bregmatic

Face presentation is characterized by complete extension of the fetal head, and the presenting diameter is the submentobregmatic diameter, which measures 9.5 cm. This extends from: Submentum (junction of neck and chin) to Bregma (anterior fontanelle)

10 cm | Incomplete flexion | Vertex

14 cm | Partial extension | Brow

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding after 6 weeks of amenorrhea. Transvaginal ultrasonography does not reveal an intrauterine gestational sac or any signs of ectopic pregnancy. Her serum β-hCG level is 1,200 IU/L, which is below the discriminatory zone. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: In a hemodynamically stable patient with a pregnancy of unknown location, the immediate priority is to determine if the pregnancy is viable. The discriminatory zone for visualizing a gestational sac via transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is typically IU/L. Since this patient’s level is 1,200 IU/L, the absence of an intrauterine sac is not diagnostic of an ectopic pregnancy. The next step is to repeat the serum β-hCG after 48 hours. A normal pregnancy should show a doubling of the level, whereas a plateauing or declining level suggests an ectopic pregnancy or early loss. Laparoscopy (Option A) and Dilatation and curettage (Option D) are invasive and reserved for higher β-hCG levels or clinical instability. Methotrexate (Option B) is only given after an ectopic pregnancy is confirmed. Therefore, expectant monitoring of the β-hCG trend is the appropriate standard of care
questions.learning: In a hemodynamically stable patient with a pregnancy of unknown location, the immediate priority is to determine if the pregnancy is viable. The discriminatory zone for visualizing a gestational sac via transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is typically IU/L.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with numbness over the chin and lower lip. Which nerve is most likely involved in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental nerve

The mental nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). It exits the skull through the mental foramen and provides cutaneous sensation to the chin, lower lip, and labial mucosa. Injury to the mental nerve results in numbness of the chin and lower lip without affecting the mandibular teeth.

Why not the other options?

• A. Great auricular nerve: Supplies the skin over the parotid region, angle of the mandible, and ear.
• C. Inferior alveolar nerve: Supplies the mandibular teeth and gives rise to the mental nerve; a lesion proximal to the mental foramen also causes dental sensory loss.
• D. Lingual nerve: Provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.
questions.learning: Mental nerve — The mental nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). It exits the skull through the mental foramen and provides cutaneous sensation to the chin, lower lip, and labial mucosa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is tumour marker of pancreatic cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carcinoembryonic antigen

Carcino Embryogenic Antigen is the tumour marker for pancreatic cancer.

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)

* Normally detected in glycocalyx of fetal epithelial cells

* May play a role in the metastasis of cancer cells

* CEA levels over 5 ng/dL: ascites fluid A/W malignancy

* Detection, recurrence, and prognosis of adenocarcinoma (lung) and colorectal carcinoma

* Elevated levels also present in cirrhosis, biliary obstruction, hepatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, smokers and post-surgical bowel sequestration with mucocele

* Benign cysts may be CEA+ even when benign

* Hepatocellular carcinoma: canalicular pattern for polyclonal CEA is 50-90% sensitive for hepatocellular carcinoma, > 95% specific

* Pancreatic adenocarcinoma: 92% sensitive for metastases vs. 0% for bile duct adenoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Onion skin fibrosis on histopathology is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Onion-skin” periductal concentric fibrosis is the histologic hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Unknown trigger (autoimmune + gut-liver axis)

↓

Chronic inflammation of intra & extrahepatic bile ducts

↓

Periductal fibrosis (concentric layers)

↓

Bile duct strictures (“beading”)

↓

Cholestasis → cirrhosis → liver failure

It reflects chronic inflammatory obliteration of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts leading to multifocal strictures. Primary biliary cirrhosis shows portal granulomas and ductopenia, not onion-skin fibrosis. This classic pattern is a high-yield buzzword for PSC.

Small bile duct showing an “onion-skin” type of periductal fibrosis

Beaded bile ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis

| Feature | PSC | PBC

| ------- | --- | ---

| Ducts involved | Intra + extrahepatic | Small intrahepatic

| Histology | Onion-skin fibrosis | Florid duct lesion

| Antibody | p-ANCA | AMA

| Association | Ulcerative colitis | Autoimmune diseases

| Imaging | Beading | Normal early

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the type of psoriasis in the given picture.
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple small, drop-like erythematous papules with fine scaling scattered over the skin. This pattern is characteristic of guttate psoriasis. The term “guttate” comes from the Latin word gutta, meaning “drop,” reflecting the raindrop-like lesions. Guttate psoriasis commonly: 1. Affects children and young adults 2. Appears suddenly, often after a streptococcal infection 3. Involves the trunk and proximal limbs 4. Shows numerous small lesions, unlike large plaques Why other options are incorrect: (B) Erythrodermic psoriasis → Diffuse redness involving almost entire body (C) Pustular psoriasis → Presence of pus-filled lesions, not seen here (D) Inverse psoriasis → Occurs in skin folds, smooth and shiny lesions without scaling

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old asymptomatic woman visits the gynecology OPD for routine cervical cancer screening. She has no history of abnormal Pap smears, is immunocompetent, and has undergone regular screening in the past. Which of the following is the preferred screening strategy for her?
options: Co-testing (Pap smear + high-risk HPV DNA test) every 5 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Co-testing (Pap smear + high-risk HPV DNA test) every 5 years

For women 30–65 years of age, the preferred cervical cancer screening strategy is co-testing with cytology (Pap/LBC) plus high-risk HPV DNA testing every 5 years. Persistent HPV infection is more clinically significant after age 30, making HPV testing highly sensitive and specific for detecting high-grade cervical lesions.

Why not the other options?

• A. LBC every 5 years – Incorrect. Cytology alone is recommended every 3 years, not every 5 years.
• C. VIA – Used mainly in low-resource settings (including India's national screening program) where laboratory-based testing is unavailable. It is feasible but less accurate than HPV-based screening.
• D. Colposcopy – A diagnostic procedure performed after an abnormal screening test, not a primary screening method.

High-Yield Screening Schedule

• 21–29 years: Pap smear (cytology) every 3 years
• 30–65 years: Co-testing every 5 years (preferred), or primary HPV testing every 5 years, or cytology alone every 3 years
• >65 years: Screening may be discontinued if prior screening has been adequate and consistently negative.
questions.learning: Co-testing (Pap smear + high-risk HPV DNA test) every 5 years For women 30–65 years of age, the preferred cervical cancer screening strategy is co-testing with cytology (Pap/LBC) plus high-risk HPV DNA testing every 5 years.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with erythematous scaly patches in the perioral region, mucosal ulcers, and impaired epithelial wound healing. What is the likely mineral deficiency associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc deficiency

Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic periorificial dermatitis (around mouth, eyes, anus), mucosal ulcers, and impaired wound healing, as seen in this child. Zinc is a cofactor for numerous enzymes involved in:

• DNA & RNA synthesis
• Cell division and tissue repair
• Protein synthesis and epithelial integrity

Deficiency results in: Acrodermatitis enteropathica (genetic zinc malabsorption)

• Impaired epithelial regeneration → erythematous scaly lesions
• Poor wound healing
• Mucosal breakdown → ulcers

Other features of zinc deficiency:

• Alopecia
• Diarrhea
• Growth retardation
• Loss of taste (hypogeusia)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Iron deficiency: Causes anemia, not characteristic dermatitis
• Calcium deficiency: Affects bones (rickets/osteomalacia)
• Copper deficiency: Causes anemia and neurologic issues, not perioral dermatitis
questions.learning: Zinc deficiency Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic periorificial dermatitis (around mouth, eyes, anus), mucosal ulcers, and impaired wound healing, as seen in this child.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A randomized trial comparing the efficacy of two drugs showed a difference between the two with a p value of <0.005. In reality, both drugs do not differ at all. This is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha error

• In this scenario, let’s take the null hypothesis as the two drugs being the same, which the questions states, is true in reality.
• The alternative hypothesis will then be that both drugs are different.
• The questions states that p value was found to be < 0.005, which is statistically significant and so the null hypothesis is rejected.
• But we already know that the null hypothesis is true and we are forced to accept the alternative hypothesis even though it is false.
• This is a type I error or alpha error.
• When an alternative hypothesis is accepted even when it is false and the null hypothesis is true, it is a type I error or false positive error.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are criteria for opting Le Fort’s operation for surgical correction of pelvic organ prolapse? I. Procidentia in old age II. Unfit for long duration surgery III. Associated uterine pathology IV. Coital function no longer required Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and IV

Le Fort’s operation (Le Fort’s partial colpocleisis) is an obliterative surgery performed for advanced pelvic organ prolapse (procidentia) in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse and are poor candidates for prolonged reconstructive surgery. The procedure closes most of the vaginal canal while leaving lateral channels for drainage of cervical and uterine secretions if the uterus is retained. The following are indications for Le Fort’s operation:

• I. Procidentia in old age: It is commonly performed in elderly women with complete uterovaginal prolapse (procidentia).
• II. Unfit for long-duration surgery: It is a short, relatively simple operation with minimal blood loss, making it suitable for women with significant medical comorbidities.
• IV. Coital function no longer required: Since the vagina is obliterated, future vaginal intercourse is not possible. Therefore, it is performed only in women who no longer desire sexual activity.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Associated uterine pathology: Le Fort’s operation is contraindicated if there is suspected or confirmed uterine, cervical, or endometrial pathology, because the uterus becomes inaccessible for future evaluation. Such patients generally require hysterectomy or another appropriate procedure.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Le Fort’s operation (Le Fort’s partial colpocleisis) is an obliterative surgery performed for advanced pelvic organ prolapse (procidentia) in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse and are poor candidates for prolonged…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man suddenly develops a severe headache described as the worst of his life, followed by vomiting and photophobia. On examination, neck stiffness and a dilated right pupil are noted. CT imaging shows hemorrhage in the subarachnoid space. What is the most common underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sudden "thunderclap" headache (the worst headache of one's life), vomiting, and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The most common cause of spontaneous SAH is the rupture of an intracranial aneurysm, accounting for approximately 50% of cases. Hypertension (Option A) is a major risk factor but is less often the direct cause of the bleeding compared to an aneurysm. Arteriovenous malformations (Option C) are a significant cause but are less frequent than aneurysms. Brain tumors (Option D) can cause bleeding via vessel erosion but are a rare cause of SAH. The dilated pupil on the right side suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third cranial nerve. Diagnosis is primarily by non-contrast CT, and management involves early surgical clipping or endovascular coiling to prevent rebleeding
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a sudden "thunderclap" headache (the worst headache of one's life), vomiting, and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: After receiving a complaint from a security guard, the police recovered a beheaded skull bone near a park. During the investigation, the police suspected that it could be that of a known missing person. The missing person's relatives were called in to confirm the identity. Which of the following techniques can be used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superimposition

The technique used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person is superimposition. The superimposition technique is applied to the skull to determine whether it belongs to the person in the photograph.

The following points can be used for comparisons such as the eyes, nasion, prosthion, zygomas, lower border of the nose, supraorbital ridges, lower border of the zygomas, angle of the jaw, external auditory meatus, teeth and the lower border of the upper jaw.

Other options:

Option B: Anthropometry is based on the principle that the skeletal dimensions do not change after the age of 21 years and the variation in the size of the different parts to one another. Descriptive data such as the color of the hair, eyes, complexion, and body marks are recorded. Body measurements are estimated such as height, anteroposterior diameter of head and trunk, the span of outstretched arms, the length of the left middle finger, left little finger, left forearm, left foot, length, and breadth of right ear, and color of left iris from the photographs.

Option C: DNA fingerprinting for forensic analysis is done to detect DNA from small amounts of samples from the crime scene. DNA fingerprinting uses restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLPs) or Polymerase chain reaction(PCR) to identify a person's unique pattern of DNA.

Option D: Cheiloscopy is also known as lip printing. Here, the fissures and grooves on the lip characteristic of a person are examined.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is considered balanced resuscitation?
options: Maintain ph by ensuring acid-base balance
Fluid resuscitation by giving colloids and crystalloids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Allow permissible hypotension

Permissive hypotension is a part of balanced resuscitation in trauma management to avoid bleeding.

Damage control resuscitation (DCR) i.e. balanced resuscitation is used in the settings of major trauma. It aims to control hemorrhage and prevent coagulopathy prior to the development of the trauma triad of death (hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy). The components of DCR include:

• Permissive hypotension until definitive surgical control
• Minimize crystalloid based resuscitation
• Early use of blood products (PRBCs, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate) in the ratio of 1:1:1
• Use of hemostatic agents such as tranexamic acid, recombinant factor 7a, prothrombin complex concentrates

DCR has the following advantages:

• Minimizes the impact of trauma-induced coagulopathy
• Limits blood product waste
• Reduces the complications that occur with aggressive crystalloid resuscitation.
questions.learning: Allow permissible hypotension Permissive hypotension is a part of balanced resuscitation in trauma management to avoid bleeding. Damage control resuscitation (DCR) i.e. balanced resuscitation is used in the settings of major trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoderm

Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak.

Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure called the gastrula. This process establishes the three primary germ layers that give rise to all tissues and organs of the body. During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.

Cells from the epiblast migrate inward (invagination) through the primitive streak.

The first group of migrating epiblast cells replaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm. The endoderm gives rise to structures like the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs.

Subsequent migrating cells spread between the epiblast and the newly formed endoderm to create the mesoderm, which forms structures like muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system.

Remaining epiblast cells that do not migrate through the primitive streak form the ectoderm, which gives rise to the epidermis and the nervous system.

Other Options:

Option B: Cardiac Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms after the endoderm and differentiates later into subtypes, including the cardiac mesoderm.

Option C: Epidermis: The epidermis arises from the ectoderm, which forms after both the endoderm and mesoderm.

Option D: Neural Groove: The neural groove is part of the ectoderm and forms during neurulation, which occurs much later than the formation of the endoderm.
questions.learning: Endoderm Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak. Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure called the gastrula.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: You are attending physiology viva. The examiner asks you who recorded the first EEG. You say "I don't know ". The examiner feels bad for you and gives you a clue that "the name sounds like something you get commonly in McDonalds". You remember the name and answer correctly. What type of memory has been implicated here?"
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Priming

In the given scenario, priming is the most appropriate answer.

The examiner is asking for a fact, and then prompting the answer, by giving a clue which sounds (phonological) like the answer. This is an example of priming.

Prime is any cue, which precedes the recall of the target word. It maybe similar to hear (sun-bun-gun) or may hold similarity to the target word (Sun- moon - star).
questions.learning: Priming — In the given scenario, priming is the most appropriate answer. The examiner is asking for a fact, and then prompting the answer, by giving a clue which sounds (phonological) like the answer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 21-year-old married woman with 10 weeks of gestation presents for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). Written informed consent for the procedure should be obtained from:
options: Both the woman and her husband
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Only the woman

Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971 (amended in 2021) in India, consent of the pregnant woman alone is sufficient for termination of pregnancy if she is 18 years or older and mentally competent. Husband’s consent is not required, irrespective of marital status.

Why not the other options?

• B. Both the woman and her husband: Incorrect. Husband’s consent has no legal requirement under the MTP Act.
• C. One of the woman’s parents: Required only if the woman is <18 years of age or is mentally ill (guardian’s consent).
• D. The police: Police permission is not required for MTP, even in pregnancies resulting from rape.

| Patient | Whose Consent is Required?

| ------- | --------------------------

| Adult (≥18 years), mentally competent | Only the woman’s consent

| Minor (<18 years) | Guardian’s consent

| Mentally ill woman | Guardian’s consent
questions.learning: Only the woman Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971 (amended in 2021) in India, consent of the pregnant woman alone is sufficient for termination of pregnancy if she is 18 years or older and mentally competent.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the causative organism of Erythrasma, a mild, localized and superficial skin infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corynebacterium minutissimum

Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. It commonly affects intertriginous areas such as the groin, axillae, inframammary folds, and toe webs, especially in diabetic, obese, and immunocompromised individuals.

The infection presents as well-demarcated, reddish-brown patches with fine scaling and is often mistaken for fungal infections. The organism produces porphyrins, which fluoresce coral-red under Wood’s lamp examination, a classic diagnostic feature.

Why not the other options?

• A. Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis: Causes caseous lymphadenitis in animals and is a rare human pathogen.
• C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae: Causes diphtheria, characterized by pseudomembrane formation and toxin-mediated systemic disease.
• D. Corynebacterium matruchotii: Part of the normal oral flora and associated with dental plaque formation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old infant was brought with complaints of jerking movement of limbs towards the body. On examination, there is a regression of developmental milestones. Electroencephalogram shows hypsarrhythmia. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

Infantile spasms (West syndrome) is an epileptic encephalopathy characterized by the triad of epileptic spasms, developmental regression, and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.

• Age: typically 3–12 months
• Seizures: brief flexor or extensor spasms (“jackknife seizures”)
• EEG: chaotic, high-amplitude pattern called hypsarrhythmia

Treatment:

• First-line: ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone)
• Alternative: oral steroids or vigabatrin (especially in tuberous sclerosis)
• Early treatment is crucial to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes
• Delay can lead to long-term cognitive impairment
