questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of moderate-severe visual impairment according to the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey 2015-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Untreated cataract

According to the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey 2015-19, the most common cause of moderate-severe visual impairment (MSVI) is untreated cataract.

MSVI is defined as presenting visual acuity of <6/18 to 3/60 in the better eye with available correction.

Most commonly, cases of visual impairment and blindness are more prevalent in patients aged 50 years and above.

Other options:

Option A: Refractive errors are the leading cause of MSVI in patients aged 49 years and below.

Options C and D: Glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy account for a very low number of visual impairment cases in patients aged 50 years and above.
questions.learning: Untreated cataract According to the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey 2015-19, the most common cause of moderate-severe visual impairment (MSVI) is untreated cataract.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 25 year old male patient presents with several purpuric skin lesions and is diagnosed with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. Which of the following tyrosine kinase inhibitors can be used in his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fostamatinib

Fostamatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of chronic immune thrombocytopenia (idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura).
Fostamatinib has activity against spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK). The major metabolite of fostamatinib, R406, inhibits signal transduction of Fc-activating receptors and B-cell receptors. The fostamatinib metabolite R406 reduces antibody-mediated destruction of platelets.
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of platelets and possibly inhibition of platelet release from the megakaryocyte. It is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX. Secondary causes of ITP include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), HIV-AIDS, and Hepatitis C.

ITP usually presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, very low platelet count, and normal peripheral blood cells. Patients typically exhibit ecchymoses and petechiae or they may incidentally discover thrombocytopenia during a routine complete blood count. Rarely, life-threatening bleeding may occur. The presence of wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages can serve as warning signs of potentially life-threatening bleeding.
The treatment of ITP is as follows:

Clinical features
Management

1.

Minor bleeding manifestations (and/or)

Platelet count > 5000/ μL

Prednisone (OR)

Anti-D immunoglobulin therapy - effective only in Rh-positive patients (OR)

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

2.

Severe ITP (any of the following):

- Significant GI / intracranial bleeding
- Platelet count < 5000/μL
- Signs of impending bleeding (retinal or large oral mucosal bleeds)

Platelet transfusion (AND)

High-dose glucocorticoids (AND)

IVIG / Anti-D immunoglobulins + Rituximab

3.
Relapse after first-line therapy
Splenectomy

4.
Unresponsive to all other therapy or relapse after splenectomy
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists - romiplostim (subcutaneous), eltrombopag (oral)

Other options :
Option A and B: Eltrombopag and Romiplostim are thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor agonists used in the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia which have failed to respond to conventional treatments. Both drugs act via the Mpl receptor to increase platelet counts and not via tyrosine kinase inhibition.

Option C: Bosutinib is a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor indicated in CML.
questions.learning: Fostamatinib Fostamatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of chronic immune thrombocytopenia (idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presented with recurrent URTI, poor growth, high-arched palate, and impaired hearing. Tympanogram is given as follows. What would be the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical scenario along with type B tympanometry curve is suggestive of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion would be the most appropriate management.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

• Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
• Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus
• Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.
• Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The given clinical scenario along with type B tympanometry curve is suggestive of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What condition causes the skull appearance as in the given radiograph?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperparathyroidism

The given X-ray of the skull shows multiple radiolucent lytic lesions, typical of the salt and pepper appearance (pepperpot appearance). This is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

In hyperparathyroidism, there is resorption of the trabecular bone of the skull (which causes the radiolucent areas) in combination with cystic areas of osteopenia. There is also a loss of definition between the inner and outer tables of the skull.

Other options:

Option B: In multiple myeloma, multiple well-defined "punched out" lytic lesions exist.

Option C: Untreated hyperthyroidism for several years can lead to osteoporosis of bones.

Option D: In Paget's disease, the pelvis, spine, skull, and proximal long bones are most frequently affected. Radiological skull changes include:

• Osteoporosis circumscripta: Large, well-defined lytic lesion
• Cotton wool appearance: Mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions of the skull
• Diploic widening: Both inner and outer calvarial tables are involved, with the former usually more extensively affected
• Tam o'Shanter sign: Frontal bone enlargement, with the appearance of the skull falling over the facial bones, like a Tam o'Shanter hat
questions.learning: Hyperparathyroidism — The given X-ray of the skull shows multiple radiolucent lytic lesions, typical of the salt and pepper appearance (pepperpot appearance).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: According to POCSO, aggravated sexual assault includes:
options: Sexual assault done by police officer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sexual assault done by police officer

Sexual assault done by a police officer is an aggravated sexual assault according to POCSO (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences).

The POCSO act defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age. It defines various forms of sexual offenses which include:

1. Sexual harassment - Threatening
2. Sexual assault - Any act with sexual intent that involves physical contact without penetration.
3. Aggravated sexual assault - Similar to sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term aggravated
4. Penetrative sexual assault - An act with sexual intent that involves physical penetration of the penis or any object into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus.
5. Aggravated penetrative sexual assault - Similar to penetrative sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term aggravated
6. Pornography

The term aggravated is used for those assaults done:

• By a person in a position of trust or authority such as a police officer, security force, relative, doctor
• In the course of communal violence
• On mentally & physically disabled
• Gang sexual assault
• Using deadly weapons
• Causing grievous hurt

Depending on if there was penetration or not, it can be aggravated sexual assault (if there is no penetration) or aggravated penetrative sexual assault (if there was penetration). Both are different.

The Act prescribes stringent punishment graded as per the gravity of the offence, with a maximum term of rigorous imprisonment for life and fine.

Note- Gang penetrative sexual assault comes under aggravated penetrative sexual assault and not under aggravated sexual assault. Therefore, option C cannot be correct in this case.
questions.learning: Sexual assault done by police officer Sexual assault done by a police officer is an aggravated sexual assault according to POCSO (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of cardiac failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-pulsatile elevation of JVP

Heart failure causes venous congestion and reduced cardiac output, producing a combination of:

• Pulmonary symptoms (left heart failure)
• Systemic venous congestion (right heart failure)

Typical symptoms include:

| System | Symptoms

| ------ | --------

| Pulmonary | Dyspnea, orthopnea, PND

| Systemic venous | Pedal edema, hepatomegaly

| General | Fatigue

Framingham Criteria for Congestive Heart Failure, a classic exam favorite used to clinically diagnose CHF. Diagnosis requires:

Either

• 2 Major criteria

OR

• 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria

Diagnostic Criteria

| Major Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) | Sudden breathlessness during sleep

| Neck vein distension (elevated JVP) | Reflects increased right atrial pressure

| Pulmonary rales (crepitations) | Due to pulmonary edema

| Cardiomegaly | Seen on chest X-ray

| Acute pulmonary edema | Severe LV failure

| S3 gallop | Rapid ventricular filling in HF

| Increased central venous pressure (>16 cm H₂O) | Venous congestion

| Hepatojugular reflux | JVP rises with liver compression

| Weight loss >4.5 kg in 5 days with treatment | Response to diuresis

| Minor Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Bilateral ankle edema | Venous congestion

| Night cough | Pulmonary congestion

| Dyspnea on exertion | Reduced cardiac output

| Hepatomegaly | Congestive hepatomegaly

| Pleural effusion | Fluid accumulation

| Vital capacity reduced by 1/3 | Lung restriction

| Tachycardia (>120/min) | Sympathetic activation
questions.learning: Non-pulsatile elevation of JVP Heart failure causes venous congestion and reduced cardiac output, producing a combination of: • Pulmonary symptoms (left heart failure) • Systemic venous congestion (right heart failure) Typical symptoms include: | System |…

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A woman, who is 4 days postpartum, presented with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Postpartum blues

Postpartum blues is the most likely diagnosis in a postpartum woman with tearfulness, mood swings, and insomnia from day 4.

Postpartum blues, also known as baby blues, is a transient mood disorder characterized by sadness, tearfulness, confusion, and dysphoria. There are no suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby. These symptoms typically develop 3-5 days after delivery. They are thought to be due to hormonal changes, the stress of giving birth, and the responsibilities of motherhood. They resolve spontaneously within 10-14 days.

Management involves reassurance, education, and support. The patient must be followed up and assessed if symptoms persist for >2 weeks to evaluate postpartum depression.

Other options:

Option A: When the symptoms of depressed mood, anxiety, insomnia, and weight changes start within 4 weeks as per DSM 5 or 6 weeks as per ICD 11, and the symptoms persist for ≥ 2 weeks, the diagnosis will be postpartum depression. The patient may have occasional thoughts of harming the baby and suicidal thoughts. It can persist for months to years when untreated.

Option C: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that usually occurs within 4 weeks after delivery (DSM 5) or 6 weeks after delivery (ICD 11). The predominant symptoms are hallucinations, delusions, suicidal thoughts, and thoughts of harming the baby. Psychotic symptoms such as insomnia, restlessness, labile mood, and agitation are seen. Lithium, antipsychotics, and an antidepressant is the treatment of choice.

Option D: Postpartum anxiety is not defined by DSM-5. However, some platforms might describe postpartum anxiety as excessive or severe worry after childbirth.

Note:  Zuranolone is the first-ever oral drug to be approved specifically for the treatment of postpartum depression. It is a neuroactive steroid that enhances the action of GABA in the brain and regulates mood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition induced by which pair of transcription factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SNAIL & TWIST

Epithelial-mesenchymal transition is induced by SNAIL & TWIST.

Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a process where epithelial cells lose their cell polarity and adhesion properties, transitioning into a more motile mesenchymal cell phenotype. This is critical in embryogenesis, wound healing, and cancer metastasis.

SNAIL and TWIST encode transcription factors whose primary function is to promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). SNAIL and TWIST downregulate E-cadherin expression.

• In EMT, carcinoma cells downregulate certain epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and upregulate certain mesenchymal markers (e.g. vimentin and smooth muscle actin).
• This favors the development of a promigratory phenotype that is essential for metastasis.
• Loss of E-cadherin expression seems to be a key event in EMT.
• EMT has been documented mainly in breast carcinoma

Other Options:

Option A: TF IIA & TF IIB: These are general transcription factors involved in the assembly of the transcription initiation complex, not specific to EMT.

Option B: Cathepsin & MMP8: These are proteolytic enzymes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, which may assist invasion during EMT but do not directly induce it.

Option D: STAT-5 & HIF-1α: While these factors are involved in cellular responses to cytokines and hypoxia, respectively, they are not directly linked to the initiation of EMT.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is the most economical method to disinfect 20 litres of water at the household level after a disaster?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlorine tablet

During disasters and emergencies, chlorination is the most economical, practical, and effective method for household-level disinfection of drinking water. Chlorine tablets are inexpensive, easy to transport, simple to use, and effective against most waterborne pathogens.

After adding the tablet, the water should be allowed to stand for at least 30 minutes before consumption.

Why not the other options?

• B. Alum: Used for coagulation and sedimentation (removing turbidity), not for disinfection.
• C. Fluorine: Used for prevention of dental caries, not for water disinfection.
• D. Boiling: Highly effective but less economical, especially for large volumes and in disaster situations due to fuel requirements.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the benefits of transitioning from Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) to Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
options: Less incidence of Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Less incidence of Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio

The benefit of transitioning from an Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) to an Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) is IPV is unlikely to cause VAPP(Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio ).

There are two types of vaccine that protect against polio: inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) and oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV).

* Sabin (OPV)

*  Salk (IPV)

OPV (Sabin) initially consisted of a mixture of live attenuated poliovirus strains of each of the three serotypes. OPV used in India contained, Type 1 virus 10 lakh, Type 2 virus 2 lakh and Type 3 virus 3 lakh TC ID50 per dose (0.5 ml). Trivalent vaccine has now been replaced by bivalent OPV, by removing the type 2 component from immunisation programmes (OPV switch) as it is implicated in the pathogenesis of cVDPV and occasionally vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP). OPV type 2 was discontinued globally in April 2016.

IPV (Salk)  is produced from wild-type poliovirus strains of each serotype that have been inactivated (killed) with formalin. The Salk vaccine or inactivated polio vaccine is trivalent. It can be administered as an IM, SC, or ID injection. It carries the advantage of not causing Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) or cVDPV as it is inactivated.

Other options:

Option B: Both OPV (Oral polio vaccine) and IPV (Inactivated polio vaccine) induce humoral IgG and IgM antibodies. OPV also induces local immunity in the lining of the intestine.

Option C: Although polio vaccine related side effects are less in IPV as compared to OPV, this is incorrect because Option A provides a better and precise statement.

Option D: Storage is not a major reason for transitioning from OPV to IPV. The storage conditions are quite similar for both of them

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man, a road traffic accident (RTA) patient with a fracture of the shaft of the femur, develops shortness of breath, a drop in SaO₂, and altered mental status 3 days later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

The clinical scenario of sudden onset breathlessness and altered mental status on 3rd day of following a femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

Fat embolism is the presence of fat globules in vital organs and peripheral circulation after fracture of the long bone or other major trauma. Fat embolism is a frequent complication after limb fractures. In most adults with closed long bone fractures, fat globules larger than 10 μm circulate in the bloodstream, and histological evidence of fat can often be detected in the lungs and other internal organs.  Clinical features of fat embolism are usually seen within 72 hours.

Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules.

Clinical features:

* Early signs are fever and tachycardia.

* Presenting features are of 2 types:

* Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation.

* Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia.

* Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva.

The classical clinical triad consists of

* respiratory distress

* petechial haemorrhages

* neurological abnormalities

Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive:

* Respiratory support (oxygen)

* Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity)

* Intravenous low molecular weight dextran

* Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis

* Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures

Other Options:

Option A: Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound(blackish) pain and crepitus

Option B: Sepsis, usually accompanied by fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and a source of infection.

Option C: Pulmonary embolism usually manifests as a sudden onset of shortness of breath, frequently accompanied by pleuritic chest pain and an increased heart rate.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.
questions.learning: Fat embolism — The clinical scenario of sudden onset breathlessness and altered mental status on 3rd day of following a femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The World health organisation(WHO) definition of blindness is ________.
options: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 1/60 in the better eye
Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 6/60 in the better eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye

The World Health Organisation has adopted the International Classification of Diseases 11 (ICD 11) definition of visual impairment and blindness. As per the new definition, blindness is defined as presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10° in the better eye.

Note: Earlier, the WHO definition of blindness was: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye ( Option B).

Refractive error is the main cause of visual impairment in individuals aged 0-49 years, followed by cataracts, amblyopia, and corneal opacity. However, in the age group >50 years, cataract is the major cause, followed by refractive errors and surgical complications of cataract.

Blindness

Presenting visual acuity <3/60

Mild visual impairment

Presenting visual acuity <6/12 – 6/18

Moderate visual impairment (MVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/18 – 6/60

Severe visual impairment (SVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/60 – 3/60

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: There is a group of 200 hypertensive patients. First group of 100 patients is given medical advice whereas a second group of 100 patients is advised lifestyle changes. Which of the following tests of significance is used to compare the blood pressure after 3 months ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Un- paired t test

The unpaired t-test is used to test the difference between two groups or means when the samples are independent of each other. Here, the blood pressure of the two groups who are given different interventions is being compared, which are independent of each other.

Pearl PF0591: Tests of Significance

How to choose which test to use?

* See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative?

* If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used.

* If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups are being tested, or more than 2 groups.

* If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.

* If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA.

The tests:

1. T Tests

* Unpaired t tests

* Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test.

* It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are.

* Paired t tests

* "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!"

* So remember paired test is mainly used in comparison of a before and after scenario

* Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test.

* It is mainly used on dependent samples For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug.

* It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars.

* T scores

* The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups.

* The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.

2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

* The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

3. Chi-Square Test

* The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.

* It is a test of proportions and associations.

* A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases.

* If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient living with HIV presents with a chronic cough, persistent fever, and marked weight loss over several months. Considering the patient’s immuno compromised state and the strong suspicion of tuberculosis, which diagnostic investigation should be prioritized to confirm TB?
questions.explanation: In a patient living with HIV who presents with classic symptoms of Tuberculosis (cough, fever, weight loss), the diagnostic priority according to modern guidelines (including India's NTEP) is CBNAAT (Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test), commonly known as GeneXpert. CBNAAT is prioritized because it is highly sensitive and can simultaneously detect the M. tuberculosis genome and rifampicin resistance in less than two hours. Culture (Option A) is the gold standard but takes weeks to produce results. Chest X-ray (Option B) is a vital screening tool but cannot provide a definitive diagnosis or resistance profile, and in HIV patients, it may show atypical patterns or even be normal. Standard PCR (Option D) is less standardized for routine TB diagnosis than the specific CBNAAT system. Early and accurate diagnosis of TB in HIV-infected individuals is critical, as TB is a leading cause of mortality in this population. CBNAAT allows for the immediate initiation of correct, resistance-based antitubercular therapy

questions.text: What is the target Maternal mortality rate and Under 5 mortality rate to be achieved by 2030 ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 70 and 25 respectively

The target maternal mortality rate and Under-5 mortality rate to be achieved by 2030 are 70 and 25, respectively.

SDG(Sustainable development goals) comprises of 17 goals and 170 targets for Agenda 2030.

The SDGs adopted in 2015 aim to reduce Under-5 mortality to as low as 25 per 1000 live births by the year 2030.

The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), also known as the Global Goals, were adopted by the United Nations in 2015 as a call to action to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure that by 2030 all people enjoy peace and prosperity.

It consists of 17 integrated sustainable development goals to be achieved by the year 2030, with priority being given to countries that are farthest behind. The SDGs are designed to end poverty, hunger, AIDS, and discrimination against women and girls.

SDG 3 deals with ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all at all ages. The important sub-targets of SDG 3 are:

Reduce global maternal mortality to <70/100,000 live births.

3.2

• Reduce neonatal mortality to at least as low as 12/1000 live births.
• Reduce under 5 mortality to at least as low as 25/1000 live births.

3.3
End epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases, combat hepatitis, water-borne diseases, and other communicable diseases

3.5
Prevention and treatment of substance abuse, narcotic abuse, and harmful use of alcohol.

3.7

3.9
Substantially reduce deaths and illnesses due to hazardous chemicals and air, water, and soil pollution and contamination.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which statement is incorrect about colostrum, the early breast milk provided to newborns?
options: It appears during the first 1-3 days postpartum
It contains a large number of antibodies
It contains high amounts of lactose and low amounts of protein
questions.explanation: The statement that colostrum contains high lactose and low protein is incorrect (Option D). Physiologically, colostrum is characterized by having higher concentrations of protein (including immunoglobulins and lactoferrin) and lower concentrations of lactose and fat compared to mature breast milk . All other statements are accurate: colostrum is the "first milk" produced during the first 1 to 3 days after delivery (Option A). It is famously yellow in color due to high beta-carotene content (Option B). Most importantly, it contains a large number of antibodies, particularly secretory IgA, which provides the newborn with essential passive immunity against enteric pathogens (Option C). This "liquid gold" is crucial for the infant's early immunological defense and gut health. Therefore, the description of its nutritional composition in Option D is the definitive error. As the milk matures, protein levels decrease and lactose levels rise to provide more energy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly explains or best represents the dose–response curve shown?
options: Drug B is the most efficacious
Drug B is the most potent
Drug C is more efficacious than drug D
Drug A is more potent than drug B
questions.explanation: A dose–response curve illustrates the relationship between drug dose and the magnitude of response. Two key properties are assessed: potency and efficacy. Potency refers to the amount of drug required to produce a given effect and is indicated by the position of the curve along the x-axis. A drug that achieves its effect at a lower dose appears more left-shifted and is therefore more potent. In the graph, Drug B is the leftmost curve, meaning it requires the smallest dose to produce a response, making it the most potent. Efficacy refers to the maximum effect (Emax) a drug can produce, represented by the height of the curve. Drug B has a lower maximal response compared to Drugs A, C, and D, so it is not the most efficacious. Drug D shows the highest efficacy, not Drug C, ruling out option (C). Drug A lies to the right of Drug B, indicating lower potency. Thus, based on its leftward position, Drug B is the most potent drug

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male who is a chronic smoker presented to the hospital with intermittent claudication pain of both thigh and buttock region on walking about 500 m. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
options: Arterial disease involving the superficial femoral artery
Arterial disease involving the profunda femoris artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement. Classically, the muscle group affected by claudication is one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease.

Intermittent claudication is a feature of chronic arterial disease or occlusion of the artery.  Aortoiliac disease affects the infrarenal aorta and iliac arteries.

Management involves smoking cessation, lifestyle modifications, and treatment of underlying diabetes or hyperlipidemia if present.

For claudication, cilostazol or pentoxyfilline is used. Cilostazol is superior to pentoxyfilline.

Surgical options include aortoiliac bypass, aortobifemoral bypass, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), which can be with or without stent placement, and thromboendarterectomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a severe headache. CT imaging of the brain shows hypodense areas in the right basal region, labeled as “X.” What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache is the classic presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH). On a non-contrast CT, acute blood appears hyperdense (bright) and typically fills the subarachnoid spaces, including the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures. When blood fills the basal cisterns, it creates the pathognomonic “Star of Death” sign. Hypodense areas may appear later if ischemia develops. Meningococcal meningitis (Option B) usually shows meningeal enhancement but not acute hyperdense cisterns. A brain abscess (Option C) appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with edema. Pneumocephalus (Option D) would show very dark areas representing air rather than bright blood. Therefore, the hyperdense filling of the basal regions on CT, combined with the history of severe headache, confirms the diagnosis of SAH

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presents with sudden onset palpitations, sweating, shortness of breath, and a choking sensation following a prior COVID-19 infection. She is excessively anxious about her health due to having tested positive earlier. This is her first such episode, lasting around 20 minutes. Physical examination, ECG, and laboratory investigations are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with sudden onset palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, and choking sensation, lasting about 20 minutes, with normal examination, ECG, and labs. These features are classic for a panic attack, which is characterized by abrupt episodes of intense fear with autonomic symptoms and no underlying organic cause. Her health anxiety after COVID-19 acts as a trigger. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD):Requires exposure to severe trauma and features like flashbacks and avoidance; not a single acute episode. (B) Bipolar disorder : Involves mood episodes (mania/depression) over days to weeks, not brief episodic anxiety attacks. (C) Depression : Characterized by persistent low mood, anhedonia, and fatigue, not sudden short-lived autonomic symptoms

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What will be the diagnosis of the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple round viral particles with a dense central core and surrounding capsid, arranged in a clustered pattern within a host cell. This morphology is characteristic of the Herpes simplex virus (HSV) on electron microscopy. HSV is a large, enveloped DNA virus with an icosahedral capsid and a distinct electron-dense core, often seen in groups within infected cells. The presence of uniform spherical particles with clear capsid outlines and internal density helps distinguish HSV from other viruses. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) HIV: Appears pleomorphic with a conical core, not uniform icosahedral particles. (B) Hepatitis B virus: Shows Dane particles with smaller spherical and filamentous forms, not clustered capsids like this. (C) Human papillomavirus: Non-enveloped virus with different capsid appearance and not typically seen in such clustered intracellular EM patterns

questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are normal age-related changes seen in the human heart, except:
options: Dilatation of the aorta with rightward shift
Increase in left ventricular cavity size
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase in left ventricular cavity size

With normal aging, the heart shows concentric LV remodeling with increased wall thickness and a reduced LV cavity size, along with left atrial enlargement due to diastolic dysfunction. The aorta dilates and elongates, often shifting rightward.

A. Increased left atrial cavity size – Normal due to age-related diastolic dysfunction.

B. Decreased left ventricular cavity size – Typical concentric remodeling of aging.

C. Dilatation of the aorta with rightward shift – Common age-related vascular change.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate next step in management for an elderly man who has been on prolonged bed rest and now presents with acute breathlessness and chest pain?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of "prolonged bed rest" (a major risk factor for Deep Vein Thrombosis) followed by "sudden onset breathlessness and chest pain" is the classic clinical presentation of a Pulmonary Embolism (PE). In a hemodynamically stable patient with a high clinical suspicion of PE, the most appropriate next action and the definitive gold standard for diagnosis is a CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) (Option A). While an ECG (Option B) should be done to rule out myocardial infarction, it often shows non-specific findings in PE. A plain CT thorax (Option C) without intravenous contrast would not be able to visualize the intravascular clots. Echocardiography (Option D) is useful for identifying right ventricular strain in severe cases but is not a primary diagnostic tool for the embolus itself. Therefore, CTPA should be prioritized to confirm the presence of emboli in the pulmonary arteries and initiate immediate anticoagulation therapy

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A person holds a fixed false belief that he owns a large amount of property and that someone he knows is attempting to take it away from him. Which type of delusion best describes this belief?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing two distinct delusions. The belief that he owns extensive property is a delusion of grandeur, which is a false and exaggerated belief in one’s own importance or wealth. The belief that someone is trying to take it away from him is a delusion of persecution, characterized by the false belief that one is being targeted, harassed, or conspired against. Delusions of reference (Option B) involve believing that neutral events (like news reports) are directed personally at oneself. Nihilistic delusions (Options C and D) involve the false belief that the self or the world does not exist. Since the patient's beliefs are focused on self-importance and being harmed by others, "grandeur and persecution" is the correct clinical description
questions.learning: This patient is experiencing two distinct delusions. The belief that he owns extensive property is a delusion of grandeur, which is a false and exaggerated belief in one’s own importance or wealth.

questions.text: All of the following are contraceptive methods used post-coitus except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Danazol

Danazol is not used as a post-coitus contraceptive.

Danazol, a synthetic derivative of ethinyl testosterone, acts by inhibiting pituitary gonadotropins. It possesses mild anabolic, anti-estrogenic, and anti-progestational properties. It is used in abnormal uterine bleeding, endometriosis, and cyclic mastalgia.

Emergency or post-coital contraceptives are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse. They are interceptives. Their main action is to make the endometrium unsuitable for implantation. They can also delay or inhibit ovulation, and prevent fertilization of the egg by sperm.

Methods of emergency contraception:

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While assessing the quality of drinking water, which of the following parameters falls outside the acceptable limits for safe potable water?
questions.explanation: According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) guidelines for drinking water, the acceptable limit for Cadmium is 0.003 mg/L. The value provided in Option A (0.03 mg/L) is exactly ten times the safe limit, making it highly toxic and unsafe for consumption. Cadmium is a heavy metal that primarily damages the kidneys and bones. The other parameters provided are all within safe ranges: the limit for Fluoride is up to 1.0 mg/L, making 0.8 mg/L acceptable (Option B). Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) have an acceptable limit of 500 mg/L, so 300 mg/L is well within range (Option C). Nitrate levels should remain below 45 mg/L; therefore, 20 mg/L is considered safe (Option D). Maintaining these standards is crucial to prevent long-term health complications such as fluorosis or methemoglobinemia. Consequently, only the cadmium level in Option A exceeds the established safety threshold

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with signs of hypothyroidism, including cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and a delayed ankle jerk reflex. Laboratory results show a TSH of 15 IU/L with low T3 and T4 levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Order a thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan
questions.explanation: The patient presents with classic clinical signs of hypothyroidism and definitive biochemical confirmation: an elevated TSH (15 IU/L, where normal is typically ) and low T3/T4 levels . This profile is diagnostic of primary overt hypothyroidism. The standard of care and most appropriate next step is to begin treatment with levothyroxine (LT4) (Option A) to restore a euthyroid state. Measuring TBG (Option B) is unnecessary as it only assesses binding capacity rather than thyroid function. A radionuclide scan (Option C) and ultrasonography (Option D) are used to evaluate thyroid anatomy, nodules, or hyperthyroidism, but they have no role in the initial management of confirmed primary hypothyroidism. Treatment aims to normalize TSH levels and resolve symptoms. Therefore, because the diagnosis is already biochemically and clinically established, pharmacological replacement is the definitive next action. Regular TSH monitoring is then used to titrate the LT4 dose

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Increased firing of _____ is responsible for the occurrence of scissoring gait.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obturator nerve

Scissoring gait is caused due to increased spasticity in the adductor muscles of the thigh, caused due to increased firing of the obturator nerve.

Scissoring gait is a type of abnormal gait pattern where the legs cross over each other with each step, resembling a scissor-like motion. This abnormality is often associated with increased firing or spasticity in the adductor muscles of the thigh, which are responsible for pulling the leg inward toward the midline of the body. The obturator nerve innervates the adductor muscles of the thigh. Increased firing or hyperactivity of the adductor muscles due to neurologic conditions can lead to scissoring gait.

Scissoring gait is a characteristic feature of cerebral palsy as shown in the GIF below-

Other Options:

* The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, which are involved in stabilizing the pelvis during walking. Dysfunction of these muscles might contribute to a Trendelenburg gait (characterized by the dropping of the pelvis on the opposite side of the affected gluteus medius muscle).

* The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus muscle, responsible for hip extension. Dysfunction of the gluteus maximus might lead to a waddling gait.

* The femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps muscles of the thigh, which are responsible for extending the knee. Dysfunction of the quadriceps might lead to a knee-buckling gait.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve Scissoring gait is caused due to increased spasticity in the adductor muscles of the thigh, caused due to increased firing of the obturator nerve.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which immunoglobulin is present in serum/ plasma at the highest concentration?
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is the most abundant antibody class in the human body, accounting for approximately 75–80% of the total serum immunoglobulins. Its high concentration is vital for providing long-term immunity against bacteria and viruses, as it can neutralize toxins and facilitate phagocytosis. IgG is also the only immunoglobulin capable of crossing the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus. IgA (Option B) is the second most common but is primarily found in secretions like breast milk and saliva. IgM (Option C) is the first antibody produced during an initial infection but is present in much lower concentrations than IgG. IgE (Option D) is involved in allergic reactions and parasitic infections and is found in only trace amounts in the serum. Understanding the relative abundance of these antibodies is fundamental for interpreting clinical serology and immunodeficiency panels. Therefore, IgG remains the dominant immunoglobulin in both serum and plasma. AAns

questions.text: A 19-year-old female patient presented to emergency unconscious. A non-contrast CT revealed hydrocephalus, requiring urgent neurosurgical intervention. The patient had nobody accompanying or any identity proof. What should the doctor do ?
options: Take consent by calling the relatives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Operate without consent

As the situation is an emergency, the person is unconscious and is not accompanied by anyone, the doctor can operate without consent.

Section 30 BNS (IPC 92) deals with acts done in good faith without consent.

The following situations would apply :

* Emergency (No need to take consent during emergencies)

* The person is incapable of giving consent

* The person has no guardian to give consent

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During the procedure shown below, which substance is taken up by the cancer cells?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan, which is a functional imaging technique used to visualize metabolic processes in the body. The most common tracer used is Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a radioactive analog of glucose. Cancer cells characteristically exhibit a high rate of glycolysis to support their rapid proliferation (the Warburg effect), and therefore avidly uptake glucose at much higher levels than normal tissues. This "hot spot" uptake allows PET scans to identify primary tumors, assess for metastatic spread, and monitor the response to treatment. Alanine (Option A), Sodium (Option C), and Calcium (Option D) are not the standard metabolic tracers used for general oncological PET imaging. Clinicians must be aware that normal tissues with high glucose demand, like the brain and heart, will also show significant uptake. Therefore, PET results must be carefully correlated with anatomical imaging like CT or MRI
questions.learning: The image depicts a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan, which is a functional imaging technique used to visualize metabolic processes in the body.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Cells with prolific smooth endoplasmic reticulum secrete_______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Steroid hormones

Cells with prolific smooth endoplasmic reticulum secrete steroid hormones.

The endoplasmic reticulum contains a complex series of tubules in the cytoplasm of the cell.

• Ribosomes are attached to the cytoplasmic side of the membrane in the rough(granular) endoplasmic reticulum. Protein synthesis and the initial folding of polypeptide chains with the formation of disulfide bonds are the functions of rough ER.
• Ribosomes are absent in the smooth (agranular) endoplasmic reticulum. Free ribosomes are found in the cytoplasm. It is the site of steroid synthesis in steroid-secreting cells and the site of detoxification processes in other cells.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a modified endoplasmic reticulum, that functions as an intracellular calcium store, which releases calcium into the cytoplasm stimulating cell contraction, proliferation, and migration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 56-year-old man suffering from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus came for a routine checkup. His lipid profile revealed increased TG (triacylglycerol) and VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein). What is the cause of this abnormal lipid profile?
options: Increased activity of lipoprotein lipase and decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase
Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
Increase in peripheral function of LDL receptors
Increased in activity of hepatic lipase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity

• Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): Breaks down stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into free fatty acids, which are transported to the liver. Increased HSL activity leads to more fatty acids reaching the liver, increasing VLDL synthesis.
• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): Hydrolyzes circulating triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons. Decreased LPL activity impairs VLDL clearance, resulting in hypertriglyceridemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Increased LPL & decreased HSL: Would lower triglycerides and VLDL, opposite effect.

C. Increase in LDL receptor function: Lowers LDL cholesterol, not VLDL or TG.

D. Increased hepatic lipase: Mainly affects HDL and IDL metabolism, not primary VLDL/TG elevation.
questions.learning: Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity • Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): Breaks down stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into free fatty acids, which are transported to the liver.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and occasional blood-stained nasal discharge. His CT and endoscopy findings are shown in the below image. What could be the underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inverted papilloma

In an elderly patient, unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and pale polypoidal mass arising from the lateral wall of the nose are suggestive of inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor).

Inverted papilloma (transitional cell papilloma) is a tumor originating from the nonolfactory mucosa of the nose (Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses. The most common site of origin is the lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus.The unilateral growth of hyperplastic papillomatous tissue into the stroma characterizes this condition. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is believed to be the cause.

It primarily affects men aged 40-70 and presents unilaterally with symptoms such as nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. Invasive growth into the sinuses or orbit can lead to proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.

On nasal endoscopy, it appears as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a nasal polyp. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are used to determine the location and extent of the lesion. MRI can also help differentiate between associated sinus secretions and the tumor mass. Biopsy is essential for diagnosis, as it is important to differentiate it from simple nasal polyps, which may be associated with or mistaken for the tumor.

The treatment of choice is medial maxillectomy, which can be performed through lateral rhinotomy, sublabial degloving approach, or preferably, an endoscopic approach. In 10%-15% of cases, the tumor is associated with malignancy. Recurrence is possible, and radiotherapy is generally not recommended due to the potential risk of inducing malignancy.

Other options:

Option B: Carcinoma maxilla arises from the lining of the maxillary sinus and its early features include additional symptoms like facial paraesthesias, pain, or epiphora and depending on the direction of spread of the growth, would cause additional symptoms.

Option C: Esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) arises from the olfactory epithelium in the upper third of the nose. It has bimodal peaks of incidence at 10–20 years and 50–60 years. Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis are the most common symptoms. The tumour also invades the orbit and the surrounding structures, which results in other symptoms like proptosis, headache, epiphora, diplopia, and blurred vision.

Option D: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is seen almost exclusively in males in the age group of 10–20 years and is very rarely seen in older people and females. Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis is the most common presentation.
questions.learning: Inverted papilloma — In an elderly patient, unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and pale polypoidal mass arising from the lateral wall of the nose are suggestive of inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of increased urinary frequency. On cystoscopic examination, a pale ureteric orifice is observed. A KUB X-ray has been provided for evaluation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with increased urinary frequency and a pale ureteric orifice on cystoscopy, which is a classic feature of genitourinary tuberculosis (GU TB). In bladder tuberculosis, chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis, reduced vascularity, and scarring, giving the ureteric orifice a pale, gaping (“golf hole”) appearance. The provided KUB X-ray supports this diagnosis by suggesting calcifications or irregularities in the urinary tract, which are commonly seen in chronic TB infection. Over time, TB can lead to a contracted bladder (“thimble bladder”), ureteric strictures, and renal involvement. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Bladder carcinoma → Typically shows irregular mass, hematuria; not pale ureteric orifice (B) Schistosomiasis → Causes calcified bladder wall (“sandy patches”), but cystoscopy differs (D) Papilloma → Benign tumor with papillary projections, not associated with pale orifice
questions.learning: The patient presents with increased urinary frequency and a pale ureteric orifice on cystoscopy, which is a classic feature of genitourinary tuberculosis (GU TB).

* A: Acebutolol

* A: Atenolol

* N: Nebivolol ( III )

* B: Betaxolol ( III )

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old man who had gastrointestinal surgery one month ago presents with a palpable bulge at the surgical site. On examination, a reducible incisional hernia measuring 12 cm is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
options: Prescribe an abdominal belt for daily use
Advice observation and reassessment in six months
questions.explanation: The patient has a large (12 cm), symptomatic incisional hernia. Because the hernia is reducible and the patient is relatively recent from their primary surgery (1 month), the most appropriate next step for definitive management is surgical repair. Modern standards dictate that for an incisional hernia of this size, a mesh repair (either laparoscopic or open) is mandatory to reduce the very high rate of recurrence associated with primary suture closure. Laparoscopic closure without mesh (Option D) is incorrect due to the high failure rate. While an abdominal belt (Option B) can provide temporary symptomatic relief, it is not a "management step" toward a cure. Observation (Option C) is generally only for asymptomatic patients who are poor surgical candidates. Laparoscopic Intraperitoneal Onlay Mesh (IPOM) is a common technique for such repairs, offering less postoperative pain and faster recovery. Preoperative optimization, including weight loss and smoking cessation, is critical for surgical success
questions.learning: The patient has a large (12 cm), symptomatic incisional hernia. Because the hernia is reducible and the patient is relatively recent from their primary surgery (1 month), the most appropriate next step for definitive management is surgical repair.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Mustard oil adulteration is most commonly associated with the addition of which of the following oils?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Argemone oil

Mustard oil adulteration with Argemone oil is a classic cause of epidemic dropsy, a toxic condition caused by the alkaloids sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine present in Argemone mexicana seeds.

• Agreement oil closely resembles mustard oil in color and appearance, making it a common adulterant.
• Consumption causes epidemic dropsy, characterized by:

• Bilateral pitting edema of the legs
• Diarrhea
• Breathlessness
• Cardiac failure
• Glaucoma (may occur)
• Skin erythema and tenderness

Why not the other options?

• B. Castor oil: Used medicinally as a laxative; not the classic adulterant of mustard oil.
• C. Linseed oil: Used industrially and in paints; not associated with epidemic dropsy.
• D. Cottonseed oil: May be used as an edible oil but is not the classic adulterant responsible for epidemic dropsy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Among the following options,which is the most common treatment for recurrent Pterygium of eye?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctival autograft

The most commonly used technique for recurrent pterygium among the following is conjuctival autograft.

A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it is made up of elastotic degenerative changes in vascularized subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts:

* cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge)

* head

* body

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism.

Treatment:

* A pterygium is best left alone unless:

* It is progressing towards the pupillary area

* Causes excessive astigmatism

* Restricts ocular motility

* Causes disfigurement.

* Excision: Simple excision of the pterygium is associated with a high recurrence rate, and should be combined with:

* Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively to prevent a recurrence. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.

* Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis.

* Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures.

* Amniotic membrane graft

* Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep.

Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also) of which conjuctival autografting has less recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure which reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning and necrosis.

Note:

A combination of conjuctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.
questions.learning: Conjunctival autograft — The most commonly used technique for recurrent pterygium among the following is conjuctival autograft. A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea.

questions.text: What are the upper age limits by which a child should start walking alone, and be able to speak single words?

• C. 15 months, 15 months respectively: Delay beyond this age alone does not necessarily indicate abnormal development.

questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with heart failure and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c of 7.8%) present with progressive dyspnea. Which is the preferred antidiabetic drug?

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In what amino acid form is ammonia transported from the brain to the liver for detoxification?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is a toxic byproduct of nitrogen metabolism, particularly dangerous to the central nervous system. In the brain, excess ammonia is detoxified by being combined with glutamate to form Glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is a non-toxic, neutral amino acid that can safely circulate in the blood to be transported to the liver (and kidneys). Once in the liver, glutamine is broken back down into glutamate and ammonia by glutaminase, and the ammonia is then converted into urea for excretion. Glutamate (Option A) itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier effectively for transport. Alanine (Option B) is the primary form of ammonia transport from skeletal muscle to the liver (via the Cahill cycle). Glycine (Option C) is involved in various metabolic pathways but not primary systemic ammonia transport. The "glutamine shuttle" is essential for preventing hyperammonemia, which can lead to cerebral edema, encephalopathy, and potentially fatal brain damage in liver failure
questions.learning: Ammonia is a toxic byproduct of nitrogen metabolism, particularly dangerous to the central nervous system. In the brain, excess ammonia is detoxified by being combined with glutamate to form Glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme glutamine synthetase.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A male patient working in the matchbox industry for the past 20 years reports to the dentist with multiple sinuses and fistulae in and around his jaw with foul-smelling discharge. Which of the following chemicals are responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phosphorus

The clinical scenario is suggestive of a phossy jaw, which occurs due to chronic phosphorus poisoning. Phossy jaw refers to osteomyelitis and necrosis of the jaw, with foul-smelling pus discharging multiple sinuses.

Frequent inhalation of phosphorus fumes causes necrosis of the lower jaw in the region of a decayed tooth. Patients initially present with toothache, followed by swelling of the jaw, loosening of the teeth, necrosis of gums, and sequestration of the bone in the mandible producing considerable facial disfigurement.

Chronic phosphorus poisoning is common among the workers of phosphorus industries (matchbox factories), who have had chronic exposure to phosphorus fumes for months to years. It is managed surgically and by prevention of further exposure to the poison.

Phosphorus is a non-metallic, inorganic irritant poison that affects cellular oxidation. It exists in two forms, white phosphorus, a highly toxic form, and red phosphorus, the non-toxic form.

Fulminant poisoning is seen when more than one gram is consumed, and death occurs within 12 hours due to peripheral vascular collapse. In acute poisoning, they present with pain in the throat and abdomen, with intense thirst, nausea, diarrhea, and severe abdominal pain. System toxicity occurs after 2–3 days and results in hematemesis, enlarged tender liver, jaundice, pruritus, and hemorrhages. The gastric and intestinal content have garlic odor and are luminous.

Gastric lavage with potassium permanganate oxidizes phosphorus into phosphoric acid and phosphates. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb the poison.

Other options:

Option A: Bromine is a corrosive substance that causes necrosis of skin and tissues.

Option B: The symptoms of antimony poisoning, both acute and chronic are similar to that of arsenic. Inhalation of fumes causes a flu-like illness called metal fume fever. In cases of chronic poisoning with heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, mercury, antimony, copper, etc., the shaft of a long bone, strands of scalp hair, fingernails or toenails, and a wedge of the quadriceps muscle should be taken for sampling.

Option C: Prolonged ingestion of fluorides results in the mottling of teeth, an increase in the density of bones, lipping of bony margins of vertebrae, which sometimes produce pressure on the spinal cord leading to paraplegia.
questions.learning: Phosphorus — The clinical scenario is suggestive of a phossy jaw, which occurs due to chronic phosphorus poisoning. Phossy jaw refers to osteomyelitis and necrosis of the jaw, with foul-smelling pus discharging multiple sinuses.

questions.text: Which nerve passes through the foramen marked in the image below?

Correct answer: D. Inferior alveolar nerve

The marked structure is mandibular foramen and inferior alveolar nerve passes through it.

The inferior alveolar nerve (IAN), a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3), it descends behind the lateral pterygoid, at the lower border of the muscle, the nerve passes between the sphenomandibular ligament and the mandibular ramus and enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen
The mandibular foramen is located above the mandibular angle, the opening through which the IAN and the vessels of the mandible pass.
The IAN continues its course through the mandibular canal and then branches off to supply the lower teeth, gums, and lower lip.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with complaints of headache, seizures and blurred vision. His BP was recorded as 220/120 mmHg. Which of the following will be the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IV labetalol

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypertensive crisis (BP > 160/110 mmHg). The preferred drug to manage a hypertensive patient in an emergency is IV labetalol.

Intravenous labetalol is the drug of choice for controlling BP in a hypertensive crisis. It is effective, has a rapid onset of action, and has a good safety profile.

Labetalol is a nonselective β blocker and vascular α blocker. It should be avoided in patients with asthma and congestive heart failure due to bronchoconstriction.

It is available in oral form for the treatment of chronic hypertension and as an intravenous formulation for use in hypertensive emergencies. It can be used in the setting of a pregnancy-induced hypertensive crisis.

Other options:

Option A: IV Hydralazine: It is a vasodilator used in the treatment of heart failure, and hypertensive emergencies, especially preeclampsia. The drug is used as a combination pill containing isosorbide dinitrate (BiDil) in the treatment of heart failure. The important side effect of hydralazine is drug-induced lupus.

Option B: Oral Nifedipine: It is a calcium channel blocker (CCB), a class of medications commonly used to lower blood pressure by relaxing the blood vessels. They work by blocking the influx of calcium into smooth muscle cells, leading to vasodilation and reduced peripheral resistance. They are safer alternatives to use in pregnant patients with Asthma as they do not cause vasoconstriction and would not worsen it.

Option D: Oral Methydopa: Methyldopa is a selective alpha-2 receptor agonist and is preferred for chronic hypertension in pregnancy based on its safety and efficacy data for both mother and fetus.
questions.learning: IV labetalol — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypertensive crisis (BP > 160/110 mmHg). The preferred drug to manage a hypertensive patient in an emergency is IV labetalol.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A firefighter presents with fever and cough. Culture (shown in the image) reveals Gram- negative, oxidase-positive bacilli, with colonies that fluoresce under UV light. Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are pathognomonic for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism is a Gram-negative, motile rod that is characteristically oxidase-positive. A defining feature is its ability to produce pigments like pyocyanin and pyoverdin, which cause colonies to fluoresce or transilluminate under ultraviolet (UV) light. Klebsiella (Option A) is Gram-negative but oxidase-negative and typically forms non-fluorescent mucoid colonies. Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) is a Gram-positive coccus that forms golden-yellow colonies and lacks UV fluorescence. Serratia (Option D) is Gram-negative and oxidase-negative; while some species produce a red pigment (prodigiosin), they do not fluoresce like Pseudomonas. P. aeruginosa is a common cause of respiratory infections, particularly in individuals exposed to environmental stressors like firefighters. Its unique biochemical profile, including the positive oxidase test and UV fluorescence, allows for definitive identification from culture samples
questions.learning: The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are pathognomonic for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism is a Gram-negative, motile rod that is characteristically oxidase-positive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis of a middle-aged patient presented with episodic headache, palpitations and increased 24-hour urinary levels of metanephrines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pheochromocytoma

Symptoms suggest: Intermittent sympathetic overactivity

Classic triad:

• Headache
• Palpitations
• Sweating

Lab clue:

• ↑ Metanephrines (very specific)

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma

Episodic headache, palpitations, and elevated urinary metanephrines are classic for pheochromocytoma. Excess catecholamine secretion produces paroxysmal sympathetic surges and hypertension. Urinary metanephrines are sensitive markers of catecholamine excess.

The other tumors do not produce this characteristic biochemical pattern.

Neuroblastoma

• Occurs in children
• Not typical in adults

Carcinoid tumor

• Causes flushing and diarrhea
• Due to serotonin secretion, not catecholamines

Brain tumor

• May cause headache
• Does not explain palpitations or elevated metanephrines

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with obstetric score G2P1 at 14 weeks is advised uterine artery Doppler. What would it detect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Early-onset preeclampsia

Uterine Artery Doppler evaluates uteroplacental blood flow during pregnancy.

It is usually performed between 11–14 weeks or 18–24 weeks. The test detects impaired placental blood flow, which is associated with:

• Early Onset Preeclampsia
• Fetal Growth Restriction

However, uterine artery Doppler is primarily used to predict early-onset preeclampsia. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler predicts early-onset preeclampsia.

Normally in pregnancy:

Spiral arteries remodel

↓

Low resistance blood flow

↓

Adequate placental perfusion

In abnormal placentation:

Poor trophoblastic invasion

↓

High resistance uterine arteries

↓

Abnormal Doppler waveform

↓

Risk of early preeclampsia

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Increased pulsatility index (PI) | High resistance

| Early diastolic notch | Poor placental perfusion
questions.learning: Early-onset preeclampsia Uterine Artery Doppler evaluates uteroplacental blood flow during pregnancy. It is usually performed between 11–14 weeks or 18–24 weeks.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a voltage-gated calcium channel present on the T tubule?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dihydropyridine receptor

Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) is a voltage-gated calcium channel present on the T tubule.

Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) is a voltage-gated calcium channel situated on the membrane of T-tubules within muscle cells. It works as a voltage sensor, it detects cell membrane depolarization triggered by an action potential. When depolarization occurs, DHPR undergoes a structural alteration, which then prompts the activation of the ryanodine receptor (RyR). This activation results in the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, instigating the process of muscle contraction.

Other options:

Ryanodine receptor (RyR): is present on the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) in muscle cells. Upon activation by calcium influx through DHPRs, RyRs release stored calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytoplasm, thereby initiating muscle contraction.

SERCA: is an ATPase enzyme situated on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, that actively transports calcium ions from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during muscle relaxation. This process facilitates the reduction of cytoplasmic calcium levels, enabling muscle relaxation after contraction and preparing it for subsequent contraction cycles.

Troponin complex acts as a key regulatory switch in the excitation-contraction coupling process, ensuring that muscle contraction occurs only when calcium ions are present and that relaxation occurs when calcium levels decrease.
questions.learning: Dihydropyridine receptor Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) is a voltage-gated calcium channel present on the T tubule. Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) is a voltage-gated calcium channel situated on the membrane of T-tubules within muscle cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC-1), in which of the following conditions can combined oral contraceptives (OCPs) be safely used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills contain:

• Estrogen (Ethinyl estradiol)
• Progestin (e.g., Levonorgestrel)

They are widely used for birth control and menstrual regulation.

Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categorizes the safety of contraceptive methods based on underlying medical conditions. The MEC classification system has four categories:

●        MEC 1: Method is absolutely safe for use

●        MEC 2: Safe for use but has certain limitations (benefits outweigh risks)

●        MEC 3: Relatively contraindicated (risks outweigh benefits)

●        MEC 4: Absolutely contraindicated (method should not be given)

HIV infection without complications is classified as MEC 1 for combined oral contraceptive pills.

For HIV-positive women:

COCs are MEC-1 (safe to use).

Reasons:

• Do not worsen HIV disease progression
• Do not significantly increase viral replication

Diabetes Mellitus - Often MEC-2 or MEC-3, especially with vascular complications.

Hyperlipidemia - COCs may increase lipid levels, so usually MEC-2 or MEC-3.

Hypertension - Estrogen-containing pills may increase thrombotic risk, so classified as MEC-3 or MEC-4 depending on severity.

Benefits of COCs

| Benefit | Effect

| ------- | ------

| Regulates menstrual cycles | Reduces irregular bleeding

| Decreases dysmenorrhea | Less painful periods

| Reduces risk of ovarian cancer | Long-term protection

| Reduces risk of endometrial cancer | Endometrial suppression
questions.learning: HIV Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills contain: • Estrogen (Ethinyl estradiol) • Progestin (e.g., Levonorgestrel) They are widely used for birth control and menstrual regulation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 500 cu ft

The minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act is 500 cu ft.

The Factories Act, 1948 states the following in the matters of Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers in a factory – the appointment of 'Safety Officers'

* > 500 Workers – there should be a Welfare Officer

* > 250 Workers – a canteen shall be provided

* > 30 female workers- Crèche

According to the Indian Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: Effective as of the 1st of July 2017, mandatory crèche (daycare) facilities for every establishment employing 50 or more employees (inclusive of males and females). As this act is more recent, it supersedes the Factory Act, 1948 with regards to the requirement for a crèche.

Maximum hours of work per week including overtime work hours is 60 hours.

Pearl PF1016: The Factories act, 1948 and The Maternity Act, 2017

The Factories act,1948

* The act defines factory as an establishment employing 10 or more workers where power is used, and 20 or more workers where power is not used.

* Age of employment –  prohibition children of < 14 years from working.

* Adolescents between 15 – 18 years

* Can be employed  only in certain industries and  work between 6 AM – 7 PM

* They should not be made to work for more than four and a half hours

* They are allowed to take leave once in every 15 days and have an accumulated leave of up to 40 days

* Hours of work for adults: maximum hours of work for an industrial worker should be not more than 48 hours per week, not exceeding 9 hours a day, if working overtime then it should be no more than 60 hrs per week

* Per capita space availability: For factories established after 1948 – min 500cuft / person

* Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers – Safety officer

* > 500 Workers – Welfare officer

* > 250 Workers – Canteen

* > 50 Workers- Crèche*

The Maternity Act, 2017 is a landmark law which has enhanced the duration of paid maternity leave:

* Working mothers- 12 weeks to 26 weeks

* Working mothers, already with 2 surviving children - 12 weeks

* Adopting mother and commissioning mothers- 12 weeks from the date on which the child is being handed over to the mother.

*for fifty women worker after the 1976 amendment.
