questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy with sensorineural hearing loss and eye defects presents to the OPD with hematuria. His renal biopsy on light microscopy was normal. Family history reveals the maternal uncle had Gr 5 CKD an is undergoing dialysis. Which of the following would be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alport syndrome

The clinical presentation of a child with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects with normal renal biopsy is consistent with Alport Syndrome. It is a hereditary nephritis, which explains the family history of chronic kidney disease.

Alport syndrome is a genetic disease caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene, which codes for the alpha chain of type IV collagen. In approximately 85% of cases, the syndrome is X-linked.

In the early years (around 5 years), patients are often asymptomatic but may have persistent microscopic hematuria. Between 5 and 10 years of age, proteinuria, and hypertension may develop, which can be managed with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. By 10 years of age, serum creatinine levels start to rise. Around 15 years, patients may experience ear, nose, and throat (ENT) manifestations, with high-frequency sensory neural hearing loss being a common feature in males. Ocular manifestations, such as anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic) and dot and fleck retinopathy (most common), typically appear around the age of 20. Anterior lenticonus is particularly correlated with the development of end-stage renal disease (ESRD). By 25 to 30 years of age, most individuals with Alport's syndrome progress to ESRD.

Gross hematuria following upper respiratory tract infections is not typically seen in Alport's syndrome and should prompt consideration of other conditions, such as IgA nephropathy.

Skin immunofluorescence to demonstrate the lack of the α5(IV) collagen chain and genetic testing can be used for the diagnosis. Light microscopy and immunofluorescence (IF) on renal biopsy may be normal. Electron microscopy reveals irregular areas of thinning and thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), along with splitting of the lamina densa, giving it a basket-weave appearance.

The mainstay of management is the control of hypertension and ACE inhibitors to slow down the progression of renal damage. Although transplant recipients develop anti-GBM antibodies, graft survival is good.

Thin GBM disease is an autosomal dominant disease characterized by persistent microscopic hematuria but no progression to ESRD or extrarenal manifestations. EM can be used to confirm the diagnosis, showing GBM thickness of less than 200 nm.

Other options:

Option B: Goodpasture syndrome is an immune-mediated disease with antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of GBM type IV collagen; it is not hereditary and the light microscopy would reveal extra capillary proliferation with crescents & necrosis.

Option C: In IgA Nephropathy, light microscopy would reveal focal mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis & mesangial widening.

Option D:  In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), there will be diffuse endocapillary proliferation and accompanying leukocytic infiltration seen in light microscopy.
questions.learning: Alport syndrome — The clinical presentation of a child with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects with normal renal biopsy is consistent with Alport Syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The following Darrow Yannet diagram is suggestive of which condition? Note : The solid line is the original fluid compartment and the colour shaded compartment within the dotted line denotes the change caused by the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenal Insufficiency

In adrenal insufficiency there is hypo-osmotic volume contraction. Aldosterone deficiency leads to increased sodium loss (loss of hyperosmotic fluid).

• The osmolarity of ECF decreases.
• ECF volume decreases because of the loss of volume.
• Water shifts into ICF; as a result of the shift, ICF osmolarity decreases until it is equal to ECF osmolarity, and ICF volume increases.
• So, loss of hypertonic fluid causes hypotonic volume contraction.

Please note that in the diagram, the horizontal axis represents volume and vertical axis represents osmolarity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent abdominal surgery during which a surgical gauze was inadvertently left inside the abdomen. The patient subsequently developed septic shock and died. This incident is best classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Never event

A never event is a serious, preventable patient safety incident that should never occur if appropriate safety systems are in place. Leaving a surgical gauze (retained surgical item/gossypiboma) inside a patient after surgery is a classic example of a never event.

• Retained surgical items (e.g., gauze, sponge, instrument) are completely preventable through proper surgical counts and safety checklists.
• In this case, the retained gauze led to sepsis, septic shock, and death, making it a classic never event.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sentinel event: Incorrect in this question. Although the patient’s death qualifies as a sentinel event, the emphasis is on the retained surgical gauze, which is specifically classified as a never event.
• C. Adverse event: Too broad; it includes any injury caused by medical management and may not be preventable.
• D. Active event: Not a recognized patient safety classification.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which fungus is most commonly associated with orbital cellulitis in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhizopus

Rhizopus is the most common fungus associated with orbital cellulitis in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis.

Diabetic patients are immunocompromised and so prone to develop opportunistic infections like mucormycosis - caused by Rhizopus and Mucor spp. Rhino-orbital- cerebral disease is the most common form of mucormycosis. It mostly occurs in diabetics. Patients initially present with eye or facial pain, facial numbness, conjunctival suffusion and swelling, and blurry vision. Infection then spreads from the ethmoid sinus to the orbit, leading to proptosis and orbital cellulitis.

Rhizopus is angioinvasive, and thus the infection may spread to the frontal lobe and cavernous sinus, leading to septicemia and thromboses. The sinus tissue in such patients often develops into a black necrotic eschar.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the Total Fertility Rate in India at present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.0

According to the Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report 2020, the Total Fertility Rate at present is 2.0.

India's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) declined from 2.1 in 2019 to 2.0 in 2020. In 2020, Bihar recorded the highest TFR at 3.0, while Delhi, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal reported the lowest at 1.4.

Over the decades, the TFR has shown a significant downward trend, dropping from 5.2 to 4.5 between 1971 and 1981, and from 3.6 to 2.0 between 1991 and 2020.

The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is expressed as the "average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if she were to experience the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her reproductive years (typically ages 15-49).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient on anti cancer therapy developed infection. Blood Analysis revealed a Total Leucocyte Count of 2000/mm3. Which of the following drug is likely to be effective in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Filgrastim

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Neutropenia due to cancer chemotherapy. Filgrastim is a recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, used in the treatment of neutropenia. It increases neutrophil production.

It is administered subcutaneously or by slow intravenous infusion only.

It is indicated in:

*

The treatment of severe neutropenia after autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and high-dose cancer chemotherapy.

*

The treatment of severe congenital neutropenias.

*

The treatment of neutropenia of patients with AIDS receiving zidovudine.

The pegylated forms, pegfilgrastim and lipegfilgrastim, are longer-acting forms.

Important adverse reactions include bone pain, local skin reaction, and cutaneous necrotizing vasculitis.

Filgrastim is the first FDA-approved drug to treat patients with radiation-induced myelosuppression and to increase survival in such patients.

OTHER OPTIONS:

Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist. It is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

Option B: Oprelvekin is a recombinant human IL-11. It increases thrombopoiesis. It is used in the treatment of thrombocytopenia due to non-myeloid malignancies. Important adverse effects are fluid retention, tachycardia, palpitation, edema, and shortness of breath.

Erythropoietin is used in the treatment of anemias associated with surgery, chronic kidney disease, AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, prematurity, and certain chronic inflammatory conditions.
questions.learning: Filgrastim — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Neutropenia due to cancer chemotherapy. Filgrastim is a recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, used in the treatment of neutropenia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which characteristic best describes an ideal therapeutic radioisotope for medical use? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strong Beta; Low Gamma emitter

An ideal therapeutic radioisotope should be a strong beta emitter with low gamma emission. Beta particles have relatively high energy and are strongly absorbed by adjacent tissue, allowing them to cause substantial damage to targeted cells (like cancer cells). Low gamma emission is preferred to minimize radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissues and healthcare workers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman undergoing infertility treatment is found to have bilateral tubal blockage on hysterosalpingography. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopic chromopertubation

The most appropriate next step in management for a patient with bilateral tubal blockage on hysterosalpingography is laparoscopic chromopertubation.

Tubal contractions, particularly cornual spasms, can give an incorrect impression of proximal fallopian tube obstruction (a false-positive result) on hysterosalpingography. Laparoscopy with chromotubation is therefore considered to confirm the diagnosis of cornual spasm. Laparoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this condition.

Laparoscopic chromopertubation involves the laparoscopic visualization of pelvic structures, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, followed by the injection of methylene blue dye through the cervix to assess tubal patency. In addition to evaluating tubal patency, laparoscopy can help diagnose peritubal adhesions, endometriosis, and other pelvic abnormalities.

Chromotubation may be performed, in which a dilute dye is injected through a Leech-Wilkinson cannula placed against the cervix or through a balloon catheter positioned within the uterine cavity. Tubal spill is evaluated through the laparoscope. Indigo carmine dye, if available, is preferable to methylene blue, as methylene blue rarely may induce acute methemoglobinemia, particularly in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is commonly done in the proliferative phase.

Other options:

Option A: Intrauterine insemination (IUI): IUI is used for treating infertility but relies on open fallopian tubes for natural fertilization.

Option B: In vitro fertilization (IVF): While IVF is an effective treatment for infertility due to tubal blockage, the immediate next step to confirm and evaluate the extent of tubal blockage is typically laparoscopic chromopertubation.

Option D: Ovulation induction: Ovulation induction aims to stimulate egg release but does not address tubal blockage.
questions.learning: Laparoscopic chromopertubation — The most appropriate next step in management for a patient with bilateral tubal blockage on hysterosalpingography is laparoscopic chromopertubation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: FISH technique helps to identify all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point mutation

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is not useful in identifying point mutation. Point mutations are identified by other means like sequencing studies and restriction fragment length polymorphism.

FISH is a method of molecular analysis of genetic lesions involving large deletions, duplications, or more complex rearrangements that are not readily amenable to detection using polymerase chain reaction or DNA sequencing approaches.

FISH uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. To perform FISH, large fragments of cloned genomic DNA spanning up to 200 kb are labeled with fluorescent dyes and applied to metaphase chromosome preparations or interphase nuclei. The probe hybridizes to its homologous genomic sequence and thus labels a specific chromosomal region that can be visualized under a fluorescent microscope.

FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy), subtle microdeletions and complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping, and gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas).
questions.learning: Point mutation Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is not useful in identifying point mutation. Point mutations are identified by other means like sequencing studies and restriction fragment length polymorphism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a dietary fiber?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gums

Gum is the best answer among the given options. Even though all of the given options are dietary fibers, the consumption of gums through diet is very low and hence, it is the best answer.

Dietary fibers consist of both soluble and insoluble forms and include lignin, pectin, inulin, cellulose, hemicellulose, etc.

Advantages of fibers:

• Forms bulk of the stool and reduces stool transit time
• Reduces incidence of carcinoma colon, DM, CAD, diverticulitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old man is brought to the hospital with auditory hallucinations and difficulty recognizing his family members. He has a history of chronic alcohol use and reports that his last alcohol consumption was 48 hours ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s auditory hallucinations and severe confusion occurring 48 hours after his last drink strongly suggest Delirium Tremens (DTs). DTs is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically peaking between 48 and 96 hours. It is characterized by altered mental status, disorientation, and autonomic hyperactivity. Alcoholic hallucinosis (Option B) involves hallucinations with an intact orientation and usually occurs earlier, within 12–24 hours. Alcohol-induced psychosis (Option C) refers to persistent psychotic symptoms due to chronic use rather than acute withdrawal instability. Schizophrenia (Option D) is a chronic disorder; the acute onset immediately following alcohol cessation makes a withdrawal syndrome far more probable. DTs is a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines and intensive care due to high mortality from cardiovascular collapse
questions.learning: The patient’s auditory hallucinations and severe confusion occurring 48 hours after his last drink strongly suggest Delirium Tremens (DTs). DTs is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically peaking between 48 and 96 hours.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba

The correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium- Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba.

Lochia is the vaginal discharge for the first fortnight during puerperium that originates from the uterine body, cervix, and vagina.

Depending upon the variation of the color of the discharge, it is named:

(1) Lochia rubra- Seen in 1–4 days after delivery. The color of the discharge is red. It consists of blood, shreds of fetal membranes and decidua, vernix caseosa, lanugo, and meconium.

(2) Lochia serosa- Seen during 5-9 days. The color is yellowish or pink or pale brownish. It consists mainly of leukocytes, wound exudate, mucus from the cervix, and micro-organisms (anaerobic streptococci and staphylococci). The presence of bacteria is not pathognomonic unless associated with clinical signs of sepsis.

(3) Lochia alba- Seen during 10–15 days. The color of the discharge is pale white. Lochia alba contains plenty of decidual cells, leukocytes, mucus, cholesterin crystals, fatty and granular epithelial cells, and microorganisms.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about iron absorption?
options: RBC protophyrin is increased in deficiency
Iron excretion is only through skin, gut and urothelial cells
Body cannot compensate if more than 10 RBC/HPF per day is lost in urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ferrireductase convert Fe2+ to Fe 3+

Ferrireductase is an enzyme that converts Fe3+ (ferric iron) to Fe2+ (ferrous iron),  not the other way around. Ferrous is the form of iron that is more readily absorbed in the gut.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Most of the iron in the diet is in the ferric (Fe3+) form, whereas it is the ferrous (Fe2+) form that is absorbed.

Body iron stores are controlled by intestinal absorption as there is no exit to iron from the body. Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) transports non-heme iron into the enterocyte. Iron absorption in the duodenum is regulated by hepcidin release from the liver in response to increases in intrahepatic iron levels. It binds to ferroportin leading to endocytosis and degradation within the enterocyte. This prevents the transfer of iron from enterocyte to plasma resulting in iron trapping within duodenal cells in the form of mucosal ferritin. The trapped iron is lost as these cells are sloughed. The iron transported by ferroportin into the plasma is transferred to other parts with the help of transferrin and stored as serum ferritin and hemosiderin. The image depicting iron absorption and storage is given below:

Other options:

Option B: RBC protoporphyrin is increased in deficiency, increased protoporphyrin levels in red blood cells can indicate iron deficiency or disorders of heme synthesis.

Option C: Iron is primarily excreted through the gut, skin, and urinary tract, but the body generally has very limited mechanisms for iron excretion compared to iron absorption and recycling.

Option D: The body’s iron homeostasis is finely tuned, and a significant loss of red blood cells, such as more than 10 ml per day, can overwhelm the body’s ability to compensate and maintain iron balance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity and posterior buccal mucosa and has a history of prolonged high-dose steroid use. What is the most appropriate drug for treating this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of black necrotic tissue in the nasal and oral cavities of an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroid user) is highly diagnostic of invasive mucormycosis. This is a surgical and medical emergency. The standard first-line antifungal agent for mucormycosis is systemic Amphotericin B (preferably in its lipid formulation). Amphotericin B is a potent broad-spectrum fungicidal drug that remains the only agent with reliable efficacy against the Mucorales fungi. Fluconazole (Option A) and Itraconazole (Option C) are not effective against these aggressive fungi and should never be used as primary therapy for this condition. Griseofulvin (Option D) is only used for superficial skin infections (dermatophytes). Management must include both immediate administration of Amphotericin B and urgent surgical debridement of the necrotic tissue to prevent intracranial extension
questions.learning: The presence of black necrotic tissue in the nasal and oral cavities of an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroid user) is highly diagnostic of invasive mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In Pap smear cytology, which of the following is the most appropriate fixative used to preserve cellular details immediately after smearing?
questions.explanation: For a conventional Pap smear, immediate fixation is critical to stabilize cellular structures and prevent air-drying artifacts. The standard fixative used is 95% ethanol, which works by precipitating proteins and maintaining the life-like appearance of the cells for microscopic examination. Formaldehyde (Options A and D) is a cross-linking fixative most commonly used for whole tissue preservation in histology but is not the primary fixative for cytological smears. 70% ethanol (Option C) is generally used as a disinfectant rather than a cytology fixative. Cells are collected from the cervical transformation zone, smeared onto a slide, and immediately immersed in or sprayed with 95% ethanol. This ensures the precise detail of the nucleus and cytoplasm is preserved for cancer screening
questions.learning: For a conventional Pap smear, immediate fixation is critical to stabilize cellular structures and prevent air-drying artifacts. The standard fixative used is 95% ethanol, which works by precipitating proteins and maintaining the life-like appearance of the…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: New Which of the following is considered as a universal methyl group donor in various biochemical reactions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S-Adenosyl Methionine

Methionine in the form of S-adenosyl methionine is used for various biochemical reactions and is considered the universal methyl group donor.

S-adenosyl methionine is made from methionine and ATP and the reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme methionine adenosyltransferase(MAT) which has 3 isoenzymes. MAT-1 and MAT-3 are seen in the liver whereas MAT-2 is seen in non-hepatic tissues.

Function of S-Adenosyl methionine:

1. Transmethylation reactions:

* Norepinephrine to Epinephrine

* Ethanolamine to Choline

* Acetyl serotonin to Melatonin

* Guanidinoacetate to Creatine

2.  DNA methylation

3.  Polyamine synthesis:

* Cadaverine

* Putrescine

* Spermidine

* Spermine
questions.learning: S-Adenosyl Methionine Methionine in the form of S-adenosyl methionine is used for various biochemical reactions and is considered the universal methyl group donor.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for the function of oxygen-sensitive channels in peripheral chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation: Potassium As detailed in Question 18, the detection of low arterial oxygen levels by peripheral chemoreceptors is fundamentally tied to Potassium (K+) ions. The closure of channels in response to hypoxia is the initiating event that leads to cellular excitation. Sodium (Na+) (Option B) is involved in the later stages of action potential generation but is not the primary ion for the "oxygen-sensitive" channel itself. Bicarbonate (HCO3 -) (Option C) and Chloride (Cl-) (Option D) are vital for acid-base balance and transport but do not serve as the primary triggers for oxygen sensing. The carotid bodies, located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries, are the most important peripheral chemoreceptors for the hypoxic drive. Their high rate of blood flow and sensitive channel mechanism allow them to continuously monitor arterial blood and send immediate signals to the respiratory centers in the medulla via the glossopharyngeal nerve whenever oxygen levels become critically low.
questions.learning: Potassium As detailed in Question 18, the detection of low arterial oxygen levels by peripheral chemoreceptors is fundamentally tied to Potassium (K+) ions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following is pressure epiphysis
questions.explanation: A pressure epiphysis is the articular end of a long bone that participates in joint formation and is responsible for transmitting the weight of the body. The head of the humerus is a classic example, as it forms the shoulder joint and bears mechanical load during arm movement. Other examples include the head of the femur and the lower end of the radius. Regarding the distractors, terms like the "elbow joint" (Option B) and "wrist joint" (Option C) refer to the entire articulation rather than a specific epiphysis. The sternum (Option D) is a flat bone and does not possess epiphyses in the same manner as long bones. Additionally, there are traction epiphyses (like the humeral tubercles) which serve as attachment points for muscles but do not transmit weight. Therefore, the head of the humerus specifically fits the functional definition of a pressure epiphysis
questions.learning: A pressure epiphysis is the articular end of a long bone that participates in joint formation and is responsible for transmitting the weight of the body.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple painful vesicular lesions on an erythematous base arranged along a dermatomal distribution over the trunk, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of multiple painful blisters (vesicles) on an erythematous base, strictly aligned along a single dermatome, is the hallmark clinical finding of Herpes Zoster (shingles). This condition is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) that has remained latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia since a primary chickenpox infection. Herpes simplex (Option A) typically presents with localized clusters of vesicles on the lips or genitals and does not follow a dermatomal pattern. Molluscum contagiosum (Option C) is characterized by painless, firm, umbilicated pearly papules rather than painful vesicles. Chicken pox (Option D) involves a widespread, pleomorphic rash (vesicles in different stages) across the entire body, rather than a localized dermatomal eruption. Diagnosis of Herpes Zoster is usually clinical, although Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells can support it. Management involves antiviral therapy like acyclovir to reduce the duration of the rash and the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia, which is the most common chronic complication
questions.learning: The presentation of multiple painful blisters (vesicles) on an erythematous base, strictly aligned along a single dermatome, is the hallmark clinical finding of Herpes Zoster (shingles).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following drain is placed after mastectomy. Identify the type of drain.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Closed

The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed type of drain commonly used after mastectomy.

Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate. This enhances wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains are prophylactic in elective surgeries and therapeutic in emergency surgeries. Drains can be -

• Open - They are based on the principle of gravity
• Semi-open - Their action is based on capillary effect
• Closed - They carry out their actions through suction

Suction drains are commonly used in chest, breast, abdominal, thyroid, and plastic surgeries. They remove intraperitoneal secretions, anastomotic leaks, and blood from hemorrhage at the surgical site. Romo Vac drain is a negative suction drain closed drain kept in the subcutaneous tissue. Romo Vac drain is indicated in modified radical mastectomy, subcutaneous swelling excision, and amputations.

Special types of drains:

• Chest drains are connected to an underwater seal to aid the exit of air from the pleural cavity. They are used in pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and hemothorax.
• After surgical exploration of the bile duct, the sphincter of Oddi goes into spasm. To facilitate drainage of bile, a T tube may be used.

Drain insertion site care: The site of insertion of the drain is kept clean by drying and patting the drain insertion site with a clean towel after bath. The dressing is changed daily with folded gauze pieces placed below and above the drain site.

Removal of drains: The catheter at the site is milked for residual collections. It is then clamped and the suture holding the catheter is cut. The tube is then gently pulled out and any clots at the perforation end are removed. The time of removal of drains for various conditions is as given below.

• Drains used in surgeries like thyroidectomy are usually removed within 24 hours. Their main purpose is to cover postoperative bleeding.
• In a mastectomy, a drain is placed for 5 days to collect serous collections.
• Drains used to cover the colorectal anastomoses are placed for 5-7 days.
• Common bile duct T-tube drains are usually placed for 10 days.
• Drains for infections are removed when the infection subsides or when the content of the drain is minimal.

After the drain is removed, a folded gauze is placed over the drain insertion area. The dressing can be removed after 24 hours. The patient may be given an antibiotic ointment to apply over the area for a week.
questions.learning: Closed — The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed type of drain commonly used after mastectomy. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A fracture of the cribriform plate has occurred. What symptom is the patient most likely to present with?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is a thin, fragile, perforated structure that forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It is in direct contact with the meninges and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A fracture in this specific area often causes a dural tear, resulting in CSF rhinorrhea, where clear fluid leaks from the intracranial space into the nose. This is often accompanied by anosmia (loss of smell) due to damage to the olfactory nerve fibers. Hearing loss (Option A) is associated with temporal bone fractures. Visual loss (Option B) or diplopia (Option D) usually results from fractures involving the orbit or sphenoid bone. CSF rhinorrhea is a significant clinical finding because it creates a potential pathway for bacteria to cause meningitis. Management involves bed rest and precautions to avoid intracranial pressure spikes while the dural tear heals
questions.learning: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is a thin, fragile, perforated structure that forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A school-going child presents with a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, mouth breathing, and impaired hearing. On examination, a high arched palate is noted. What is the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical picture is suggestive of adenoid hypertrophy. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

Indications of adenoidectomy:

* Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome, or speech abnormalities, i.e. (rhinolalia clausa)

* Recurrent rhinosinusitis

* Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid hyperplasia

* Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia

* Dental malocclusion. Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent their recurrence after orthodontic treatment
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The given clinical picture is suggestive of adenoid hypertrophy. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Causes of AUB are subdivided by the acronym PALM-COEIN. What are the characteristics of PALM causes? I. Structural lesions II. Diagnosed by ultrasound III. Confirmed by histopathology Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and III

The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification is the standard system used to classify the causes of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) in reproductive-aged women.

The PALM group includes structural causes that can usually be identified by imaging and confirmed by histopathological examination, whereas the COEIN group comprises non-structural causes. All the statements regarding PALM causes are correct:

• I. Structural lesions: PALM includes structural abnormalities of the uterus.
• II. Diagnosed by ultrasound: Most PALM lesions can be detected by transvaginal ultrasonography, saline infusion sonography, hysteroscopy, or MRI.
• III. Confirmed by histopathology: Tissue diagnosis confirms conditions such as endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, adenomyosis (after hysterectomy), and polyps.
questions.learning: I, II and III — The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification is the standard system used to classify the causes of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) in reproductive-aged women.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young boy presents with joint swelling following a fall. Laboratory tests reveal a normal PT and an elevated aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemophilia

This patient with a history of joint swelling on minor trauma and an abnormal coagulation panel points to a probable diagnosis of haemophilia.

This condition is caused by an X-linked recessive mutation leading to a deficiency of Factor VIII of the coagulation factors. This leads to a prolonged partial thromboplastin time. Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and thus the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug.

Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular haematomas, haemarthroses, haematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. Retroperitoneal haemorrhages can accumulate large volumes of blood and may cause hypovolemic shock.

Laboratory findings in haemophilia:

* Factor VIII – reduced

* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) - prolonged

* Platelet count – normal

* Bleeding time – normal

* Prothrombin time – normal

Other options:
Option B: von Willebrand disease often shows an elevated aPTT and normal PT, but the bleeding time is increased.
Option C: IDA would show low haemoglobin and iron, not coagulation abnormalities.
Option D: Platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard–Soulier syndrome, etc.) often have a normal aPTT.

Pearl PF0779: Parameters of the coagulation pathway and its uses

Parameters of the coagulation pathway and its uses

Parameter
Uses

Prothrombin Time (PT)
It is used to monitor the functioning of the extrinsic and the common coagulation pathways. Normal PT is 12–16 seconds.

Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
It is used to monitor the functioning of the intrinsic and the common coagulation pathways. Normal aPTT is 26–34 seconds. A relatively rare cause of prolonged aPTT is the presence of antibodies against coagulation plasma proteins called inhibitors. It can be seen due to the following reasons: Hemophilia A and B patients receiving clotting factors to control their bleeding episodes, Pregnancy, Autoimmune diseases, Malignancies (lymphoma, prostate cancer), and Dermatologic conditions.

Thrombin time (TT)
It is used for testing the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin and depends on adequate fibrinogen levels.

Bleeding time (BT)
It is the time taken for a standardized skin puncture to stop bleeding. It tests the ability of blood vessels to constrict and platelets to form a hemostatic plug.

Fibrin degradation products (FDPs)
They are used to assess the fibrinolytic activity, and they are increased in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby in the NICU is being evaluated for his features of microcephaly and hepatomegaly. CT scan revealed nodular periventricular calcifications. Congenital CMV infection is suspected. Which of the following samples is the best to detect the organism using PCR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine

Among the following options, urine is the best sample to be sent for the diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.

In congenital CMV infections, the investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first three weeks of life (after this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection). Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine is a more reliable sample than blood.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester. 90% of the infected babies are asymptomatic and have lesser chances of having late sequelae.

The clinical manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss.

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness.

questions.learning: Urine Among the following options, urine is the best sample to be sent for the diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. In congenital CMV infections, the investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about vitamin K?
options: Deficiency of vitamin K leads to hypercoagulability.
It is a water soluble vitamin.
Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.
Menaquinone is the dietary source of vitamin K found in green vegetables.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.

Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. This is due to the loss of normal bowel flora that synthesizes menaquinones (vitamin K2).

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:

• Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
• Menaquinones (Vitamin K2) are synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
• Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.
questions.learning: Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding gums, petechiae, delayed wound healing, and similar clinical features. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of bleeding gums, petechiae (small red skin spots), and poor wound healing is the classic presentation of scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential cofactor for the enzymes prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which are required for the cross-linking of collagen fibers. Deficient collagen synthesis leads to fragile blood vessels and weakened connective tissue. Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) primarily causes ocular issues like night blindness and Bitot's spots. Vitamin B6 deficiency (Option B) is associated with neuropathy and seizures. Vitamin B3 deficiency (Option C) causes pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Because Vitamin C is uniquely required for structural collagen integrity, its absence directly results in the hemorrhagic and healing defects described in the patient
questions.learning: The clinical triad of bleeding gums, petechiae (small red skin spots), and poor wound healing is the classic presentation of scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperphosphatemia

Refeeding syndrome is associated with Hypophosphataemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia.

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially lethal condition that can occur with rapid and excessive feeding of patients with severe underlying malnutrition due to starvation, alcoholism, delayed nutritional support, anorexia nervosa, or massive weight loss in obese patients.

* It can occur with either enteral or parenteral nutrition, but is more common with the latter.

* Symptoms: Electrolyte abnormalities can result in cardiac failure and dysrrhythmias, respiratory failure, neurologic disturbances, and renal and hepatic dysfunction.

Prevention and treatment:

* Correct underlying electrolyte and volume deficits.

* Additionally, thiamine should be administered before the initiation of feeding. Caloric replenition should be instituted slowly and should gradually increase over the first week.

* Vital signs, fluid balance, and electrolytes should be closely monitored and any deficits corrected as they evolve.
questions.learning: Hyperphosphatemia Refeeding syndrome is associated with Hypophosphataemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Refeeding syndrome is a potentially lethal condition that can occur with rapid and excessive feeding of patients with severe underlying malnutrition…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child was brought to the OPD following a sting on his toe. On examination, he had tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, hypersalivation, and dilated pupils. Local examination of the wound showed mild erythema. He remembers the animal having a curved tail upwards. Which of the following has most likely bitten him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scorpion

The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite.

Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite. Systemic toxicity occurs in <10% of stings but is more commonly seen in infants and children. The venom is a clear, colorless toxalbumen and is generally classified as either hemolytic or neurotoxic.

The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator resulting in the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It also has a direct effect on the myocardium.

It can present as neurotoxicity with restlessness or seizure-like activity, abnormal oculomotor function, loss of pharyngeal muscle control leading to respiratory compromise. Tongue fasciculations and hypersalivation are also common. Cardiovascular toxicity from systemic envenomation includes tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock.

If the scorpion has hemolytic venom, the reaction is mainly local, with edema, pain, and reddening. This usually lasts for one to two hours.

Treatment:

* Pain- Paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids

* Sedation for agitation, oculomotor abnormalities, uncoordinated neuromuscular activity, muscle spasms- Benzodiazepines

* Hypertension and pulmonary edema -Prazosin counteract the adrenergic surge that can lead to these effects

* Cardiogenic shock- Antivenom, prazosin, nitroglycerin, dobutamine

* Cholinergic effects- Atropine

* Supportive care wound care

Note: Massive amounts of catecholamines are also released by a species of spider called the Black Widow spider which is fatal if bitten.
questions.learning: Scorpion — The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite. Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient with thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion is done when the platelet level drops below a threshold. To proceed with surgery, platelet transfusion is done to achieve a platelet level of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 50,000

In an otherwise healthy patient, surgery can safely be performed in patients with platelet counts higher than 50,000/mm3. The risk of bleeding increases significantly if the platelet count is below this level. When platelet transfusions are used to treat thrombocytopenia, the platelet count rises by 10,000/mm3 for every unit transfused.

Thrombocytopenia is defined as a platelet count less than 1,50,000/mm3. It may be the result of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), drug-induced thrombocytopenia, rheumatological diseases (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), pregnancy and chronic liver disease. The initial step if the patient has low platelet count is to repeat the test and examine the peripheral smear.

Anemia is also a common preoperative hematological disorder. The optimal preoperative hemoglobin concentration varies between 7.5 to 10 g/dL across the individuals, with inter-individual differences due to co-morbid conditions in the patients. Patients with anemia or suspected anemia must undergo a battery of investigations to determine the type of anemia and how best to correct it. Preexisting anemia is a risk factor for postoperative death and complications such as AKI, stroke and infections.
questions.learning: 50,000 In an otherwise healthy patient, surgery can safely be performed in patients with platelet counts higher than 50,000/mm3. The risk of bleeding increases significantly if the platelet count is below this level.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structure lying in the floor of inferior horn of lateral ventricle are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tail of caudate nucleus

The correct answer is Tail of caudate nucleus.

The floor of the inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle is formed by the hippocampus, fimbria, and collateral eminence.

The tail of the caudate nucleus runs in the roof of the inferior horn, along with the stria terminalis, and therefore is not a floor structure.
questions.learning: Tail of caudate nucleus — The correct answer is Tail of caudate nucleus. The floor of the inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle is formed by the hippocampus, fimbria, and collateral eminence.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following medications would be most helpful for a chronic smoker attempting to quit smoking?
questions.explanation: Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation primarily includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and two first-line non-nicotine medications: Bupropion and Varenicline. Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, effectively reducing nicotine withdrawal symptoms and the urge to smoke. Varenicline acts as a selective partial agonist at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It works by providing low-level stimulation to ease withdrawal while simultaneously blocking nicotine from binding, which prevents the rewarding effects of smoking. Mirtazapine (Option B) is an antidepressant with no established role in standard smoking cessation protocols. Clinical trials have demonstrated that both Bupropion and Varenicline significantly increase quit rates compared to placebo, with Varenicline often being the most effective single agent. Consequently, Option D is correct as it encompasses both validated pharmacotherapeutic options
questions.learning: Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation primarily includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and two first-line non-nicotine medications: Bupropion and Varenicline.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient following a road traffic accident presented with subcutaneous emphysema. On auscultation, there was no air entry on the right side. Vitals were unstable. What will be your immediate management?

e-FAST- Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
options: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)
Wide bore needle decompression and IV fluids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)

The given clinical scenario of a patient with h/o road traffic accident (RTA) with no air entry on the right side and hemodynamic instability suggests a diagnosis of tension pneumothorax. This is managed by immediate decompression by insertion of a needle in the appropriate place.

Pneumothorax refers to the presence of excess air in the pleural space. Entrapment of air occurs by:

1. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax - due to the spontaneous rupture of apical pleural blebs or cystic spaces immediately below the visceral pleura.
2. Secondary pneumothorax - due to the rupture of dilated cystic spaces in lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
3. Tension pneumothorax -  a one-way valve mechanism that directs airflow into the pleural space leading to a higher than atmospheric pressure environment, and prevents expansion of the lung.

Tension pneumothorax is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea, tachycardia, and hypotension. On examination, the trachea is deviated away from the side of the injury, and breath sounds are absent on the affected lung. A patient can develop subcutaneous emphysema as a complication, secondary to the pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax is a surgical emergency and the excessive pressure has to be immediately relieved. Tension pneumothorax is managed by immediate needle decompression in the 5th intercostal space (ICS), followed by definitive management with a chest tube inserted in the same space.

Other options:

Option B: While IV fluids are a part of the resuscitation protocol, hypotension in a tension pneumothorax is due to an obstructive type of shock, increasing circulating volume will have minimal effect on improving blood pressure. The management of the primary cause, tension pneumothorax, takes higher precedence as the next immediate step.

Option C: Intubation is performed when the patient is unresponsive post chest tube insertion.

Option D: Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (eFAST) is not required before emergency decompression as tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, but it can be performed following chest tube insertion.
questions.learning: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS) The given clinical scenario of a patient with h/o road traffic accident (RTA) with no air entry on the right side and hemodynamic instability suggests a diagnosis of tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A male patient has a history of vestibular schwannoma, and histopathological examination of brain lesions reveals psammoma bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are slow-growing, extra-axial tumors arising from the arachnoid cap cells. Histologically, they are famously characterized by psammoma bodies—concentric, laminated calcifications. The presence of both a vestibular schwannoma and a meningioma is a hallmark of Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2). Regarding the distractors, GBM (Option B) is a highly aggressive intra-axial tumor characterized by pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation, not psammoma bodies. Pilocytic astrocytoma (Option C) is a low-grade tumor typically found in children's cerebellums, showing Rosenthal fibers rather than calcified bodies. Oligodendroglioma (Option D) shows a "fried-egg" cellular appearance and irregular calcification but lacks the classic laminated psammomatous structure. Therefore, the combination of specific histological calcifications and the associated schwannoma confirms meningioma, often in the context of a genetic syndrome
questions.learning: Meningiomas are slow-growing, extra-axial tumors arising from the arachnoid cap cells. Histologically, they are famously characterized by psammoma bodies—concentric, laminated calcifications.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A tumor biopsy shows a mutation that renders CDK constitutively active regardless of cyclin binding status. Which immediate consequence on the cell cycle restriction point would this produce, independent of p53/p21 status?
options: Rb would remain hypophosphorylated, enforcing permanent G1 arrest
Rb would become hyperphosphorylated, releasing E2F and driving G1-S transition irrespective of growth factor signaling
p53 would compensate by inducing apoptosis directly without involving p21
Cyclin levels would become irrelevant, but CDK would still require growth factor-bound tyrosine kinase receptor signaling to phosphorylate Rb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rb would become hyperphosphorylated, releasing E2F and driving G1-S transition irrespective of growth factor signaling

CDKs are constitutively expressed but normally inactive without cyclin binding — they require phase-specific cyclins for activation. A mutation causing constitutive CDK activity bypasses this regulatory requirement entirely → Rb is hyperphosphorylated regardless of growth factor signaling or p21-mediated inhibition → E2F released → G1-S transition proceeds unchecked. This models oncogenic CDK dysregulation (e.g., cyclin D-CDK4/6 pathway dysregulation in many cancers, therapeutically targeted by CDK4/6 inhibitors like palbociclib).

| Component | Normal regulation | Constitutively active CDK

| --------- | ----------------- | -------------------------

| CDK | Inactive without cyclin | Active regardless of cyclin

| Growth factor dependency | Required for cyclin expression | Bypassed

| Rb phosphorylation | Regulated by cyclin-CDK activity | Hyperphosphorylated unconditionally

| E2F | Released only when appropriate | Constitutively released

| Restriction point | Enforced | Lost
questions.learning: Rb would become hyperphosphorylated, releasing E2F and driving G1-S transition irrespective of growth factor signaling CDKs are constitutively expressed but normally inactive without cyclin binding — they require phase-specific cyclins for activation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A clinician touched the eyes of a patient with a piece of cotton, and rapid blinking of the eyes occurred in response. What is the structure responsible for carrying the above sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The response of blinking when the clinician touches the patient's eye with a piece of cotton is known as the corneal reflex. The sensation is transmitted by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), while the motor response is controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII).

The corneal reflex is an involuntary, protective response that causes blinking when the cornea is stimulated, such as by a light touch. It serves as a defence mechanism to prevent foreign objects from entering the eye and causing damage. The reflex involves two main components: sensory input and motor output. The sensation of touch or irritation on the cornea is detected by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically its nasociliary branch, which sends the signal to the brainstem.

The motor response, which is the blinking of the eyelids, is mediated by the facial nerve (Option B). The facial nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is responsible for closing the eyelids. This reflex is important for protecting the eye from potential damage, and any disruption to the trigeminal or facial nerves can impair the corneal reflex, leading to difficulty in protecting the eye from injury.

Other options:

Option B: The Facial Nerve (CN VII) is a major nerve responsible for controlling the muscles of facial expression including orbicularis oculi, which is responsible for forced closing of the eyelid. Although orbicularis oculi and facial nerve is a part of corneal reflex, its is not responsible for carrying the sensation and hence cannot be the answer.

Option C: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) plays a key role in several eye reflexes, particularly in the pupillary light reflex and the accommodation reflex. The pupillary light reflex mediates pupil constriction in response to light exposure by controlling the sphincter pupillae muscle. In the accommodation reflex, it coordinates the convergence of the eyes and the constriction of the pupils when focusing on a near object.

Option D: The optic nerve (CN II) plays a crucial role in sensory input for several reflexes. In the pupillary light reflex, it detects light entering the eye and sends the signal to the brain, triggering pupil constriction via the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Additionally, the optic nerve is involved in the accommodation reflex, where it helps detect the visual stimulus, prompting changes in eye focus and pupil constriction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which among the following is an ideal treatment for a 55-year-old female with simple hyperplasia of the endometrium with atypia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Simple hysterectomy

Simple hysterectomy is the best treatment in a case of atypical endometrial hyperplasia in a peri-menopausal and post-menopausal female.

Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia carries 29% risk of developing into endometrial carcinoma and hence, must be treated with total abdominal hysterectomy (simple hysterectomy ). The presence of any concomitant endometrial cancer must be ruled out by doing fractional curettage (or dilatation and curettage) before doing a hysterectomy.

If a premenopausal woman does not desire to undergo hysterectomy, progesterone can be given and the patient is followed up every 3-6 months. If the atypia persists during the follow-up hysterectomy should be performed.

The table below summarizes the management of patients with endometrial hyperplasia

Management of Endometrial hyperplasia

Hyperplasia without atypia

Pre-menopausal women
Progesterone therapy

Postmenopausal women:

• Simple hyperplasia without atypia
• Complex hyperplasia without atypia

• Follow up without therapy
• Progesterone therapy

Hyperplasia with atypia

Pre-menopausal women

If patient wishes to preserve uterus,give High-dose progesterone therapy

If atypia persists, then perform Total abdominal hysterectomy

Peri-menopausal women
Total abdominal hysterectomy

Post-menopausal women
Total abdominal hysterectomy +BSO (bilateral salphingo-ophorectomy)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old G4A3 woman had a history of miscarriage at 8 weeks, the second miscarriage at 11 weeks with no cardiac activity, and the third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks with preterm delivery due to early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome.

APLA is an autoimmune disorder commonly associated with fetal death, preterm delivery, early-onset preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency and thromboses. Pregnancy loss usually occurs before 10 weeks.

Diagnosis of APLA requires at least 1 clinical criterion and 1 laboratory criterion.

• Obstetric criteria

• One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond 10 weeks or
• Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency requiring delivery before 34 weeks, or
• Three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks

• Laboratory criteria

• Presence of lupus anticoagulant, or
• Anticardiolipin antibodies, or
• Anti-β2 glycoprotein antibody

Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), also referred to as a recurrent miscarriage or habitual abortion, is historically defined as 3 consecutive pregnancy losses prior to 20 weeks from the last menstrual period.

Common causes include:

• Parental chromosomal abnormalities
• Untreated hypothyroidism
• Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
• Uterine anatomic abnormalities,
• Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Other options:

Option A: There is no history of STD or skin lesions suggestive of syphilis and according to Kassawitz rule, in women with untreated syphilis having a series of pregnancies, the likelihood of fetal infection in later pregnancies becomes less; usually, only the first pregnancy is an abortion, the following pregnancy losses will be stillbirths in the next trimester rather than recurrent pregnancy loss.

Option C: TORCH infections may play a role in sporadic spontaneous pregnancy loss, rather than recurrent pregnancy losses.

Option D: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) refers to the onset or first recognition of diabetes during pregnancy, usually at the 24-28 weeks screening test. Women with uncontrolled overt or pregestational diabetes with elevated HbA1c or preprandial glucose in the first trimester have an increased risk for early miscarriage, but there is a history or lab findings suggestive of gestational diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome — The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Overestimates GFR

Creatinine clearance (CrCl) is a commonly used clinical estimate of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). However, it slightly overestimates the true GFR because, in addition to being freely filtered by the glomerulus, creatinine is also secreted in small amounts by the proximal renal tubules. In contrast, inulin clearance is the gold standard for measuring GFR because inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed, secreted, synthesized, nor metabolized by the kidneys.

Why not the other options?

• A. Underestimates GFR: Incorrect. Creatinine clearance overestimates, rather than underestimates, GFR due to tubular secretion.
• C. Gold standard for GFR measurement: Incorrect. The gold standard is inulin clearance, not creatinine clearance.
• D. Equal to inulin clearance: Incorrect. Creatinine clearance is slightly higher than inulin clearance because of tubular secretion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of severe head injury following a road traffic accident (RTA) and a poor Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. CT scan of the brain appears normal, but the patient dies within a few hours. Brain biopsy shows multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

The clinical vignette of an initially poor GCS score and later death following a high-energy accident(RTA) with a normal CT scan and brain biopsy showing multiple haemorrhages is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury is a type of primary brain injury commonly associated with high-energy accidents. It is caused by damage to axons throughout the brain due to rotational acceleration followed by deceleration. There is disruption and shearing of axons leading to microhemorrhages. Most commonly, it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death.

The immunohistochemistry marker with beta-amyloid precursor protein is considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.

The histological features :

Initially, there will be dilation of the axons, followed by the formation of club-shaped structures known as retraction balls. These retraction balls later decrease in number over 2-3 weeks, followed by microglial cell proliferation.

Later in the course, astrocytosis and demyelination will be observed.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

* CT may be normal.

* MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain. It detects the micro-bleeds within the brain.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebral contusion occurs due to traumatic brain injury, at the sites that come in direct contact with the skull. Imaging may show microhemorrhages and edema. Usually, no treatment is required.

Option C: Subdural hemorrhage is caused by rupture of cerebral bridging veins. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.

The image below shows a CT of a subdural hemorrhage.

Option D: Extradural hemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura mater tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They are confined by cranial sutures.

The image below shows a CT of an extradural hemorrhage.

Pearl PF1100: Diffuse Axonal Injury

Features of diffuse axonal injury

Mechanism
Primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration-decceleration injury (this leads to deformation of the axons by stretching them)

Pathology

Changes in permeability of the axolemma

Axonal swelling

Intracellular calcium accumulation

Proteolysis

Collapse of the cytoskeleton

Histology

'Retraction balls or globes' - bulbous and clubbed axons. Seen earliest at 12-18 hours.

Immuno-histochemistry

Beta-amyloid precursor protein - considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.

Retraction balls:

* The force generated by violent shaking or rotational injury (as in a passenger ejected from the moving vehicle) can produce stretching of axons in cerebral white matter.

* Microscopic examination does not show any axonal injuries up to 12 hrs after injury

* After 12 hrs the axons first appear dilated then club shaped and finally appear as round balls known as retraction balls which indicates transected axons.

* The number of retraction balls begins to decrease after 2-3 weeks after injury and cluster of microglial cells appear followed by astrocytosis and demyelination.

Image shows scattered axonal retraction balls stained with Congo Red (arrows):
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury — The clinical vignette of an initially poor GCS score and later death following a high-energy accident(RTA) with a normal CT scan and brain biopsy showing multiple haemorrhages is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a pillar of primary health care?
questions.explanation: The four primary "pillars" (or principles) of primary health care, as defined by the Alma-Ata Declaration, are: Equitable distribution (Option D), Community participation, "Intersectoral coordination" (Option B), and "Appropriate technology" (Option C). Therefore, "Health education" (Option A) is "not" technically one of the pillars. Instead, health education is one of the "eight essential components" of primary health care. Other components include nutrition, safe water/sanitation, maternal/child health, immunization, and local disease control. Equitable distribution ensures health services are accessible to all regardless of status. Intersectoral coordination means that health programs must work with agriculture, education, and other sectors to be effective. Appropriate technology means using methods that are scientifically sound, locally acceptable, and affordable. Differentiating between the principles (pillars) and the actual elements (components) is a common requirement for public health and social medicine examinations
questions.learning: The four primary "pillars" (or principles) of primary health care, as defined by the Alma-Ata Declaration, are: Equitable distribution (Option D), Community participation, "Intersectoral coordination" (Option B), and "Appropriate technology" (Option C).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus delivers a full-term infant. Which of the following complications is the newborn at risk of developing due to maternal diabetes?
questions.explanation: Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) are at a high risk for several neonatal complications. The most common acute metabolic issue is neonatal hypoglycemia (Option D) . During pregnancy, the fetus is exposed to high maternal glucose, which crosses the placenta and triggers fetal pancreatic hypertrophy and hyperinsulinemia. After birth, the maternal glucose supply is suddenly cut off, but the baby's insulin levels remain high, leading to a rapid drop in blood sugar. IDMs are also at risk for hypocalcemia (not hypercalcemia, Option C) and various congenital heart defects, most notably ventricular septal defects or transposition of the great arteries (Tetralogy of Fallot, Option B, is less specifically linked than these). Hyperglycemia (Option A) would not occur in a hyperinsulinemic neonate. Therefore, close monitoring of blood glucose levels in the immediate postpartum period is mandatory for all IDMs to prevent neurological injury from hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) are at a high risk for several neonatal complications. The most common acute metabolic issue is neonatal hypoglycemia (Option D) .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends a routine follow-up visit. Investigations show normal serum creatinine and potassium levels, but microalbuminuria is present, and her HbA1c is 8%. Her blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits, and she is currently being treated with metformin. What should be the next step in her management?
options: Stop Metformin and start a different OHA
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits microalbuminuria, which is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy. Starting an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the critical next step, even if blood pressure is normal, because these drugs provide renoprotection by lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing the progression of albuminuria. Thiazide diuretics (Option A) may be used for edema but do not offer the same kidney-protective benefits. Insulin (Option B) is considered if HbA1c remains despite oral agents, which is not the case here. Metformin should only be stopped (Option C) if the eGFR falls below 30 ml/min, whereas this patient has normal creatinine. Early intervention with RAAS blockade significantly reduces the long-term risk of end-stage renal disease and major cardiovascular events in diabetics

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) mainly indicate in the context of water quality management?
questions.explanation: The Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) is used in water quality management to predict whether water will be scale-forming or corrosive. It does this by comparing the actual pH of the water with the pH at which the water is saturated with calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Positive LSI (> 0): Water is supersaturated with CaCO₃ → scale formation likely Negative LSI (< 0): Water is undersaturated → corrosive, tends to dissolve metals and pipe material LSI = 0: Water is in equilibrium (neither scaling nor corrosive) LSI incorporates several chemical parameters, including pH, calcium hardness, alkalinity, temperature, and indirectly total dissolved solids. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option B: Total dissolved solids are measured separately, not by LSI alone 2. Option C: Water hardness alone does not determine scaling or corrosion 3. Option D: Biological contamination is unrelated to LSI and assessed microbiologically Thus, LSI primarily indicates the balance between scaling and corrosion in water systems

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is not used for brachytherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine-131

I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which a radioactive source is placed directly into or near the target tissue to deliver localized radiation treatment. It is commonly used for treating various types of cancer.

Other options:

A) Iodine-125: This radioactive isotope is commonly used in brachytherapy for treating prostate cancer. It emits low-energy gamma rays that can effectively target and treat the cancerous tissue.

C) Cobalt-60: This isotope is not typically used in brachytherapy but rather in external beam radiation therapy. Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

D) Iridium-192: This is a commonly used radioactive isotope in brachytherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays and is used for treating various types of cancer, such as cervical, prostate, and breast cancer. Iridium-192 is often used in temporary brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is temporarily placed in the body and then removed after a specific period of treatment.

In summary, while Iodine-125 and Iridium-192 are commonly used in brachytherapy, Cobalt-60 is primarily used in external beam radiation therapy. Iodine-131 is not typically used in brachytherapy but has other medical applications, such as thyroid cancer treatment and diagnostic imaging.
questions.learning: Iodine-131 I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
You are working in a primary health center (PHC) situated in a high seismic zone. Which of the following will you do as part of preparedness for an emergency?

1. Disaster preparedness by making sure all financial and other resources are available
2. Increase public awareness through campaigns and loudspeakers
3. Conduct a simulation for the disaster and assess the response
4. Follow instructions given over the phone or radio by higher officials
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

Steps 1, 2, and 3 are done as part of preparedness for an emergency by someone working in a PHC situated in a high seismic zone.

Emergency preparedness refers to long-term development activities that strengthen the capacity of a country to effectively manage all kinds of emergencies. It involves the following steps:

1. Disaster preparedness by making sure all financial and other resources are available
2. Increase public awareness through campaigns and loudspeakers
3. Conduct a simulation for the disaster and assess the response
4. Evaluate the risk of disaster
5. Information sessions coordination with news media
6. Adopt standards and regulations

Disaster risk management is a systematic process using administrative decisions, policies, and strategies to lessen the impacts of natural hazards and disasters. The steps are:

• Response - This includes activities such as:

• Search, rescue, and first aid: This step is important since the organized relief services will be able to address only a small fraction of demand after a major disaster.
• Field care: This includes making health care available regardless of facilities and operating status.
• Triage: Classifying the injured based on the severity of the injuries and chances of survival with medical intervention.
• Tagging: Tags with name, age, triage category, diagnosis and treatment are put for identification purposes.
• Identification of the dead: The dead bodies should be shifted from the disaster site to the mortuary.

• Rehabilitation - This includes measures that lead to the restoration of pre-disaster conditions. These measures include water supply restoration, food safety, basic sanitation, personal hygiene, and vector control.
• Mitigation - This includes measures to prevent disasters from causing emergencies or to lessen the likely effects of emergencies. Some of them are flood mitigation, land use planning, improved building codes, and the reduction and protection of vulnerable populations or structures.
• Preparedness - This is a program that aims at strengthening the capacity of a country to manage all types of emergencies efficiently. Its objective is to ensure that appropriate measurements are taken for the relief and rehabilitation of disaster victims.

Some measures that should be followed by all in case of an emergency include:

• Avoiding telephone use, unless it is to call for help
• Listen to and carry out the radio or loudspeaker broadcast messages
• Carry out the official instructions given over the radio or by loudspeaker
• Keep a family emergency kit ready

Note: Vaccination of the general population post-disaster against typhoid, cholera, and tetanus is not recommended.
