questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The O2 saturation with respect to PO2 is shown by the curve marked as 5. What happens to the oxygen Hb dissociation curve on transfusion of stored RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2

When stored RBCs are transfused, the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve typically shifts to the left but still retains its sigmoid shape as represented by the curve marked as 2.

This is due to reduced levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in stored red blood cells. 2,3-BPG is a metabolite in RBCs that binds to hemoglobin and reduces its affinity for oxygen.

During storage, metabolic processes in RBCs slow down, leading to a depletion of 2,3-BPG. Lower 2,3-BPG levels make hemoglobin hold onto oxygen more tightly, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. Hence, this increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the left.

Other Options:

Option B and C: show a right shift to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.↑ in 2,3-BPG seen in increased anaerobic glycolysis leads to the right shift of the curve. Storage of blood causes depletion of 2,3-BPG, hence leading to left shift instead of right.
questions.learning: 2 When stored RBCs are transfused, the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve typically shifts to the left but still retains its sigmoid shape as represented by the curve marked as 2.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Statement NOT true about β-oxidation of fatty acids:
options: CAT I and CAT II transport fatty acids
CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation

β-oxidation of fatty acids occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and long-chain fatty acids require the carnitine shuttle for mitochondrial transport.

Carnitine Shuttle Steps:

1. CPT-I (CAT-I): Converts fatty acyl-CoA → acyl-carnitine in the cytosol/outer mitochondrial membrane.
2. Acyl-carnitine is transported into mitochondria.
3. CPT-II (CAT-II): Converts acyl-carnitine → fatty acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing carnitine.

Key points:

• ATP is used earlier for fatty acid activation to fatty acyl-CoA.
• Carnitine is released inside mitochondria after reconversion.
• CoA remains within the mitochondrial matrix, not released in the cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation.
questions.learning: CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation β-oxidation of fatty acids occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and long-chain fatty acids require the carnitine shuttle for mitochondrial transport.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with difficulty ingesting liquids more than solids. What is the most likely characteristic finding on imaging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rat tail appearance

The clinical scenario of a female patient having more difficulty swallowing liquids than solids suggests achalasia cardia, with the characteristic imaging finding being the Rat tail sign.

Achalasia is a primary oesophagal motility disorder. It is characterized by the absence of oesophagal peristalsis and impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation in response to swallowing. These abnormalities cause a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction.

Esophageal manometry shows:

* Incomplete LES relaxation in response to swallowing.

* High resting LES pressure.

* Absent esophageal peristalsis.

On performing a timed barium study, barium will be retained for more than five minutes. The fluoroscopic examination will reveal a dilated oesophagus that tapers to form a bird's beak at the gastroesophageal junction as seen in the image above. Endoscopy and biopsy are usually carried out to rule out cancer. 24-hour pH monitoring is used in the diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Medical management with sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, and calcium-channel blockers for symptomatic relief. Pneumatic dilatation and Botox injection

Surgical management is the treatment of choice :

* Laparoscopic Heller's myotomy is the definitive management - The major complication associated with this procedure is gastro-oesophageal reflux. So it is best to combine it with partial anterior fundoplication (Heller–Dor operation).

* Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is a recently introduced, advanced natural-orifice approach for myotomy.

* Open Esophageal Myotomy - rarely done.

Other options:

Option A: Apple core sign is characteristically seen in the barium enema of carcinoma colon as shown below.

Option B: Barium enema radiograph of diverticulosis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth as shown below.

Option C: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that shows the string sign of Kantor on barium enema as shown below.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

Pearl PF0315: Manometric findings in oesophageal disorders

Manometric Findings in Nutcracker Esophagus

* Peristaltic esophageal contractions 2 standard deviations above normal

* Amplitude > 180 mmHg and duration > 7seconds.

* Normal peristaltic sequence

Manometric Findings in Diffuse Esophageal Spasm

* Simultaneous, multipeaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mm Hg) or long duration (>2.5 sec)

* These erratic contractions occur after more than 20% of wet swallows.

* Intermittent normal peristalsis

Manometric Findings in Hypertensive Lower Esophageal Sphincter-

* Elevated LES pressure > 26mmHg and normal relaxation of LES

* The esophageal body may be hyper-peristaltic or normal.

Manometric findings in Achalasia Cardia

* Incomplete LES relaxation

* Aperistalsis in the esophageal body

* Elevated LES pressure ≥26 mmHg

* Increased intraesophageal baseline pressures relative to gastric baseline

Manometric findings in ineffective esophageal motility disorders

* Decreased or absent amplitude of esophageal peristalsis (<30 mmHg)

* Increased number of non-transmitted contractions
questions.learning: Rat tail appearance — The clinical scenario of a female patient having more difficulty swallowing liquids than solids suggests achalasia cardia, with the characteristic imaging finding being the Rat tail sign.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the anomaly shown below?
options: It occurs due to the persistance of prechordal plate
It occurs due to the defective migration of primordial cells to the genital ridge
It contains skin, cartilage and bone
It is a benign tumor of coccyx
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It occurs due to the persistance of prechordal plate

The image shows a sacrococcygeal teratoma, which occurs due to the persistence of pluripotent cells of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers. These germ layers are formed from the primordial germ cells of the epiblast, which are pluripotent. The process begins with the formation of the primitive streak on the epiblast, which develops into the primitive node in the cranial region, and a primitive pit. The cells from the epiblast, migrate towards the primitive streak and invaginate into the primitive pit and organizes itself into cells arranged in three layers, which eventually develop into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The prechordal plate simply refers to the cells that have invaginated in the cranial region.

Sacrococcygeal teratomas occur due to remnants of pluripotent cells from the primitive streak due to defective migration of the cells (Option B). As these cells are from the epiblast, teratomas contain tissues from all germ layers which may include skin, hair, cartilage and bone (Option C). These tumors are benign in nature (Option D), but may rarely become malignant. If they occur in the cranial end of the primitive streak, they form oro-pharyngeal teratomas (as shown below), whereas if they occur in the caudal end of the primitive streak in the coccygeal region, they are called sacro-coccygeal teratomas.
questions.learning: It occurs due to the persistance of prechordal plate The image shows a sacrococcygeal teratoma, which occurs due to the persistence of pluripotent cells of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Classical galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme:
questions.explanation: Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by the inability to metabolize galactose, a sugar found in milk. The "classical" form of the disease is specifically caused by a deficiency of the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). This deficiency leads to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in various organs, including the liver and brain. Aldose reductase (Option A) converts excess galactose into galactitol, which contributes to cataract formation in untreated patients. Galactokinase deficiency (Option B) causes a milder form of the disease primarily characterized by early cataracts. UDP galactose-4-epimerase deficiency (Option D) is an extremely rare variant. Classical GALT deficiency presents in infancy with jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and sepsis if milk is not removed from the diet. Therefore, GALT is the definitive enzyme lacking in the classical presentation of this syndrome

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of both arms. Punctate pitting was noted on examining the nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

The presentation of erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of arms and punctate pitting of the nails are suggestive of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin with systemic manifestations. Plaque psoriasis is the most common type.

* The peak occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, and scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

* Koebner or isomorphic phenomenon- describes the appearance of new lesions along the site of trauma (linear lesions)

Nail findings are commonly seen across all types of psoriasis. Patients present with pits, ridges, and grooves of the nail plate. In the case of nail bed involvement subungual oil drops, subungual hyperkeratosis, and distal onycholysis can be seen.

The characteristic histopathological finding in psoriasis consists of multiple neutrophilic foci in the parakeratotic stratum corneum i.e Munro’s microabscesses and spongiform neutrophils in the spinous layer of the epidermis i.e spongiform pustules of Kogoj.

The topical application of steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and emollients is the mainstay of management. Phototherapy and oral methotrexate, acitretin, and cyclosporine can also be used.

Other options:

Option B: Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder affecting the skin and mucosal membranes. The lesions of Lichen planus can be described as 5Ps — purple, polygonal, pruritic, plane-topped (flat), papules and are shown in the image below. White streaks forming a lacework in buccal mucosa is a characteristic feature and are known as Wickham’s striae. Nail involvement includes hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, and pterygium unguis due to adhesion between the dorsal nail fold and the nail bed.

Option C: Atopic dermatitis or eczema is a relapsing chronic inflammatory skin disease. Patients present with itchy erythematous papules/ papulovesicular lesions in flexural regions as shown below. Nail involvement is in the form of coarse pitting and ridging.

Option D: Pityriasis rosea is an acute self-limiting papulosquamous disorder. It is commonly seen in children and young adults. The first manifestation of the disease is usually the appearance of the herald patch, which is larger and more conspicuous than the lesions of the later eruption covered by fine scales. Later the center tends to clear and assumes a wrinkled, atrophic appearance and a tawny color, with a marginal collarette of scale attached peripherally, with the free edge of the scale internally - called a Hanging curtain sign.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

Pearl PF1460: Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

I. In Mild Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* Coal tar

* Dithranol

* Potent topical steroid

* Vitamin D analogue

Second line

* Local NB-UVB or PUVA

* Excimer laser

II. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* NB-UVB or PUVA

Second line

* Acitretin

* Apremilast

* Ciclosporin

* Fumaric acid esters (where available)

* Methotrexate

Third line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Secukinumab

* Ustekinumab

III. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis with Psoriatic Arthritis

First line

* Apremilast

* Methotrexate

Second line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Ustekinumab

Third line

* Combination therapy
questions.learning: Psoriasis — The presentation of erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of arms and punctate pitting of the nails are suggestive of psoriasis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Rh negative mother, ICT negative was given Anti D during 28 week of pregnancy. Which of the following is the ideal one
options: No need additional dose since she is ICT negative
Give another dose of Anti D 72 hour postpartum irrespective of baby blood group
Give another dose of Anti D 72 hour postpartum depending on the baby blood group
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give another dose of Anti D 72 hour postpartum depending on the baby blood group

Anti-D should be given postnatally within 72 hours & all women who deliver Rh D-positive baby should have quantification of fetomaternal hemorrhage to guide appropriate dose of anti D prophylaxis.

RCOG and NICE guidelines for Anti–D prophylaxis:

1. All Rh-negative women should be offered Anti-D

First trimester indications: (50 mcg)

• Chorionic villus sampling
• Miscarriage
• Termination of pregnancy
• Ectopic pregnancy

2nd & 3rd-trimester indications (300 mcg)

• Amniocentesis, Cordocentesis
• Obstetric hemorrhage
• Abdominal trauma
• External cephalic version

2. All Rh D-negative women should be given a single dose of 1500 units (300 mcg) of anti D between 28 - 30 weeks of pregnancy.

3. Postnatally within 72 hours

4. All women who deliver Rh D-positive baby should have quantification of fetomaternal hemorrhage to guide appropriate dose of anti D prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant woman was prescribed indomethacin. Which of the following effects does the drug have on the fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Premature closure of ductus arteriosus

Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman.

Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants. It is given intravenously. One of its limiting factors is the development of renal toxicity in neonates.

Indomethacin is a nonselective COX inhibitor. It has anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic properties. It can be used in the management of conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, gouty arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, etc. But its use is limited due to the high rate of intolerance and availability of safer agents.

Adverse effects: Diarrhea with ulcerative bowel lesions, acute pancreatitis, and hepatitis are seen. Frontal headache is the most frequent CNS effect. Dizziness, light-headedness, vertigo, and mental confusion can occur. Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and rarely aplastic anemia can also occur.

Note:

Prostaglandin analogs are indicated in the maintenance of patency of the ductus arteriosus.
questions.learning: Premature closure of ductus arteriosus Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman. Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS): 1. Type 1 CRPS may be precipitated by a traumatic event such as a fracture. 2. Type 1 CRPS is associated with peripheral nerve damage. 3. Type 2 CRPS is associated with peripheral nerve damage. 4. Budapest criteria are used for diagnosis of CRPS. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

1. Type 1 CRPS may be precipitated by trauma such as fracture: Correct

• CRPS type 1 can occur after fractures, surgery, or other trauma.
• There is no demonstrable nerve injury.

2. Type 1 CRPS is associated with peripheral nerve damage: Incorrect

• By definition, CRPS type 1 occurs without a confirmed peripheral nerve injury.
• It was formerly called reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD).

3. Type 2 CRPS is associated with peripheral nerve damage: Correct

• CRPS type 2 occurs following identifiable peripheral nerve injury.
• It was formerly called causalgia.

4. Budapest criteria are used for diagnosis: Correct

• The Budapest clinical criteria are used to diagnose CRPS based on sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, and motor/trophic features.
questions.learning: Type 1 CRPS may be precipitated by trauma such as fracture: Correct • CRPS type 1 can occur after fractures, surgery, or other trauma. • There is no demonstrable nerve injury.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with easy bruising, prolonged bleeding, and dental caries and is found to have a vitamin deficiency. Which vitamin supplementation would be most appropriate for treating her condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of easy bruising and prolonged bleeding is highly suggestive of a coagulopathy resulting from a Vitamin K deficiency. Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for the gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Without Vitamin K, these factors are produced in an inactive form, leading to a significantly increased risk of bleeding. Vitamin B1 (Option A) deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Vitamin B9 (Option B, folate) deficiency results in megaloblastic anemia but not primary bleeding issues. Vitamin D (Option C) is essential for bone health and its deficiency causes rickets or osteomalacia; while the question mentions "dental caries" (which can be seen in Vitamin D or C lack), the primary acute presentation of "prolonged bleeding" points decisively to Vitamin K. Supplementation with Vitamin K is the most appropriate treatment to restore normal clotting function and prevent life-threatening hemorrhage

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered to be the best for the detection of Clostridium difficile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay

A combination of glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay can be used for the detection of Clostridium difficile.

Clostridium difficile is a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus that causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). Enzyme immunoassay to detect glutamate dehydrogenase is less specific compared to toxin detection for diagnosis. So a combination of the two can be used for diagnostic confirmation.

The condition is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use, which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin. The spores are spread by contact with the feces of affected individuals or asymptomatic carriers. It can persist on surfaces for months. Risk factors include poor hand hygiene, old age, and gastrointestinal surgery.

The spores germinate in the small intestine and produce two toxins—toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). These interfere with the epithelial-cell barrier function and result in diarrhea and pseudomembrane formation. The pseudomembranes appear as small whitish-yellow plaques initially which later coalesce to involve the entire colon wall. It contains necrotic leukocytes, fibrin, and cellular debris. The anamnestic IgG response determines which patients develop the disease or remain asymptomatic.

Symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. The diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical criteria and detection of toxin or the organism in stool samples. This can be done by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or by culture.

Discontinuation of any ongoing antimicrobials and adequate hydration are general measures that are recommended. Oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin is the first-line treatment. Oral metronidazole can be used when these are not available.

Other options:

Option A: Aerobic culture of stool is the most sensitive test and is highly specific. It is not used practically as the turnaround time is slow.
questions.learning: Glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay — A combination of glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay can be used for the detection of Clostridium difficile.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the use of Shakir's tape?
questions.explanation: Shakir's tape (also known as Mid-Upper Arm Circumference or MUAC tape) is a simple, cost-effective, and portable tool used for the rapid assessment of nutritional status in children. It is a classic example of appropriate technology, which refers to health solutions that are easy to use, locally adaptable, and accessible to non-medical personnel (like ASHA workers) in resource-limited settings. The tape is color-coded (Red <11.5 cm indicates severe malnutrition) for easy interpretation. Regarding the distractors, intersectoral coordination (Option A) and community participation (Option D) are principles of primary health care that involve teamwork between sectors or citizens, while equitable distribution (Option B) refers to the fair allocation of resources. While the tape facilitates community-level screening, its inherent nature as a simplified diagnostic device classifies it as appropriate technology
questions.learning: Shakir's tape (also known as Mid-Upper Arm Circumference or MUAC tape) is a simple, cost-effective, and portable tool used for the rapid assessment of nutritional status in children.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden onset of hematemesis. He has been taking aspirin for his arthritis and drinks alcohol occasionally. He gives a history of occasional abdominal pain. On examination, there is no abdominal mass or tenderness. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peptic ulcer

This patient with a history of aspirin use, now presenting with abdominal pain and a sudden onset of hematemesis most likely has a bleeding peptic ulcer.

Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) accounts for around 2/3rd of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The major causative factors are Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs. Prostaglandins protect gastric and duodenal mucosa from acid and pepsin. They increase mucin and bicarbonate secretion and increase mucosal blood flow. They also promote epithelial cell proliferation. NSAIDs like aspirin disrupt these naturally protective mechanisms and increase the risk of peptic ulcer formation in the stomach and the duodenum.

They present with abdominal pain, bleeding, or signs of peritonitis due to perforation. Significant hemorrhage occurs when duodenal or gastric ulcers penetrate branches of the gastroduodenal or left gastric arteries, respectively.

Other options:

Option A: Mallory-Weiss tears are partial-thickness tears of the mucosa and submucosa occurring near the gastroesophageal junction. They occur in patients with a history of repeated emesis and are classical in alcoholic patients after a period of intense retching and vomiting following binge drinking.

Option B: Esophagitis commonly occurs due to repeated exposure of mucosa to the acidic gastric secretions in gastroesophageal reflux disease. It results in chronic blood loss and commonly presents as anemia or guaiac-positive stools. Ulcerations of superficial mucosa due to esophagitis generally do not bleed acutely.

Option D: Esophageal varices commonly occur due to portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis. A history of liver disease or the stigmata of portal hypertension and cirrhosis would suggest variceal bleeding.
questions.learning: Peptic ulcer — This patient with a history of aspirin use, now presenting with abdominal pain and a sudden onset of hematemesis most likely has a bleeding peptic ulcer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked area in the image given (arrow pointing to the space between the uterus and rectum).
questions.explanation: The marked area in the pelvic image is the Pouch of Douglas, also known as the rectouterine pouch. It is the lowest and most dependent point of the peritoneal cavity in a standing female, located between the posterior wall of the uterus and the anterior wall of the rectum. Morrison’s pouch (Option A) is the hepatorenal space in the upper abdomen, which is the most dependent part when lying supine. The vesicouterine pouch (Option B) is located anteriorly between the uterus and the bladder, situated higher in the pelvic cavity. The ischioanal fossa (Option D) is a fat-filled space located on either side of the anal canal, below the pelvic diaphragm. The Pouch of Douglas is a clinically significant site for the accumulation of fluids like blood, pus, or ascites

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Oral contraceptive pill prevents all except?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer significant protective benefits against several malignancies but are associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, particularly with long-term use. This is likely due to hormonal influences on HPV persistence. Conversely, OCPs are well-documented to prevent epithelial ovarian cancer (Option B) by suppressing ovulation and endometrial cancer (Option C) by providing a progestin-dominant environment that counteracts estrogen's proliferative effects. Evidence also suggests a modest protective effect against colon cancer (Option D). Because the use of OCPs does not protect against cervical malignancy and may instead elevate the risk, Option A is the correct "except" choice in this profile. Regular screening remains essential for OCP users to monitor for cervical neoplasia
questions.learning: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer significant protective benefits against several malignancies but are associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, particularly with long-term use.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A person living with HIV (PLHIV) presents with multiple dog bite injuries characterized by puncture wounds. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: According to the Rabies management guidelines, a punctured wound with bleeding or multiple bites constitutes a Category III exposure. For individuals living with HIV (PLHIV) or those with compromised immunity, immediate and comprehensive management is mandatory. This includes local wound treatment, which involves immediate washing with soap and water for at least 15 minutes to reduce viral load. Rabies Immune Globulin (RIG) must be administered to provide passive immunity; Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) is preferred as it is free from the danger of sensitization. Finally, the Rabies vaccine series must be initiated to stimulate active immunity. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because they provide only partial protection, which is insufficient for Category III bites, especially in an immunocompromised patient. Therefore, the combination of local care, passive immunization, and active vaccination is the only correct clinical course to prevent fatal rabies
questions.learning: According to the Rabies management guidelines, a punctured wound with bleeding or multiple bites constitutes a Category III exposure. For individuals living with HIV (PLHIV) or those with compromised immunity, immediate and comprehensive management is…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Who is primarily responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning, maintaining their records, and distributing oral contraceptives under the national health system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multipurpose worker(female)

According to the national health system, the Multipurpose worker(female)/ANM is primarily responsible for registering couples for family planning, maintaining records, and distributing oral contraceptives at the sub-centre level.

The Health Worker Female (ANM) is instructed to utilize information from the eligible couple register and child register for the family planning programme. She maintains the eligible couple registers and updates them regularly. In addition, she distributes conventional contraceptives and oral contraceptives to couples, provides facilities to depot holders, and helps prospective acceptors in availing family planning services. Other responsibilities include:

* Provide a continuous supply of contraceptives through depot holders.

* Assist and accompany prospective acceptors to higher centers for family planning services when required.

* Offer follow-up services, manage side effects, give treatment for minor complications, and refer cases needing higher care.

* Establish and guide depot holders for contraceptive distribution in the community.

Other options:

Option A: ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist. Even though ASHA workers are sometimes involved in maintaining list of eligible couples and distribution of contraceptives, among other responsibilities, the registration of eligible couples is primarily done by the female multipurpose worker

Option C: Village Health Guide (VHG) was a national community health worker initiative launched in 1977 in India, aiming to deploy locally selected volunteers—most often women—trained to deliver basic preventive, promotive, and limited curative services at the village level.

Option D: Anganwadi workers are community-based functionaries under the ICDS scheme responsible for health check-ups, including growth chart maintenance, immunization, supplementary nutrition, health education, and preschool education. They also provide referral services, acting as the primary link between the community and health services for young children and women.

Pearl PF0294: ASHA

ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist.

An ASHA must be a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old and have a formal education till 10th standard preferably if they are in good numbers. This may be relaxed upto 8th standard only if no suitable person with this qualification is available. She is part of the primary health care at the village level.

National norm: In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA, but in remote areas, one ASHA per habitation is the norm. In urban areas, 1 ASHA worker is assigned to a population of 1000-2500. This norm is also mandated by each state, differently, according to their requirements.

Responsibilities of ASHA:

* Health education and awareness

* Reproductive and child health and family planning

* Facilitate the access to health services

* Promotion of sanitation and household toilet construction

* Provision of primary medical care for minor ailments

* Provider of DOTS

* Depot holder of essentials like ORS, iron and folic acid tablets, condoms, disposable delivery kits, etc.

* Dispersal of health information on her community to higher centres

* Some responsibilities are integrated with Anganwadi workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife
questions.learning: Multipurpose worker(female) According to the national health system, the Multipurpose worker(female)/ANM is primarily responsible for registering couples for family planning, maintaining records, and distributing oral contraceptives at the sub-centre level.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient develops hyperthermia, g eneralized muscle rigidity, and increased end-tidal CO₂ (EtCO₂) shortly after administration of succinylcholine and sevoflurane during anaesthesia. Which of the following is the drug of choice for management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dantrolene

This presentation is classic for malignant hyperthermia, triggered by succinylcholine and volatile agents like sevoflurane. The definitive treatment is dantrolene, which inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reversing muscle rigidity, stops the hypermetabolic crisis, and rising EtCO₂.
questions.learning: Dantrolene — This presentation is classic for malignant hyperthermia, triggered by succinylcholine and volatile agents like sevoflurane. The definitive treatment is dantrolene, which inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reversing…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with COPD is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. Which of the following preoperative measures is most effective in reducing the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Smoking cessation

Recognize that preoperative smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative pulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing elective surgery. Smoking cessation improves mucociliary clearance, reduces airway reactivity and sputum production, and enhances pulmonary function, particularly when stopped ≥4–8 weeks before surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Give antibiotics: Not indicated unless there is evidence of an active respiratory infection.
• B. Wait for 3 months: Routine postponement is not recommended; optimization, including smoking cessation, is more beneficial.
• D. Oxygen therapy: Corrects hypoxemia but does not reduce the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications in stable COPD patients.
questions.learning: Smoking cessation Recognize that preoperative smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative pulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing elective surgery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant presents with fever and poor feeding. Lumbar puncture reveals cloudy CSF with predominantly neutrophilic pleocytosis, and CSF culture shows bacitracin resistance. Which organism is the most likely cause of this neonatal meningitis?
questions.explanation: In a two-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF findings of high neutrophils and low glucose confirm acute bacterial meningitis. The critical microbiological clue is bacitracin resistance; while Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) is bacitracin-sensitive, GBS is characteristically resistant. Pneumococcus (Option A) and Meningococci (Option D) are common causes of meningitis in older children and adults but are less frequent in the immediate neonatal period compared to GBS and E. coli. GBS is typically acquired from the maternal birth canal during delivery. Management involves emergency intravenous antibiotics, usually a combination of ampicillin and an aminoglycoside or cefotaxime. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis given to GBS-colonized mothers has significantly reduced the incidence of early-onset neonatal GBS disease. Recognizing the combination of neonatal age and bacitracin resistance is essential for rapid etiological identification on medical board examinations
questions.learning: In a two-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF findings of high neutrophils and low glucose confirm acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents after a stab injury to the neck just above the clavicle. His pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate surgical exploration

Penetrating neck injuries are managed based on the patient’s hemodynamic status and the presence of hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury.

This patient has:

• Penetrating neck trauma
• Hypotension (BP 90/70 mmHg)
• Tachycardia (120/min)

These findings indicate hemodynamic instability, which is an indication for immediate surgical exploration without delaying for imaging.

Why not the other options?

• B. Supportive treatment and observation: Appropriate only for stable patients without concerning signs.
• C. CT angiography of the neck: Investigation of choice only in hemodynamically stable patients.
• D. MRI neck: Not used in the acute trauma setting.
questions.learning: Immediate surgical exploration Penetrating neck injuries are managed based on the patient’s hemodynamic status and the presence of hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young boy presents with joint swelling after a fall. Lab investigations show normal PT and raised aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Joint swelling (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is a classic indicator of a coagulation factor deficiency, most notably hemophilia. Laboratory findings of a normal PT combined with a prolonged aPTT confirm a defect in the intrinsic pathway. Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) and Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) both manifest with this specific pattern. Von Willebrand Disease (Option A) also shows a raised aPTT but is typically characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding (like epistaxis) rather than deep joint bleeds. Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C) causes fatigue and pallor but has no effect on coagulation times. Platelet function disorders (Option D) lead to mucosal bleeding and petechiae, while both PT and aPTT usually remain within normal limits. Thus, the isolated aPTT elevation and hemarthrosis identify hemophilia
questions.learning: Joint swelling (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is a classic indicator of a coagulation factor deficiency, most notably hemophilia. Laboratory findings of a normal PT combined with a prolonged aPTT confirm a defect in the intrinsic pathway.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the retractor shown in the below image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mastoid retractor

The instrument shown in the image is Mollison’s mastoid retractor. It is used in mastoidectomy to retract soft tissues after incision and elevation of flaps. It is self-retaining and hemostatic.

Jansen’s self-retaining mastoid retractor (shown below) is also used in mastoidectomy and is similar to Mollison’s retractor.

Option A: Joll retractor (shown below) is a self-retaining retractor used in thyroid surgery.

Option D: Langenbeck retractor is useful for holding open wounds, as in an open appendicectomy and they are often used in pairs (one in each of the assistant’s hands).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient with a long history of chronic smoking presents with breathlessness. Pulmonary function tests reveal a reduced FEV₁%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A history of chronic smoking combined with an obstructive pattern on spirometry—specifically a decrease in FEV1 and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%)—is characteristic of COPD. COPD includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema, both of which involve irreversible airflow limitation. In contrast, pulmonary fibrosis (Option B) and interstitial lung disease (Option C) are restrictive lung diseases; they typically show a normal or even increased FEV1/FVC ratio because the forced vital capacity (FVC) decreases more than the FEV1. While asthma (Option D) also causes an obstructive pattern, it is distinguished from COPD by its significant reversibility after bronchodilator use and is less directly linked to chronic smoking in late adulthood compared to COPD. Therefore, given the specific risk factor of smoking and the obstructive findings, COPD is the most likely clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: A history of chronic smoking combined with an obstructive pattern on spirometry—specifically a decrease in FEV1 and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%)—is characteristic of COPD.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: If a person accused of committing a crime is produced before a criminal court and it is determined that the accused is below a specified age, the court directs that the case be transferred to the juvenile court. What is the age limit for such a transfer?
questions.explanation: Under Indian law, the relevant legislation is the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which defines a juvenile (or child) as any person below 18 years of age. When an accused is produced before a criminal court and it is determined that they are under 18 years at the time of the offence, the case is transferred to the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) instead of being tried in a regular criminal court. The objective is to focus on reform, rehabilitation, and reintegration rather than punishment. The age of 18 is internationally recognized as the threshold for adulthood in criminal responsibility under juvenile justice systems. Even if the offence is serious, the procedure initially shifts to the juvenile system, though in heinous offences (16–18 years), further assessment may occur. Other options are incorrect: 1. 21 and 24 are not recognized legal limits in juvenile justice law. 2. 17 is incorrect because the legal cutoff is below 18, not 17
questions.learning: Under Indian law, the relevant legislation is the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which defines a juvenile (or child) as any person below 18 years of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Budd-Chiari Syndrome (BCS)?
options: Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus.
Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.

Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium. The obstruction leads to hepatic congestion, portal hypertension, and impaired liver function.

The classic clinical triad consists of:

• Abdominal pain/discomfort
• Ascites
• Hepatomegaly

Why not the other options?

• A. It principally affects young males: BCS is more common in young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance in many populations due to associations with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and myeloproliferative disorders.
• B. Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus: The obstruction most commonly involves the hepatic veins. IVC obstruction can occur but is not the defining or usual mechanism.
• C. Quadrate lobe (Segment 4 and 5) undergoes hypertrophy: The caudate lobe (Segment I) undergoes hypertrophy because it has independent venous drainage directly into the IVC, allowing it to remain relatively spared.
questions.learning: Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features. Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because his parents have noticed that he persistently avoids using his right eye. Detailed ophthalmic evaluation confirms amblyopia of the right eye. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is a reduction in vision that occurs because the brain favors the other eye. In this 3-year-old boy, the right eye is amblyopic. The primary treatment to improve vision in the affected eye is "patching" or occlusion therapy. Specifically, the strong eye (the left eye) is covered for several hours a day to force the brain to process images from the weaker right eye, thereby strengthening the neural pathways. Option B is incorrect because occluding the right eye would further worsen its vision. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate as amblyopia requires active intervention during the "critical period" of visual development (before age 7–8) to be effective. Surgical correction (Option D) may be necessary if the amblyopia is caused by strabismus (misaligned eyes), but occlusion is still required to treat the resulting visual deficit. Early intervention is crucial to prevent permanent vision loss in the amblyopic eye and to ensure normal binocular vision
questions.learning: Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is a reduction in vision that occurs because the brain favors the other eye. In this 3-year-old boy, the right eye is amblyopic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A histological section is shown, with an arrow indicating a large, flask-shaped cell located in the middle layer. Identify the cell marked by the arrow.
questions.explanation: The histological section shows the cerebellar cortex, which consists of three layers: molecular, Purkinje, and granular. The marked area is a Purkinje cell, identifiable by its large, flask-shaped body arranged in a single row between the other two layers. These cells provide the only output from the cerebellar cortex and have an inhibitory effect on deep nuclei. Stellate and basket cells (Options A and B) are smaller inhibitory interneurons located in the outer molecular layer. Granular cells (Option D) are small, densely packed excitatory neurons found in the innermost granular layer. Purkinje cells are unique for their extensive dendritic branches that extend into the molecular layer. Identifying these cells is fundamental for understanding the architecture and inhibitory coordination of the cerebellum
questions.learning: The histological section shows the cerebellar cortex, which consists of three layers: molecular, Purkinje, and granular. The marked area is a Purkinje cell, identifiable by its large, flask-shaped body arranged in a single row between the other two layers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a boundary of the Gastrinoma triangle? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Second and third part of duodenum
Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein

The Gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's Triangle) is an anatomical region where gastrinomas are most commonly found. This triangle is formed by specific anatomical boundaries that define the area where these tumors typically develop. The splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein are not components of this triangle's boundaries, making this the incorrect option.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which part of the fallopian tube does fertilization occur? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ampulla

Ampulla:

• The ampulla is the widest section of the fallopian tube and is the most common site for fertilization.
• This region provides an optimal environment for the sperm to meet the ovum and for the subsequent fertilization process to occur.
• The ampulla is also the most common site of ectopic pregnancy, where a fertilized egg implants and grows outside the main cavity of the uterus.

The fallopian tube has four main parts:

1. Infundibulum: The funnel-shaped opening near the ovary with finger-like projections called fimbriae.
2. Ampulla: The widest and longest part where fertilization typically occurs.
3. Isthmus: A narrow section adjacent to the uterus.
4. Interstitial (or intramural): The part that traverses the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which will you not see in twin pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MADC (Monoamniotic Dichorionic)

Twin pregnancies are classified based on:

• Chorionicity → number of placentas
• Amnionicity → number of amniotic sacs

| Type | Chorion | Amnion | Frequency

| ---- | ------- | ------ | ---------

| Dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) | 2 | 2 | Most common

| Monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) | 1 | 2 | Common in identical twins

| Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) | 1 | 1 | Rare

MADC = Monoamniotic Dichorionic

This means:

• Two placentas (dichorionic)
• Only one amniotic sac (monoamniotic)

This is embryologically impossible because:

• Each chorion normally develops its own amniotic sac.
• If two chorions exist, there must be two amniotic sacs.

Thus monoamniotic dichorionic twins cannot exist.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following is true regarding creatinine clearance?
options: It is less than inulin clearance
It is more than inulin clearance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is more than inulin clearance

The true statement is creatinine clearance is more than inulin clearance.

Creatinine is partially secreted and never reabsorbed. Clearance of creatinine (CCr) can also be used to determine GFR; since creatinine is secreted by the tubules, thus the clearance of creatinine will be slightly higher than inulin. Hence, it overestimates GFR.

Inulin is completely filtered and never reabsorbed. Hence, it can be used for GFR estimation.

PAH(para amino hippuric acid) at low plasma concentrations is completely filtered and secreted. Hence, it can be used for the estimation of renal blood flow.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young adult presents with a deformed nose after falling from a ladder. The CT scan shows a displaced nasal fracture. What is the ideal time to reduce the fracture in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-7 days following injury

The ideal time for reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema from the injury has subsided.

The presence of edema interferes with the accurate reduction of the fracture. In most cases, the deformity is due to edema. So, ice packs and head elevation are advised initially after injury. After 3-5 days, the edema would subside and the underlying deformity will be apparent on clinical assessment.

After 2 weeks it is difficult to reduce since the process of callus formation and the bony and fibrous union would have started.
questions.learning: 5-7 days following injury The ideal time for reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema from the injury has subsided.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What were the target goals for Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to be achieved by 2023?
questions.explanation: India’s National Health Policy (NHP) 2017, aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), set specific targets to be achieved by 2023: Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): < 70 per 100,000 live births Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): ≈ 28–30 per 1,000 live births Thus, the combined target is correctly represented as 70/30. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Option B (30/70): Reverses the indicators (MMR and IMR). 2. Option C (100/30): Reflects older benchmarks; many states had already reduced MMR below 100 before 2023. 3. Option D (30/100): Inconsistent with national priorities and epidemiological realities. Achieving the 70/30 target depends on improving institutional deliveries, quality antenatal and postnatal care, strengthening Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs), and effective implementation of programs like Janani Suraksha Yojana. These targets are key indicators of progress in maternal and child health

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Select the correct option regarding Mobile Medical Units (MMUs).

1. MMUs are run by the government
2. MMUs are run by external agencies with medical supplies given by the government.
3. MMUs are run by the government and medical supplies are also given by the government.
4. MMUs are run by external agencies and medical supplies are also given by the external agency.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, and 3

Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct. MMUs can be run by either Government or an external agency, but the drugs and medical supplies are to be provided always by Government only.

Mobile Medical Units (MMU) is a major initiative under NRHM to provide a range of health care services for people living in remote, inaccessible, un-served, and underserved areas in both rural as well as urban areas, with the aim of taking healthcare services to the doorsteps of such people.

There are 3 models of operationalizing MMUs:

1. Government operated MMU
2. Operation of MMU on outsourcing basis by an external agency but capital expenditure, drugs, and supplies provided by Government.
3. Outsourcing by an external agency which provides both capital expenditure and operational expenditure. However, drugs and supplies are to be provided by Government.

MMUs provide primary care services for common diseases (communicable and non-communicable), RCH services, screening tests, and referral to higher facilities and specialists as required. Clinical services are provided by a Medical Officer and team, and mobilization and outreach services are provided by ANMs and ASHA.
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 3 Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct. MMUs can be run by either Government or an external agency, but the drugs and medical supplies are to be provided always by Government only.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Warthin Finkeldey cells are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rubeola

Warthin-Finkeldey cells are multinucleated giant cells that are present in the prodromal stage of measles (rubeola), HIV lymphadenitis, and various benign and malignant lymphoid conditions.

The cytopathic effect of measles consists of multinucleate syncytium formation with numerous acidophilic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions.

The image given below shows the Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells:

Measles is an infection caused by Paramyxovirus which is a single-stranded enveloped RNA virus. It spreads 4 days before and 5 days after the appearance of the rash through body secretions.

Clinical features include mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. The Koplik spots are red lesions with bluish-white spots seen in the inner cheeks at the level of premolars. The red maculopapular rashes begin on the forehead, behind the ears, and on the upper neck on the 4th day. It then spreads towards the torso, and extremities and reaches the palms and soles.

The diagnosis is mainly made clinically but a serological demonstration of IgM antibodies and IgG antibodies is also used. Complications include pneumonia, croup, and tracheitis. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a fatal complication of chronic measles diagnosed by elevated IgG levels in cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.learning: Rubeola Warthin-Finkeldey cells are multinucleated giant cells that are present in the prodromal stage of measles (rubeola), HIV lymphadenitis, and various benign and malignant lymphoid conditions.

questions.text: Arlt’s line is seen in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trachoma

Arlt’s line is a conjunctival sign seen in trachoma.

It is a characteristic white conjunctival scar usually formed at the junction between the lower third and upper two-third of the superior tarsus.

Clinical signs in trachoma:

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child was brought with pedal edema and cheilosis. Cardiomegaly was present. What is the vitamin deficiency associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

The given clinical presentation with pedal edema and cardiomegaly is suggestive of wet beriberi due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.

Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy, irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes and proprioception. As the disease progresses, increased intracranial pressure, meningismus and coma develop.

Wet beriberi results due to cardiac and renal dysfunction which leads to fluid accumulation. It is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, and edema. It is commonly seen in the refugee camps where people consume polished rice-based monotonous diets.

Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy in adults.

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

Other options:

Option A: Riboflavin deficiency can present with cheilosis, but it does not typically cause pedal edema and cardiomegaly.

Option C: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency can cause neurological symptoms, anemia, and dermatitis but is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

Option D: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency leads to pellagra, characterized by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. It is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient undergoes surgery of the lateral part of the base of the skull. Postoperatively, the patient presents with aspiration but does not have a change in voice. Which of the following is the reason?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior laryngeal nerve injury

In the given clinical scenario, the patient experiences aspiration but does not exhibit any change in voice following base of skull surgery. This suggests an injury to the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN).

In SLN injury, only the cricothyroid muscle is involved which is used only in high-pitch vocalization, normal speech will not be affected. SLN also provides sensory supply to the mucosa above vocal cords, hence its lesion would lead to increased susceptibility to aspiration.

Other options:

Option B: The glossopharyngeal nerve does not provide sensory or motor supply to the larynx.

Option C and D: The patient also has normal vocalization which rules out recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) and high vagal injury. RLN supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, therefore an RLN lesion would lead to disordered vocalization. A high vagal injury would mean that both the SLN and RLN functions are affected, therefore that can also be ruled out.
questions.learning: Superior laryngeal nerve injury — In the given clinical scenario, the patient experiences aspiration but does not exhibit any change in voice following base of skull surgery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weakness, and pallor, and investigations reveal a microcytic anemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia worldwide, especially in a young female of reproductive age, is Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). Clinically, IDA presents with symptoms of impaired oxygen delivery such as fatigue, generalized weakness, and visible pallor. The microcytosis occurs because hemoglobin synthesis is impaired due to a lack of iron, forcing red blood cells to undergo extra divisions to maintain concentration, resulting in smaller cells. Chronic kidney disease (Option B) typically presents with normocytic anemia due to decreased erythropoietin production. Hemolytic anemia (Option C) usually presents as normocytic or macrocytic with signs of increased cell destruction like jaundice. Alcoholism (Option A) is more frequently associated with macrocytic anemia due to folate deficiency or direct toxic effects. Diagnosis of IDA is confirmed by a low serum ferritin level, high total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and low transferrin saturation. Management involves identifying the source of iron loss (such as heavy menstruation or GI bleeding) and providing oral or parenteral iron supplementation

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Drug resistance is most seen with which STI?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gonorrhoea

Gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) is the STI most notorious for rapidly developing antimicrobial resistance.

• Mechanisms of resistance:

o    β-lactamase production (penicillin resistance)

o    Altered penicillin-binding proteins

o    Efflux pumps & porin mutations

• Drugs with rising resistance: Penicillin, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, even some cephalosporins
• Current treatment:

o    Ceftriaxone (last reliable first-line in many settings)

o    Often combined with anti-chlamydial therapy

Why not others:

• Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) → still highly sensitive to penicillin
• Chancroid (H. ducreyi) → some resistance but not as notorious
• Donovanosis → relatively predictable response to antibiotics

questions.text: A patient requires Ceftriaxone 180 mg. You have a 2 ml syringe with 10 divisions per ml. The vial contains 500 mg/5ml of ceftriaxone. How many divisions in the 2 ml syringe will you fill to give 180 mg ceftriaxone?

• 500 mg of drug is in 5 ml and hence 100 mg in 1ml. Thus 180 mg in 1.8 ml
• 10 divisions for each ml

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of programmed cell death primarily involves the action of caspase-1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis

Pyroptosis is a form of programmed inflammatory cell death mediated by activation of caspase-1. Occurs in:

• Macrophages
• Infected cells

Caspase-1 is activated via inflammasomes and leads to cleavage of IL-1β and IL-18. This causes pore formation in the cell membrane, cell swelling, and membrane rupture.

Pathogen / Danger signal

↓

Inflammasome activation

↓

Caspase-1 activation

↓

Gasdermin pore formation

↓

Cell swelling + membrane rupture

↓

Release of IL-1β, IL-18 → Inflammation

Apoptosis involves caspase-3, 6, 9. Necroptosis is caspase-independent, and necrosis is unregulated cell death.

| Feature | Apoptosis | Pyroptosis | Necroptosis | Necrosis

| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------

| Type | Programmed | Programmed | Programmed | Uncontrolled

| Inflammation |  No | Yes | Yes | Yes

| Key enzyme | Caspase 3,9 | Caspase-1 | RIPK3 | None

| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells | Swells | Swells

| Membrane | Intact | Ruptures | Ruptures | Ruptures

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with unilateral ptosis with hypotropia in the same eye. He was given an IV injection, following which the symptoms go away. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

Only Myasthenia gravis among the conditions mentioned above, would show dramatic improvement after administration of an IV injection like Anti-Cholinesterase, edrophonium.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that is characterized by generalized muscle weakness and rapidly progressing fatigue that improves after short periods of rest. Ocular myasthenia gravis causes progressive external ophthalmoplegia which affects only the extraocular muscles. Early ocular manifestations include failure of convergence & ptosis which is mostly bilateral and increases on prolonged fixation or attempts to look upwards. In the initial phase, there can be unilateral myogenic ptosis, which improves after short rest rapidly.

Diagnosis of myasthenia gravis can be made by performing the tensilon test where the symptoms improve for a short period on administering a short acting Anticholinesterase drug such as edrophonium.

Note:
Single most sensitive test for Myasthenia Gravis - Single fiber Electromyography
The single most specific test for Myasthenia Gravis - AChR antibodies

Option B: 6th nerve palsy- isolated 6th nerve palsy presents with convergent squint with limitation of abduction in the affected eye, due to the lateral rectus muscle palsy.

Option A: 3rd Cranial nerve palsy presents with

• ptosis due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle(LPS)
• Abduction and depression in the primary position(down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus(6th nerve supply) and superior oblique muscles(4th nerve supply)
• Dilated pupil and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy(involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply)
• Limited adduction, elevation due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus .

Option D: Horner syndrome, also called oculosympathetic paresis, is produced by a lesion anywhere along the sympathetic pathway supplying the head, neck and eyes. It is characterized by the classical triad of ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis(reduced ipsilateral sweating). Other features include mild enophthalmos, hypochromic heterochromia and anisocoria that is accentuated in dim light.

Tests for confirmation of Horner's syndrome -

• Cocaine drops (2-4%)
Horner pupil does not dilate
Normal pupil dilates
• Apraclonidine drops (0.5-1%)
Horner pupil dilates - due to upregulation of α1 receptors in the dilator pupillae.
Normal pupil does not dilate
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis Only Myasthenia gravis among the conditions mentioned above, would show dramatic improvement after administration of an IV injection like Anti-Cholinesterase, edrophonium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 39 weeks gestation presents to labor and delivery with regular painful uterine contractions for the past 5 hours. She denies any rupture of membranes or vaginal bleeding. Fetal movements have been perceived normally. On initial examination, the cervix is 4 cm dilated, 80% effaced, with the fetal vertex at 0 station. She requests pain relief and receives epidural analgesia. Two hours after epidural placement, repeat examination shows the cervix to be 5 cm dilated and 100% effaced with the vertex at 0 station. A subsequent examination 2 hours later reveals no change in cervical dilation or fetal descent. Fetal heart rate tracing demonstrates: • Baseline: 138/min • Variability: moderate • Accelerations: present • Decelerations: sporadic early decelerations only Uterine activity on tocometry shows contractions occurring every 6–8 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor
Continue expectant management for another 2 hours
Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor
Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor

This patient is in the active phase of labor and has demonstrated inadequate labor progress after epidural analgesia.

Active Labor Arrest Criteria

• No cervical change despite:

• ≥6 cm dilatation and
• Adequate uterine contractions for ≥4 hours, or
• Inadequate contractions despite oxytocin for ≥6 hours

This patient does not yet meet criteria for active-phase arrest because contractions are inadequate.

Interpretation:

• Labor progress is inadequate due to hypotonic uterine contractions (power dysfunction)
• There is no evidence of fetal distress or cephalopelvic disproportion

Management:

• Oxytocin augmentation should be initiated to increase contraction frequency and strength
• Continuous fetal and uterine monitoring should be maintained

Why other options are incorrect?

• Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor: Cesarean delivery is not indicated because active-phase arrest requires adequate contractions before diagnosing labor arrest
• Continue expectant management for another 2 hours: Expectant management may unnecessarily prolong labor when contractions are inadequate
• Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening: Misoprostol is used for cervical ripening and labor induction, not for augmentation of established labor
questions.learning: Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor — This patient is in the active phase of labor and has demonstrated inadequate labor progress after epidural analgesia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hematological findings are seen in pregnant women with thalassemia trait?
options: Low serum total iron binding capacity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Raised HbA₂ and low MCV

Thalassemia trait (thalassemia minor) is characterized by microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to reduced synthesis of globin chains. During pregnancy, it is an important differential diagnosis of microcytic anemia, as it can be mistaken for iron deficiency anemia. In β-thalassemia trait, the hallmark laboratory findings are:

• Raised HbA₂ (>3.5%)
• Low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)

Why not the other options?

• B. Low MCHC: MCHC may be mildly reduced but is not the characteristic diagnostic finding. Low MCV with raised HbA₂ is much more specific.
• C. Low serum total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)

• TIBC is usually normal in thalassemia trait.
• Low TIBC is more suggestive of anemia of chronic disease.

• D. Low HbA₂ and raised MCV

• This is the opposite of the findings in β-thalassemia trait.
• Raised MCV is seen in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, not thalassemia.
questions.learning: Raised HbA₂ and low MCV Thalassemia trait (thalassemia minor) is characterized by microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to reduced synthesis of globin chains.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: With respect to long-term patency and durability of grafts used in coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, which graft material is known to provide the most long-lasting outcomes?
questions.explanation: In coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), the durability of the graft is measured by its long-term patency rate. The Internal Mammary Artery (IMA), specifically the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), is the gold-standard graft material known for providing the most durable outcomes. IMA grafts have an exceptional 10-year patency rate of over 90% because their arterial wall is resistant to atherosclerosis. The long saphenous vein (Option A) is commonly used for multiple bypasses but has a significant risk of late occlusion, with only about 50% remaining patent after 10 years. PTFE (Option C) is a synthetic material used in peripheral grafts but is unsuitable and prone to failure in small-caliber coronary bypasses. The gastroepiploic artery (Option D) is an alternative arterial graft but is technically difficult and less durable than the IMA. Therefore, the internal mammary artery is the definitive superior choice for longevity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with an acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. The patient undergoes coronary angiography with stent placement in the left circumflex artery, and he is started on therapy with a beta blocker and antiplatelet agents. On day 3 of hospitalization he experiences chest pain. The pain, described as sharp and radiating to his neck and shoulders, is exacerbated by coughing and swallowing. Temperature is 37.5⁰C (99.5⁰F), blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular, and respirations are 20/min. The lungs are clear on auscultation. There is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's chest pain?
options: Pericardial inflammation due to autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue
Pericardial inflammation due to concomitant viral infection
Pericardial inflammation overlying the necrotic segment of myocardium
Recurrent thrombosis of the culprit coronary vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pericardial inflammation overlying the necrotic segment of myocardium

This patient’s day-3 post-STEMI, sharp, pleuritic chest pain radiating to the neck/shoulders and worsened by coughing is classic for early post-MI pericarditis (epistenocardiac pericarditis). It occurs due to direct inflammation of the pericardium overlying the necrotic myocardium, typically within 1–3 days after MI.

A. Pericardial inflammation due to autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue – This is Dressler syndrome, which occurs weeks to months later.

B. Pericardial inflammation due to concomitant viral infection – Would cause pericarditis independent of recent MI timing.

D. Recurrent coronary thrombosis of culprit coronary vessel – Causes ischemic, pressure-like chest pain, not pleuritic pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for an elderly diabetic female patient, based on the findings shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The clinical context—an elderly diabetic patient with a necrotic, black orbital and nasal mass—is pathognomonic for Rhino-cerebral Mucormycosis (Option B). This is an aggressive, invasive fungal infection caused by molds of the order Mucorales. These fungi thrive in the acidic, high-glucose environment of diabetic patients (particularly during DKA) and are angioinvasive, leading to vascular thrombosis and subsequent tissue necrosis (black eschar). Rhinosporidiosis (Option A) typically presents as painless, friable, strawberry-like polyps in the nose. A foreign body (Option C) would cause localized inflammation but not widespread necrotic destruction. Aspergillosis (Option D) can cause invasive sinusitis but is generally less hyper-acute and aggressive than mucormycosis. Therefore, the specific combination of demographic risk and necrotic visual evidence makes Mucormycosis the definitive diagnosis. Management requires immediate intravenous Amphotericin B and aggressive surgical debridement of all dead tissue
questions.learning: The clinical context—an elderly diabetic patient with a necrotic, black orbital and nasal mass—is pathognomonic for Rhino-cerebral Mucormycosis (Option B).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is wrong about DIC?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased fibrinogen

In disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), fibrinogen levels are decreased due to increased bleeding.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acquired syndrome characterized by the widespread activation of blood clotting factors within blood vessels, resulting in a loss of clotting control. The primary mechanism of DIC involves the uncontrolled generation of thrombin through multiple pathways which leads to sustained coagulation activation, the formation of fibrin, and the consumption of clotting factors and platelets.

Infections are the most frequent cause of DIC.

Laboratory investigations in DIC:

• Decreased platelet count
• Prolonged PT/TT
• Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
• Decreased fibrinogen
• Elevated fibrin degradation products (D-dimers)
• Peripheral smear: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia in DIC with schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells)

The treatment involves platelet transfusion when platelet counts are below 10,000-20,000/μL. Replacement of fibrinogen and coagulation factors is with fresh frozen plasma (FFP) along with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.

In cases of low-grade DIC associated with solid tumors or acute promyelocytic leukemia low doses of continuous-infusion heparin has been effective.
