questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Name the outlet forceps from the following:
questions.explanation: In the classification of obstetric instruments, Wrigley forceps are specifically categorized as outlet forceps. They are shorter and lighter than standard forceps, designed for use only when the fetal head is on the perineum (at the station or lower) and the scalp is visible at the introitus. Their primary use is to assist in the final stages of delivery, often for maternal exhaustion or non-reassuring fetal heart patterns. Piper forceps (Option B) are specialized long-curved forceps used exclusively for the delivery of the after-coming head in breech presentation. Kielland's forceps (Option C) are designed for rotation of the fetal head from malpositions like occipitoposterior or transverse. Das forceps (Option D) are a general-purpose Indian modification of the Simpson forceps, typically used for low or mid-cavity deliveries. Choosing the correct forceps based on the station and position of the head is vital for procedural safety, as Wrigley’s minimal size reduces the risk of maternal pelvic floor trauma

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Addison's disease can present with symptoms similar to which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Depression

Addison's disease presents most similarly to depression. Apathy, social withdrawal, impaired sleep, decreased concentration, and prominent fatigue is frequently seen which is usually mistaken for depression.

Following infection, trauma, or surgery, a patient with previously unrecognized Addison's disease may suffer from an Addisonian crisis. Such patients present with either shock or hypoglycemia. This is a medical emergency requiring urgent medical referral.

Endocrinopathy
Differential psychiatric diagnosis

Addison's disease
Depression

Hyperthyroidism
Mood disorder, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder

Hypothyroidism
Depression, hypomania, delusions, schizophrenia (myxedema madness).

Hypoparathyroidism
Delirium is the most common.

Hyperparathyroidism
Depression, anxiety, paranoid delusions. Tetrad of "painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones".

Hypoglycemia
Anxiety, depersonalization, derealisation, aggressive behavior, amnesia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with fetal bradycardia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maternal fever

Normal fetal heart rate:

| Parameter | Range

| --------- | -----

| Normal baseline FHR | 110–160 bpm

| Bradycardia | <110 bpm

| Tachycardia | >160 bpm

Bradycardia generally indicates fetal hypoxia or cardiac abnormalities.

Causes of Fetal Bradycardia

1. Placental Abruption

In Placental Abruption:

• Placenta separates prematurely.
• Causes acute fetal hypoxia.

2. Fetal Head Compression

Head compression during labor causes:

• Vagal stimulation
• Resulting in early decelerations on CTG.

These appear as temporary fetal heart rate slowing.

3. Congenital Heart Disease

Congenital cardiac defects can affect the fetal conduction system, producing:

• Complete heart block
• Persistent fetal bradycardia

Example:

• Congenital AV block
• Seen in maternal lupus (anti-Ro antibodies).

Maternal fever, especially in chorioamnionitis, causes:

• Increased fetal metabolic rate
• Sympathetic stimulation

Result:➡ Fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following health programmes supports DANIDA?
questions.explanation: The Danish International Development Agency (DANIDA) specifically supports the National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) in India. Its assistance focuses on providing high-quality eye care services, particularly cataract surgeries, and developing the necessary infrastructure and professional training to reduce preventable blindness. Regarding the distractors, the TB control program (Option A) has historically been assisted by SIDA (Swedish International Development Agency) and the World Bank. Malaria eradication efforts (Option C) are primarily supported by USAID and the Global Fund. HIV/AIDS programs (Option D) receive significant backing from NACO and international agencies like UNAIDS and the Global Fund, rather than DANIDA. Therefore, DANIDA’s primary contribution to India’s public health landscape is through the NPCB

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A boy, upon disturbing a bee hive, received several stings. After a few minutes, he developed symptoms of shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. This is an example of ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE-mediated reaction

Anaphylaxis following a bee sting is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity. Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions.

Immediate (type I) hypersensitivity:

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity:

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles
questions.learning: IgE-mediated reaction Anaphylaxis following a bee sting is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity. Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops pneumonia with skin lesions. Microscopy of specimen from skin lesions showed broad based budding with a thick capsule. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blastomycosis

In this case of an immunocompromised patient with pneumonia and skin lesions, the microscopy of specimens from skin lesions showing broad-based budding with a thick capsule suggests the diagnosis of Blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermitidis.

Blastomycosis is a chronic infection, characterized by the formation of suppurative and granulomatous lesions, especially, in the lungs and skin.

Blastomycosis predominantly affects individuals in regions where the fungus Blastomyces is endemic, such as the Midwest and southeastern United States. It is most common in North America and so is also called North American Blastomycosis.

The disease has a broad demographic impact, occurring in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. However, those with impaired immune systems—such as patients with AIDS, those on glucocorticoid therapy, or those receiving TNF-α inhibitors—are at higher risk for severe or disseminated disease involving the skin, bone, or central nervous system. Healthy individuals may experience a range of symptoms from mild pulmonary illness to more severe forms of pneumonia. It is more commonly observed in males aged 30-50 years, possibly due to occupational or recreational exposures.

Blastomycosis can present in three forms:

1. Pulmonary disease:

• Presents with cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever
• Hilar lymphadenopathy may be present
• Focal or diffuse consolidation, miliary lesions, or abscess formation may occur.
• Resembles TB and Histoplasmosis

2. Cutaneous disease:

• Involvement of face and exposed parts of the skin
• Skin lesion: ulcerated verrucous granulomas with an advancing border and central scarring. The border is filled with microabscesses and has a sharp, sloping edge.

3. Disseminated disease:

• Multiple skin lesions are the most common presentation
• Highly fatal
• The genitourinary tract (especially the prostate) is frequently involved
• Bone involvement resembles chronic osteomyelitis.

It can be diagnosed based on culture findings. Characteristic findings include the presence of thick-walled round yeast cells with a single broad-based bud when cultured at 37°C. (figure of 8 appearance)

Treatment of localised mild/moderate disease includes Itraconazole (6 months) and for disseminated/ severe disease- amphotericin B.

The image given below shows the skin lesions and microscopy of broad-based budding by Blastomyces dermitidis.

Other options

Option B: Histoplasmosis is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. It has tiny oval yeast cells with narrow-based budding within the macrophages with an underlying granulomatous response. This is a dimorphic fungus that exists in the yeast form in body tissues and cultures maintained at 37°C, and in the filamentous mould form in cultures at room temperature (25°C).

Option C: Coccidiomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis which is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It occurs as a spherule in tissues and culture at 37°C and as the mycelial form in soil and culture at room temperature. They are endemic to the arid desert regions of the southwestern USA and California. Infection is acquired by inhaling dust containing arthrospores of the fungus.

Option D: Candidiasis is caused by candida species which are yeast-like fungi. They exist as yeast and pseudohyphae. It appears as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Candida albicans form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 48-year-old man presents with chronic gait imbalance, numbness in the feet, and generalized muscle weakness. He reports long-term self-administration of high-dose multivitamins for over a year. Based on his symptoms and history, which vitamin toxicity is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: While most B-vitamins are water-soluble and safely excreted, Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is unique because chronic megadosing (typically) can lead to severe sensory neuropathy. This toxicity characteristically manifests as foot numbness, "pins and needles" sensations, and significant imbalance (sensory ataxia) due to damage to the dorsal root ganglia. This perfectly matches the patient's symptoms of imbalance and numbness. Vitamin D toxicity (Option A) causes hypercalcemia, leading to kidney stones and confusion. Vitamin C toxicity (Option C) is rare but may cause diarrhea or kidney stones. Vitamin A toxicity (Option D) causes headache, bone pain, and skin changes. The paradoxical nature of B6 is a classic board exam topic: while it is used to treat certain neuropathies (like those from isoniazid), excessive intake is a well-documented cause of nerve damage. Therefore, the combination of sensory deficits and a history of multivitamin megadosing identifies B6 as the toxic agent
questions.learning: While most B-vitamins are water-soluble and safely excreted, Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is unique because chronic megadosing (typically) can lead to severe sensory neuropathy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Which of the following findings are seen in a high-resolution CT scan of fungal pneumonia?

1. Interlobular septations
2. Peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation
3. Pleural effusion
4. Cavitatory lesions with surrounding ground glass opacities
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of fungal pneumonia shows interlobular septations, peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation, and pleural effusion. HRCT of fungal pneumonia shows a nodule (not a cavity) with surrounding ground-glass opacities.

A nodule surrounded by ground-glass attenuation on HRCT imaging is seen in aspergillosis, candidiasis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, coccidioidomycosis, and paracoccidioidomycosis. Cavitation on HRCT is seen in cases of community-acquired pneumonia due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, S. aureus, and gram-negative bacilli.

Aspergillosis is a fungal disease caused by Aspergillus sp. Pulmonary aspergillosis has been categorized into saprophytic, allergic, and invasive forms.

HRCT findings of various types of aspergillosis are as follows:

• Aspergilloma (saprophytic) shows a mass with soft-tissue attenuation, which is separated from the thoracic wall by airspace called the air crescent sign. Multiple nodules and bilateral involvement may be seen.
• Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA-allergic) shows hypodense mucous plugs.
• Angioinvasive aspergillosis shows multiple nodules surrounded by a halo of ground-glass attenuation (‘halo sign’) or pleural-based wedge-shaped areas of consolidation.

The following is an HRCT image of aspergilloma showing the air crescent sign:

The following CT image of aspergilloma shows the halo sign:

Candidiasis pneumonia caused by Candida sp. in immunocompromised patients shows multiple bilateral nodular opacities, areas of consolidation, and ground-glass opacities on HRCT.  Pleural effusion, thickening of the bronchial walls, and cavitation are less commonly seen.

Paracoccidioidomycosis (PCM), is a disease caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. On HRCT, ground-glass opacities, nodules, the ‘halo’ and ‘reversed halo’ signs, interlobular septal thickening, airspace consolidation, cavitation, and fibrosis.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of fungal pneumonia shows interlobular septations, peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation, and pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with generalised edema and was found to have hypercholesterolemia. Urine analysis shows protein 3+ and fat bodies. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nephrotic syndrome

The clinical scenario showing a child with generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, massive proteinuria, and fat bodies in urine is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome.

Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by nephrotic range proteinuria/heavy proteinuria >3.5 g/24 hr or urine protein: creatinine ratio > 2 and is associated with a triad of hypoalbuminemia (≤2.5 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia (cholesterol > 200 mg/dL).

Nephrotic syndrome in children is primarily idiopathic, with minimal change disease being the most common glomerular lesion. Podocyte injury or genetic mutations in podocyte proteins can lead to nephrotic-range proteinuria.

Edema is the most common presenting symptom. They have elevated levels of cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoproteins (LDL), and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL). It is caused by both increased lipid synthesis and decreased lipid catabolism.

They are prone to infections especially by encapsulated bacteria due to factors such as urinary losses of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement factors (C3, C5, factors B and D). Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state due to vascular stasis, increased platelet, increased hepatic production of fibrinogen, and urinary losses of antithrombotic factors such as antithrombin III and protein S.

The diagnosis is confirmed by performing a urinalysis and urine protein: creatinine ratio. The recommended initial treatment for nephrotic syndrome is a daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) of prednisolone for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks.

Definitions regarding the course of nephrotic syndrome:

• Remission is characterized by a urine protein: creatinine ratio of <0.2 or <1+ protein on urine dipstick testing for 3 consecutive days
• Response in nephrotic syndrome is defined as achieving remission within the initial 4 weeks of corticosteroid therapy
• Relapse is indicated by an increase in urine protein: creatinine ratio >0.2 or a reading of 2+ and higher for 3 consecutive days.
• Frequently relapsing: ≥2 relapses in 6 months or 4 relapses in 12 months.
• Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome: Relapse during steroid tapering or within 2 weeks of discontinuation.
• Steroid resistance: Failure to achieve remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone for 4 weeks and alternate days for the next 4 weeks.

Other options :

Option B: Nephritic syndrome classically presents with tea- or cola-colored urine (hematuria), edema, hypertension, and oliguria.

Option C: Goodpasture disease is an autoimmune condition characterized by pulmonary hemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and elevated anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody levels.

Option D: IgA nephropathy is an immune complex-mediated disease, with a predominance of IgA within glomerular mesangial deposits. They present with gross hematuria and proteinuria.
questions.learning: Nephrotic syndrome — The clinical scenario showing a child with generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, massive proteinuria, and fat bodies in urine is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor receives two court summons—one to appear as a witness in a murder case and another to give expert medical testimony. Which summons should the doctor attend as a priority?
options: Appearance for providing medical expert opinion
questions.explanation: A criminal court summons in a murder case carries a legal imperative and higher priority over other civil or expert witness duties. Legal attendance is mandatory unless a legitimate legal excuse is provided. While providing an expert medical opinion is professionally significant, a direct court order in a criminal matter represents a primary legal obligation that the doctor must prioritize. Appearance for expert opinion (Option B) is considered important but is typically subordinate to a direct criminal court summons. The timing of receipt (Option C) is irrelevant, as the chronological order of summonses does not override the legal gravity and mandatory nature of a criminal case involving a serious offense like murder. Therefore, the doctor must attend the criminal court first to fulfill their judicial duty in the murder trial, ensuring compliance with the law's highest mandates
questions.learning: A criminal court summons in a murder case carries a legal imperative and higher priority over other civil or expert witness duties. Legal attendance is mandatory unless a legitimate legal excuse is provided.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Giemsa stain of a thin peripheral smear is prepared. Which of the following cannot be diagnosed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coxiella burnetii

The diagnosis of Coxiella burnetii cannot be done using a Giemsa stain of a thin peripheral smear.

It is done mainly by serology, which shows a rise in the titer of specific antibodies to C. burnetii.

Microorganisms such as Histoplasma, Leishmania, Toxoplasma, and Pneumocystis can also be detected with Giemsa, and in gastric tissues, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) appear thin and distinctly blue. Giemsa’s stain is frequently used for diagnostic purposes in haematology to differentiate the nuclear and cytoplasmic morphology of platelets, RBCs, WBCs, and parasites.
questions.learning: Coxiella burnetii — The diagnosis of Coxiella burnetii cannot be done using a Giemsa stain of a thin peripheral smear. It is done mainly by serology, which shows a rise in the titer of specific antibodies to C. burnetii.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes routine ultrasonography, which reveals a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst. Her tumor markers and other serological investigations are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate approach to management?
options: Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs)
questions.explanation: In a 35-year-old asymptomatic woman with a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst and normal tumor markers, the most appropriate management is watchful waiting with follow-up CA-125 monitoring. Since all tumor markers are normal and the cyst is unilocular with no suspicious features, immediate surgery is not warranted. Serial CA-125 monitoring along with repeat ultrasonography after 3 months is the recommended conservative approach to assess for resolution or change in characteristics. Why other options are wrong: (A) Laparotomy is incorrect because laparotomy is reserved for suspicious, complex, or malignant ovarian masses. An asymptomatic unilocular cyst with normal markers does not justify major surgery. (B) Follow-up with OCPs is incorrect because OCPs are useful for functional cysts which are typically smaller (<5 cm). A 6 cm cyst in a 35-year-old warrants monitoring with tumor markers rather than OCP suppression therapy alone. (C) Ovariotomy is incorrect because surgical removal of the ovary is not indicated as first-line management for a simple unilocular cyst with normal tumor markers in a premenopausal woman
questions.learning: In a 35-year-old asymptomatic woman with a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst and normal tumor markers, the most appropriate management is watchful waiting with follow-up CA-125 monitoring.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During the procedure of epidural anesthesia, which spinal structure is not traversed or penetrated by the needle?
questions.explanation: Epidural anesthesia involves the injection of local anesthetic into the epidural space, which lies just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the "Dura" (Option D) should "not be penetrated" by the needle. If the dura is punctured, it results in a "dural tap" or "wet tap," which can lead to a post-dural puncture headache. To reach the epidural space using a midline approach, the needle must pass through several structures in order: skin, subcutaneous tissue, the "supraspinous ligament" (Option A), the "interspinous ligament" (Option B), and the "ligamentum flavum" (Option C). The clinician identifies the epidural space using the "loss of resistance" technique once the needle passes through the dense ligamentum flavum. In contrast, spinal (subarachnoid) anesthesia requires the penetration of the dura and arachnoid mater to reach the cerebrospinal fluid. Precise knowledge of spinal anatomy is vital for the safe and successful performance of regional anesthesia techniques in obstetric and surgical patients
questions.learning: Epidural anesthesia involves the injection of local anesthetic into the epidural space, which lies just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the "Dura" (Option D) should "not be penetrated" by the needle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Fast vibration sense is mediated by ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pacinian corpuscles

Fast vibration sense is mediated by Pacinian corpuscles.

Pacinian corpuscles are the largest cutaneous mechanoreceptors. They are present in the dermis of glabrous and hairy skin. They are composed of a nerve ending that is encapsulated by concentric layers of connective tissue, giving them an onion-like appearance. The sensory nerves from cutaneous mechanoreceptors are myelinated Aα and Aβ fibers. These receptors respond to fast vibration and deep pressure and adapt very rapidly

Option A: Merkel's disc responsible for sensing sustained touch and pressure

Option B: Meissner's corpuscles respond to texture and slow vibration. They are present in dermal papillae and are used in 2-point discrimination.

Option C: Ruffini endings sense skin stretch and fluttering vibration.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Water’s view is used to best visualize which of the following sinuses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maxillary sinus

Water’s view is used to best visualize the maxillary sinus. Frontal and ethmoidal sinuses can also be visualized. Sphenoid sinus can be seen in Water's view with open mouth.

It is also known as the occipitomental view. The X-ray beam is angled at 37°-45° to the orbitomeatal line.

The recommended imaging views for different sinuses are as follows:

• Ethmoidal sinus: Rheese's view
• Frontal sinus: Caldwell's view
• Sphenoid sinus: Hirtz view
questions.learning: Maxillary sinus Water’s view is used to best visualize the maxillary sinus. Frontal and ethmoidal sinuses can also be visualized.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with lower urinary tract symptoms, including weak urinary stream, hesitancy, and nocturia. On digital rectal examination (DRE), a hard, irregular prostate is palpated. He has no significant past medical history but reports mild back pain over the past few weeks. The physician suspects prostate cancer. Which enzyme is elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acid phosphatase

Prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) is commonly increased in prostatic cancer.

The form of acid phosphatase that is found in the prostate gland is called prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP). PAP is a glycoprotein that is synthesized by the epithelial cells of the prostate gland. It is secreted into the prostatic fluid, where it plays a role in the liquefaction of semen.

PAP is also a potential target for monoclonal antibody therapy. Sipuleucel-T is a cell-based approach to induce an immune response against prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) that is commonly expressed in prostatic cancer.

Option A: Alkaline phosphatase is increased in primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma.  Similarly, cancers that metastasize to the bones or primary bone cancers like osteosarcoma.

Option C: Lactate dehydrogenase elevations can occur in a range of malignancies. It is often observed in hematological cancers like lymphomas and leukemias, reflecting the rapid cell turnover characteristic of these diseases. Lung cancers, both small cell and non-small cell types, can also lead to increased LDH levels.

Option D: Alpha-fetoprotein is a protein that is produced by the liver and yolk sac during fetal development. Alpha-fetoprotein levels are typically elevated in certain types of cancer, such as liver cancer and testicular cancer, but not in prostate cancer.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not recommended in an 8 yr old child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss?
options: Sitting in front row of the class
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion

Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is not recommended in bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).

Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is done in the management of serous otitis media.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.
• Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Option B: Cochlear implant is an electronic device which helps in hearing for those with profound sensorineural hearing loss, who cannot benefit from hearing aids. It has two components :

• External component : speech processor and transmitter
• Internal component : receiver / stimulator and electrode array

Sound signals received by the processor is then conducted to the stimulator via the transmitter. It is then decoded and sent to the electrode array which is placed over the scala tympani. Scala tympani then transmits the signal to the spiral ganglion, which in turn stimulates the auditory nerve cells. Thus, sound is conducted to the brain.

Option C: Hearing aids are used in the management of SNHL. Hearing aids are of the following types

• Conventional hearing aids
• Bone-anchored hearing aids (BAHAs)
• Implantable hearing aids (vibrant soundbridge)

Option D: Sitting in the front row of class is recommended in SNHL to help the child hear the class better.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is not recommended in bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is done in the management of serous otitis media.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presented with vomiting after having fruit juice. What sugar is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fructose

An infant who develops vomiting after ingestion of fruit juice most likely has Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (HFI), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by aldolase B deficiency. Symptoms typically appear after the introduction of fruits, fruit juices, or sucrose-containing foods (usually after 4–6 months of age). Accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate in the liver depletes intracellular phosphate and ATP, leading to hypoglycemia, vomiting, hepatomegaly, and liver dysfunction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucose: Normally well tolerated and is not associated with vomiting in hereditary fructose intolerance.
• C. Sucrose: Although sucrose can precipitate symptoms because it contains fructose, the offending sugar is the fructose component.
• D. Galactose: Causes symptoms in classic galactosemia, which begin soon after initiation of milk feeding, not after fruit juice introduction.
questions.learning: Fructose — An infant who develops vomiting after ingestion of fruit juice most likely has Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (HFI), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by aldolase B deficiency.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child came to the casualty with difficulty in walking and pain in the perianal region. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, yellow needle-shaped crystals are seen under the microscope. What is the test done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Barberio’s test

Barberio’s test is a micro chemical test for detection of semen, based on identification of spermine crystals.

• Reagent: Saturated picric acid
• Positive result: Yellow, needle-shaped crystals (spermine picrate)
• Indicates presence of seminal fluid

Clinical/forensic relevance:

• Used in sexual assault cases, including perianal/anal specimens
• Helps confirm presence of semen

Differentiation from other tests:

• Florence test: Brown rhombic crystals (choline)
• Acid phosphatase test: Screening test for semen (enzyme-based)
• Teichmann test: Confirms blood (hemin crystals)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following method is employed to measure the viral load?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Real time PCR

Viral load can be measured by the real time-PCR technique.

Real time-PCR assays are commonly used for viral load quantification of HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and CMV.

Other options:

• Western blotting is used for the detection of protein.
• ELISA is an immunosorbent assay used to detect antigens of infectious agents present in clinical specimens.
• Immuno electrophoresis includes electrophoretic separation of antigens followed by an antigen-antibody reaction.
questions.learning: Real time PCR Viral load can be measured by the real time-PCR technique. Real time-PCR assays are commonly used for viral load quantification of HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and CMV.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following supply the marked structure except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diagonal artery

The structure marked is the right ventricle. It is not supplied by the diagonal artery.

The diagonal artery is a branch of the anterior interventricular artery supplying the left ventricle. This is present in about 30-50% of the population.

The right ventricle is mostly supplied by the right coronary artery and its branches such as the marginal artery.

The anterior interventricular artery gives off 1-2 anterior right ventricular branches.
questions.learning: Diagonal artery — The structure marked is the right ventricle. It is not supplied by the diagonal artery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with normal bone age compared to chronologic age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Familial short stature

Here, the child with short stature has a normal US:LS ratio (1.1:1 at 12 years is within normal limits) and no other abnormalities, which makes familial short stature highly likely. Children with familial short stature have normal bone age compared to chronological age.

Familial short stature refers to short stature that is inherited within families. The parents are also shorter in stature, and there is usually no underlying pathology affecting growth and development. Therefore, bone age assessments are typically consistent with chronologic age in children with familial short stature.

Short stature can be defined as growth below the expected genetic potential or below -2 SD for age and sex. If a child's stature is less than -3 SD below the average for their age and gender, it is more likely to indicate pathological short stature. A child's height between -2 and -3 SD is more likely due to physiological, i.e. familial or constitutional short stature.

The 2 types of normal variants of short stature are as follows:

* Constitutional delay: Bone age < Chronological age

* Familial short stature: Bone age = Chronological age

Bone age is more than chronological age in precocious puberty. Bone age is less than chronological age in constitutional delay, undernutrition, endocrinologic short stature, and systemic illness.

Other options:

Option A: In constitutional delay, bone age is delayed compared to chronological age. These children have a delayed growth pattern and delayed puberty, but will eventually reach their genetic potential height.

Option C: Endocrinologic short stature entails conditions like growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism typically cause delayed bone age compared to chronologic age.

Option D: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding for fibroblast growth factor receptor type 3. It typically manifests at birth with short limbs, a long, narrow trunk, and a large head with midfacial hypoplasia and a prominent forehead (disproportionate short stature).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant was brought by his mother with complaints of inability to open the eyes in light and excessive watering. The clinical picture is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital glaucoma

The clinical history of inability to open eyes in light (photophobia), excessive watering, and the image showing hazy cornea are suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

Primary congenital glaucoma refers to abnormally high intraocular pressure (IOP) which occurs as a result of a developmental anomaly of the angle of the anterior chamber. It is not associated with any other ocular or systemic anomaly. It can be classified as follows:

• True congenital glaucoma: The IOP is elevated during intrauterine life.
• Infantile glaucoma: Manifests prior to age 3.
• Juvenile glaucoma: The IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age. It is the least common type.

The CYP1B1 gene is implicated in the pathogenesis of congenital glaucoma.

Clinical presentation: Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm form the classic triad of symptoms of congenital glaucoma. A corneal haze is seen due to diffuse edema secondary to raised IOP. Buphthalmos occur as a result of stretching due to elevated IOP prior to the age of 3 years. Haab striae that are curvilinear healed breaks in Descemet's membrane are seen. Corneal scarring can also occur.

Evaluation under general anesthesia is generally required. IOP measurement, anterior chamber examination, optic disc examination, corneal diameter measurement, gonioscopy, and refraction should be evaluated.

Management is essentially surgical with goniotomy or trabeculotomy. If angle surgery fails, trabeculectomy, tube shunt implantation, and ciliary body ablative procedures are performed.

Other options:

Option A - In ophthalmia neonatorum, there will be inflammation of the conjunctiva. Clinical presentation includes conjunctival discharge, hyperemia chemosis, swollen eyelids, tender eyeball. Corneal involvement is rare which may occur in the form of superficial punctate keratitis.

Option C - In mucopolysaccharidosis, there will be bilateral cloudy cornea.

Option D - In cataract, there will be opacification of lens presenting as whitish reflex/ leukocoria.
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma — The clinical history of inability to open eyes in light (photophobia), excessive watering, and the image showing hazy cornea are suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought with evisceration of bowel loops from a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastroschisis

The most probable diagnosis for the evisceration of bowel loops, coming out of a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus is gastroschisis. It occurs when there is a failure in the closure of the body wall in the abdominal region.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly) allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines. The abdomen is wrapped with transparent plastic wrap, a nasogastric tube is inserted, and fluid resuscitation is initiated.

Depending on the severity, primary closure under general anesthesia or gradual reduction using a preformed silo may be performed. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Other options:

Option A: In omphalocele bowel loops fail to return from the physiologic umbilical hernia. Since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, the omphalocele is also covered by the amnion.

Option B: Congenital umbilical hernia occurs due to the incomplete closure or weakness of the muscular umbilical ring. It presents as a soft swelling covered by skin that protrudes during activities like crying, coughing, or straining, and it can be easily pushed back through the fibrous ring at the umbilicus. The hernia contains the omentum or segments of the small intestine.

The image below shows an umbilical hernia:

Option D: Ectopia vesicae/bladder exstrophy is a congenital abnormality that occurs when the lower abdominal wall does not form properly and the bladder protrudes from the abdominal wall, with its mucosa exposed.

The image below shows ectopia vesicae/bladder exstrophy
questions.learning: Gastroschisis — The most probable diagnosis for the evisceration of bowel loops, coming out of a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus is gastroschisis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Infectivity is also known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secondary attack rate

Infectivity is also known as the secondary attack rate.

Infectivity is the ability of an infectious agent to cause a new infection in a susceptible host. In diseases that are directly transmitted, it is measured by the secondary attack rate, which is the proportion of susceptible individuals that develop the infection after exposure to a primary case. It measures the communicability of the disease.

Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/ (Total number of susceptible close contacts).

Once a person gets infected, the time interval between invasion and appearance of the first sign or symptom is called as incubation period. During incubation, the agent multiplies in the host and builds up till it is sufficient to present as a disease.

As it is difficult to precisely calculate the incubation period, the gap in time between the onset of the primary case and the secondary case is used to calculate the incubation period. This is called serial interval.

Pearl PF1806: Case Fatality Rate

* Case fatality rate =  (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100

* It is a good indicator of severity or killing power of a disease.

* It is used mostly in acute and infectious diseases.

* No time interval is used.

* Case fatality rate is closely related to virulence.

* Limitation of CFR is that its usefulness for chronic diseases is limited because the period from onset to death is variable.

* It is expressed in percentage.

* CFR is an incidence proportion and not a true rate.

* CFR may vary for the same disease in different epidemics.

*

Case fatality of a few diseases:

* Rabies - 100% especially after symptoms manifest

* Ebola - 25 to 90%, average - 50%

* Yellow fever - 15 to 50%

* Chicken pox - 0.001%

* Diseases with a high case fatality rate: Tetanus, Rabies, Botulism, Ebola.

* Diseases with a low case fatality rate: Leprosy, Trachoma, Lymphatic filariasis.

Pearl PF0956: Morbidity Measurements in Epidemiology

Morbidity Measurements in Epidemiology

Incidence rate = ( Number of new cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time ) x 1000

Incidence rate of spells of sickness = ( Number of spells of sickness starting in a specified period /Mean number of people exposed to that risk in the specified time ) x 1000

Attack rate = ( Number of new cases of a disease in a specified period of time /Total population at risk during the given time ) x 100

Secondary attack rate = ( Number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the incubation period/Total number of exposed or susceptible contacts ) x 100

Prevalence = ( Number of all cases (new+old) of a specified disease at a given point in time/ Estimated population at the same point in time ) x 100
questions.learning: Secondary attack rate Infectivity is also known as the secondary attack rate. Infectivity is the ability of an infectious agent to cause a new infection in a susceptible host.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with left testicular carcinoma. Which of the following lymph nodes is the first to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Para-aortic lymph nodes

In a patient with testicular carcinoma, para-aortic lymph nodes are the first to be involved.

The lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels. The contralateral para-aortic lymph nodes are sometimes involved in tumor spread, but the inguinal lymph nodes are affected only if the scrotal skin is involved.
questions.learning: Para-aortic lymph nodes — In a patient with testicular carcinoma, para-aortic lymph nodes are the first to be involved. The lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the tarsal bone labeled in the image below.
questions.explanation: The green circle in the lateral weight-bearing X-ray highlights a bone situated anterior to the calcaneus and on the lateral aspect of the midfoot. This is the classic anatomical position of the cuboid bone. The cuboid articulates posteriorly with the calcaneus, medially with the navicular and lateral cuneiform, and anteriorly with the 4th and 5th metatarsal bases. Its wedge-shaped appearance on lateral X-ray confirms its identity. Why Other Options are Wrong: (A) Calcaneus — This is the largest tarsal bone forming the heel. It lies posterior and inferior to the circled area, not in the midfoot region. (C) Navicular — Located on the medial side of the midfoot, articulating with the talus posteriorly. The circled bone is lateral, ruling out navicular. (D) Talus — Sits superiorly, articulating with the tibia and fibula forming the ankle mortise, far above the circled region
questions.learning: The green circle in the lateral weight-bearing X-ray highlights a bone situated anterior to the calcaneus and on the lateral aspect of the midfoot. This is the classic anatomical position of the cuboid bone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the normal conjunctival flora?
questions.explanation: The normal ocular surface is colonized by a variety of microorganisms that form the commensal flora. Staphylococcus epidermidis is widely recognized as the most frequently isolated and abundant species of the normal conjunctival flora in healthy individuals. It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that generally maintains a symbiotic relationship with the host. While Staphylococcus aureus (Option A) can be found in a small percentage of healthy eyes, it is more commonly associated with pathogenic states like blepharitis or conjunctivitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) and Haemophilus influenzae (Option D) are not typically considered part of the normal resident flora; they are more often transient colonizers or primary pathogens responsible for acute bacterial conjunctivitis, particularly in the pediatric population. Understanding the normal flora is clinically essential because these commensals can become opportunistic pathogens following ocular surgery or trauma. Preserving this delicate microbial balance is one reason why the indiscriminate use of topical antibiotics is generally discouraged
questions.learning: The normal ocular surface is colonized by a variety of microorganisms that form the commensal flora. Staphylococcus epidermidis is widely recognized as the most frequently isolated and abundant species of the normal conjunctival flora in healthy individuals.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young patient presented with hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus and tetany. Which of the following marked areas in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the image of pharyngeal pouches, "3" points to the thymus (derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch). Since in the above question, the thymus is absent, option 3 will be the most appropriate answer.

DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by the hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22. It is characterized by multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. It is also known as velocardiofacial syndrome (palate, facial, and cardiac defects).

It has variable presentations including Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency, Cardiac defects, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia (CATCH-22).
questions.learning: 3 The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 28-year-old male presents with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination throughout the day, as well as having to wake up several times at night to urinate. When questioned further, he admits to having sustained a head injury one month prior. His fasting blood glucose is within normal limits. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Desmopressin

The clinical vignette suggests the probable diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus, which is treated with desmopressin.

Diabetes insipidus of central or nephrogenic origin is characterised by low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a syndrome characterised by the excretion of abnormally large volumes of dilute urine. The 24-hour urine volume exceeds 40 mL/kg body weight, and the 24-hour urine osmolarity is <280 mOsm/L. There will be a slight increase in plasma osmolarity/sodium that stimulates thirst (polydipsia). Hence, clinical symptoms and signs of dehydration are uncommon unless thirst and/or water intake are also impaired.

Desmopressin is the drug of choice for neurogenic diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin is a selective vasopressin V2 receptor agonist. V2 receptors are present throughout the collecting ducts. The V2 receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor, which, when activated, results in a signaling cascade of adenyl cyclase, prompting an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) in the renal tubule cells, ultimately resulting in increased water permeability. This activity leads to a decrease in urine volume and an increase in urine osmolality. Extrarenal V2-like receptors are involved in the release of coagulation factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, which increases platelet aggregation. Desmopressin is used for the management of nocturnal polyuria, hemophilia A, central diabetes insipidus, and von Willebrand disease. Desmopressin can be administered orally at high doses and is contraindicated in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Its major adverse effect is water intoxication. It can also give rise to flushing and transient headaches.

In post-traumatic DI, patients lose their ability to concentrate urine due to the failure of anti-diuretic hormone secretion in acceleration-deceleration injury, leading to ischaemia and discontinuity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This leads to hypotonic polyuria with low osmolality. When this is associated with altered mentation and damage to the central osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus, thirst regulation is also impaired, preventing adequate fluid intake to compensate for the losses, leading to severe hypernatremia.

DI can be central or nephrogenic.

* Central DI occurs due to damage to the neurohypophysis in the posterior pituitary. It is characterised by decreased ADH. It can be treated with desmopressin, an ADH analogue.

* In nephrogenic DI, ADH levels may be normal or increased because the kidney has become resistant to its effects. Nephrogenic DI requires treatment with a thiazide diuretic, amiloride, a low-sodium diet, and indomethacin.

Other options:

Option A: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits the NaCl symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride. It may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Option B: The drug of choice for chronic SIADH is the oral administration of a vaptan (e.g., tolvaptan). They are selective V2 receptor antagonists that act by increasing urinary water excretion by blocking the antidiuretic effect of AVP.

Option C: Insulin is used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not classified as a paired cartilage in the laryngeal structure?
questions.explanation: The human larynx consists of nine cartilages: three unpaired and three pairs of cartilages. The thyroid cartilage is the largest and is an unpaired cartilage that forms the "Adam's apple". The other unpaired cartilages are the cricoid and the epiglottis. Option A (Arytenoid), Option C (Corniculate), and Option D (Cuneiform) are all paired cartilages. The arytenoids are particularly important as they provide the attachment points for the vocal cords and are involved in their movement. The corniculate cartilages sit atop the arytenoids, and the cuneiform cartilages are located within the aryepiglottic folds to provide structural support. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for surgery, intubation, and managing laryngeal trauma. The thyroid cartilage is composed of hyaline cartilage and, unlike the elastic epiglottis, it is prone to calcification with age. Its unpaired nature means that structural damage to the thyroid cartilage often results in significant compromise of the airway and vocal production
questions.learning: The human larynx consists of nine cartilages: three unpaired and three pairs of cartilages. The thyroid cartilage is the largest and is an unpaired cartilage that forms the "Adam's apple".

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with dysphagia and odynophagia. Endoscopic examination of the esophagus reveals plaques. What is the most likely causative organism?
options: Thin septate hyphae with acute angle branching
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae

In an HIV-positive patient, dysphagia and odynophagia with white esophageal plaques is characteristic of Candida esophagitis.

• Caused by Candida albicans
• Microscopy shows budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae
• Occurs in advanced immunosuppression (low CD4 count)
• Endoscopy shows white, adherent plaques in the esophagus

Differentiation:

• Thin septate hyphae with acute angle branching → Aspergillus (lung disease, not esophagus)
• Acid-fast bacilli → tuberculosis
• Squamous cell cancer → irregular mass/ulcer, not fungal plaques

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding use of ACE inhibitors in hypertension is true?
options: They decrease blood pressure by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance
They decrease blood pressure by decreasing cardiac output
They increase blood pressure by increasing peripheral vascular resistance
They increase blood pressure by increasing cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. They decrease blood pressure by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance

The Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System (RAAS) regulates blood pressure.

Sequence:

1️⃣ Kidney releases renin

2️⃣ Renin converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I

3️⃣ ACE converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II

Angiotensin II causes:

• Vasoconstriction
• Aldosterone secretion
• Sodium retention

ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure primarily by reducing angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction. ACE inhibitors also increase: Bradykinin levels

Because ACE normally breaks down bradykinin.

This leads to:

• Vasodilation
• Side effects like dry cough

This leads to a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance (afterload).

Cardiac output is usually preserved, not reduced.

Hence, BP reduction occurs due to vasodilation, not changes in cardiac output.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If the percentage of thymine residues in DNA is 28%. What is the percentage of cytosine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 22%

The percentage of cytosine in the DNA is 22%.

As per the Chargaff's rule, in the DNA molecules, the concentration of deoxyadenosine (A) equals that of thymidine (T), and the concentration of deoxyguanosine (G) equals that of deoxycytidine (C). Therefore, A=T and G=C.

In the question, the concentration of thymine is given as 28%, therefore the concentration of adenine is also 28%, both of which add up to 56%. The remaining 44% (100-56) of the DNA consists of G-C base pairs. Of which the guanine constitutes 22% and the cytosine constitutes another 22%.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes bronchoscopy, and a perforation occurs at 25 cm. Which anatomical structure is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: During bronchoscopy, the distance measured from the upper incisors helps localize structures in relation to the trachea and esophagus. At approximately 25 cm from the incisors, the arch of the aorta lies in close relation to the trachea and left main bronchus. Therefore, a perforation occurring at this level is most likely to damage the aortic arch. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Diaphragm – Located much lower, around 40 cm from the incisors. (C) Pharyngoesophageal junction – Situated at about 15 cm from the incisors. (D) T10 – Corresponds to the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm, again much lower than 25 cm. Hence, the structure most likely to be damaged at 25 cm during bronchoscopy is the arch of the aorta
questions.learning: During bronchoscopy, the distance measured from the upper incisors helps localize structures in relation to the trachea and esophagus. At approximately 25 cm from the incisors, the arch of the aorta lies in close relation to the trachea and left main bronchus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which murmur is depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ejection systolic

The image given above is of an ejection systolic murmur.

This murmur starts after S1, increases in intensity to reach the peak, and ends before A2.

Ejection systolic murmur(ESM) is most commonly heard in aortic stenosis and in pulmonary stenosis. They are differentiated based on the difference in symptoms, site of murmur, etc.

Auscultation of ESM in aortic stenosis.

* In the early stages, an early systolic ejection sound may be heard. It disappears when the valve becomes calcified and rigid.

* As the stenosis worsens, the LV systole gets prolonged and there is delayed closure of the aortic valve. This leads to the narrowing of S2 sound, and in severe cases, it might lead to the paradoxical splitting of S2.

* S4 and S3 sounds may be heard in severe cases when the diastolic and systolic functions of the left ventricle have been reduced.

* Murmur: The murmur in aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur. The murmur radiates to the neck and base of the heart. It is augmented by squatting and reduced by the strain of the Valsalva maneuver.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A young child presents with acute diarrhea, and the clinician suspects Shigella infection rather than cholera, opting to treat with ciprofloxacin. Apart from the presence of blood in the stools, which additional clinical feature would most strongly support a diagnosis of Shigella infection?
questions.explanation: Shigellosis is a form of invasive bacillary dysentery. Unlike cholera, which is a non-invasive secretory diarrhea characteristically described as "painless" and "afebrile," Shigella infection is characteristically "inflammatory and febrile". Therefore, the "presence of fever" (Option D) strongly supports a diagnosis of Shigella or other invasive pathogens over cholera. Abdominal cramps (Option B) can occur in both, though they are often more severe in dysentery. Vomiting (Option C) is a hallmark of cholera but can also occur in Shigella. Rectal pain or "tenesmus" (Option A is absence, which is incorrect) is a classic symptom of dysentery. Shigella causes mucosal invasion and ulceration, leading to the triad of fever, abdominal pain, and small-volume stools containing blood and mucus. Clinical differentiation is vital because cholera requires massive fluid resuscitation, while dysentery like Shigellosis often requires specific antibiotic therapy with agents like ciprofloxacin
questions.learning: Shigellosis is a form of invasive bacillary dysentery. Unlike cholera, which is a non-invasive secretory diarrhea characteristically described as "painless" and "afebrile," Shigella infection is characteristically "inflammatory and febrile".

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless ocular ulcer. Examination reveals a long, branching corneal ulcer with desquamated epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless corneal ulcer is a hallmark of reduced corneal sensation, often due to damage to the trigeminal nerve. The finding of a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium without the classic "terminal bulbs" seen in viral infections identifies it as a neurotrophic ulcer. This condition results from impaired trophic support and lost sensory supply, leading to poor healing and epithelial breakdown. Fungal ulcers (Option A) are typically painful and follow vegetative trauma, showing feathery margins. Dendritic ulcers (Option B) are usually caused by herpes simplex virus and are typically painful unless sensation is already lost; they feature distinct terminal bulbs. Bacterial ulcers (Option C) are acutely painful and purulent with stromal infiltration. Thus, the painless nature and branching pattern specifically point to a neurotrophic etiology

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with hyperuricemia and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. What is the mechanism of action of the first-line drug commonly prescribed for this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of hyperuricemia and joint swelling is diagnostic of gout. For the long-term management of chronic gout (urates lowering therapy), the first-line agents are xanthine oxidase inhibitors (XOIs), such as Allopurinol or Febuxostat. These drugs work by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase, which is responsible for the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby reducing the systemic production of urate. Option A (Pyrimidine antimetabolite) refers to drugs like Methotrexate used in RA, not gout. Option B describes the mechanism of Colchicine, which is used for acute gout flares, not long-term control. Option C (Uricosuric drugs) like Probenecid increase renal uric acid excretion but are second-line due to side effects and efficacy limitations. XOIs are effective in reducing the total body urate pool, preventing tophi formation, and reducing the frequency of future gouty attacks. Monitoring renal function is essential when prescribing Allopurinol

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with an intentional tremor, has difficulty performing the heel-to-shin test, and repeatedly misses the target on the finger- to-nose test. Based on these findings, what is the likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of intentional tremor (tremor that worsens as the target is approached), dysmetria (repeatedly missing the finger-nose test), and ataxia (demonstrated by the failed heel-to-shin test) is the classic triad of cerebellar dysfunction. The cerebellum is the brain's primary center for coordinating smooth, precise movements and maintaining balance. Lesions in the basal ganglia present differently: the Caudate (Option B) and Globus Pallidus (Option C) are involved in Parkinson's disease, showing resting tremors and bradykinesia. The Subthalamic nucleus (Option D) is associated with hemiballismus (violent, flinging movements). Intentional tremor is specifically a "kinetic" tremor characteristic of cerebellar strokes, tumors, or multiple sclerosis. Clinical evaluation of coordination is the cornerstone of the neurological exam for localizing the lesion to the posterior fossa. Management involves addressing the underlying cause and physical therapy for rehabilitation
questions.learning: The clinical combination of intentional tremor (tremor that worsens as the target is approached), dysmetria (repeatedly missing the finger-nose test), and ataxia (demonstrated by the failed heel-to-shin test) is the classic triad of cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In biomedical waste management, which category of waste is disposed of in a yellow- colored bag?
questions.explanation: According to the Biomedical Waste Management Rules in India, the yellow bag is used for highly infectious, non-plastic waste. This includes anatomical waste, soiled cotton, plaster casts, and blood bags. Waste in yellow bags is typically disposed of through incineration. Gloves (Option B) and recyclable contaminated plastic waste are placed in red bags. Sharps (Option C), such as needles and blades, are placed in white, translucent, puncture-proof containers. Urine bags (Option D), if emptied and treated, are generally considered recyclable plastic waste belonging in red bags. Proper segregation at the source is vital to prevent environmental contamination and healthcare-associated infections. Therefore, because blood bags are considered highly hazardous infectious waste that requires high-temperature destruction, they must be discarded in the yellow bag
questions.learning: According to the Biomedical Waste Management Rules in India, the yellow bag is used for highly infectious, non-plastic waste. This includes anatomical waste, soiled cotton, plaster casts, and blood bags.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A boy presents with multiple bullous lesions on the trunk and periostitis evident on X-rays. What is the next appropriate investigation to perform?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a neonate or young child with multiple bullous lesions (syphilitic pemphigus) and radiological evidence of periostitis (bone inflammation) is highly diagnostic of Congenital Syphilis . The most appropriate next step in the diagnostic workup is to perform a VDRL test on both the mother and the child (Option A). This non-treponemal screening test is used to detect antibodies against Treponema pallidum. PCR for TB (Option B) and HBsAg (Option C) or general ELISA (Option D) are unrelated to this specific orthopedic-cutaneous presentation. Congenital syphilis is also associated with findings like snuffles, Hutchinson's teeth, and saber shins later in life. Therefore, because the combination of bullae and periostitis is pathognomonic for fetal-maternal transmission of spirochetes, VDRL is the definitive next investigation. Prompt diagnosis is essential for initiating penicillin therapy to prevent further systemic damage and long-term sequelae
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a neonate or young child with multiple bullous lesions (syphilitic pemphigus) and radiological evidence of periostitis (bone inflammation) is highly diagnostic of Congenital Syphilis .

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The upper part of the uncinate process commonly attaches to?
questions.explanation: The uncinate process is a thin, curved bony hook belonging to the ethmoid bone that forms part of the lateral nasal wall. Its upper part commonly extends to attach to the middle turbinate (middle nasal concha). This structure is essential in forming the drainage pathway for the frontal and maxillary sinuses through the ostiomeatal complex. The superior turbinate (Option B) is located higher in the nasal cavity than the uncinate process, so there is no anatomical attachment between them. The inferior turbinate (Option C) is a separate bone located much lower in the nasal passage. The bulla ethmoidalis (Option D) is an ethmoid air cell situated behind the uncinate process; while they form the boundaries of the hiatus semilunaris inferior, they do not serve as an attachment site for one another. Thus, the middle turbinate is the standard attachment point
questions.learning: The uncinate process is a thin, curved bony hook belonging to the ethmoid bone that forms part of the lateral nasal wall. Its upper part commonly extends to attach to the middle turbinate (middle nasal concha).

Correct answer: B. Neuropathic ulcer

There is a lack of sensation over the pressure points, leading to unnoticed microtrauma, wounds or cuts which develop into an ulcer. Causes of neuropathic ulcers include diabetic neuropathy, B12 deficiency, alcoholism, hypothyroidism, leprosy, peripheral nerve injury, transverse myelitis and myelomeningocele.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iritis is seen in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rheumatoid arthritis

Iritis is seen in all the above conditions except rheumatoid arthritis.

Iritis or iridocyclitis is also known as anterior uveitis.

Anterior uveitis is seen in:

• Ankylosing spondylitis
• Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
• Psoriasis
• Reactive arthritis
• Systemic lupus erythematosus
• Leprosy

Posterior uveitis is seen in:

• Vogt-Koyanagi Harada syndrome
• Diseases like toxoplasmosis, cysticercosis, coccidioidomycosis, toxocariasis, histoplasmosis
• Infections- Candida, Pneumocystis carinii, Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, and Cytomegalovirus
• Cat-scratch disease, Whipple’s disease, and brucellosis

Both anterior and posterior uveitis is seen in:

• Sarcoidosis
• Behcet's disease
• Inflammatory bowel disease
• Herpes infections, Syphilis, Lyme disease, TB, onchocerciasis

Intermediate uveitis/pars planitis is seen in multiple sclerosis.
questions.learning: Rheumatoid arthritis Iritis is seen in all the above conditions except rheumatoid arthritis. Iritis or iridocyclitis is also known as anterior uveitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following management methods/techniques: 1. System analysis 2. Organizational design 3. Personnel management 4. Information systems Which of the above methods/techniques are based on behavioural sciences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

The behavioural science approach to management applies principles of psychology, sociology, anthropology, and organizational behavior to improve the effectiveness of individuals and organizations. It emphasizes human behavior, motivation, leadership, communication, and teamwork in achieving organizational goals.

• 1. System analysis ✗

• System analysis is based on the systems approach, focusing on organizational processes, workflows, and interrelationships rather than human behavior.

• 2. Organizational design ✓

• Organizational design involves structuring roles, authority, communication, and teamwork, all of which are based on behavioral science principles.

• 3. Personnel management ✓

• Personnel management deals with recruitment, motivation, performance appraisal, leadership, and employee welfare, making it a core application of behavioral sciences.

• 4. Information systems ✓

• Modern Management Information Systems (MIS) incorporate behavioral aspects such as communication, decision-making, user interaction, and organizational behavior, and are therefore considered part of the behavioral science approach in management.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 The behavioural science approach to management applies principles of psychology, sociology, anthropology, and organizational behavior to improve the effectiveness of individuals and organizations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of reversible dementia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lewy body dementia

Lewy body dementia causes irreversible dementia.

Dementia is an acquired deterioration in cognitive abilities that impairs the successful performance of activities of daily living. The most commonly lost cognitive function is episodic memory, that is, the ability to recall events specific in time and place.

Causes of dementia are:

Reversible

• Hypothyroidism
• Thiamine deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency
• Normal pressure hydrocephalus
• Subdural hematoma
• Brain tumor
• Chronic infection
• Autoimmune encephalopathy

Irreversible

• Alzheimer's disease
• Huntington's disease
• Lewy body dementia
• Vascular dementia
• Creutzfeld-Jacob disease
• Frontotemporal dementia
• Parkinson's disease
questions.learning: Lewy body dementia Lewy body dementia causes irreversible dementia. Dementia is an acquired deterioration in cognitive abilities that impairs the successful performance of activities of daily living.
